security.instrument: LB 1402 (2024), § 7 (repealing Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 77-7101 to 77-7113); Referendum Measure 435 (Nov. 5, 2024); Neb. Const. art. VII, § 11
security.note: A protection was repealed twice inside two years: the tax credit scholarship act by statute operative October 31, 2024, and the appropriation-funded scholarship by referendum on November 5, 2024, both within two years of this coding. Repeal within the last two years is the anchor for 0, and a restrictive constitutional provision is in force besides.

formation.note: It is unlawful to operate a private elementary or secondary school without a license, but section 394.211(1)(d) exempts elementary and secondary educational institutions operated by churches, religious organizations, and faith-based ministries from the whole Act. The exempt school files the exemption with the State Board on a form or in a signed letter, the exemption expires two years after the last day of the month of filing, and the superintendent inspects for health, safety, and building compliance. A filing the state records rather than evaluates is the anchor for 3; a nonreligious private school would fall to the anchor for 1.

autonomy.note: Section 394.130 requires instruction in the subjects required by law for public school pupils, under the prescribed regular state courses or through courses prepared by the private school and approved by the state board, and provides that nothing in the section may be construed to interfere with the right of private schools to give religious instruction. Section 394.150 requires instruction in both constitutions and a passing examination for a diploma. Broad subject areas prescribed with content, texts, and staffing the school's own is the anchor for 3; the anchor for 2 is not taken because no state assessment exists for nonpublic students, no teaching license is required of an exempt school, and the showing required by section 394.160 reaches only the person giving constitutional instruction and is satisfied by examination or credentials.

portability.note: A scholarship organization may provide grants only on behalf of pupils in a household whose income is not more than 300 percent of the federally designated poverty level, funded by a capped credit against the modified business tax. A narrow, income-limited program is the anchor for 2. The education savings account program created by 2015 Nev. Stat. ch. 332 was repealed by 2019 Nev. Stat. ch. 537, § 39.5, and is not counted.

household.note: The parent files a written notice of intent with the superintendent of the resident district containing the child's particulars and an educational plan; the superintendent is not authorized to require additional information or assurance, and must issue a written acknowledgment that is deemed proof of compliance with the compulsory attendance law. No assessment or portfolio review is required. Notice required with no assessment is the anchor for 3; the anchor for 1 is not taken because the plan is filed rather than approved.

security.instrument: Nev. Const. art. 11, § 10; Schwartz v. Lopez, 132 Nev. Adv. Op. 73 (2016)
security.note: Article 11, section 10 forbids the use of public funds of any kind for sectarian purpose and remains in force. Schwartz v. Lopez sustained the education savings account program against it on the reasoning that the funds become private once deposited, and the legislature then repealed the program in 2019. A restrictive constitutional provision in force is the anchor for 1; the repeal was more than two years ago, so the anchor for 0 is not taken.

formation.instrument: RSA 193:1, I(a); N.H. Code Admin. Rules Ed 401.02, Ed 403, Ed 404
formation.note: RSA 193:1, I(a) discharges the parent's duty by attendance at an approved New Hampshire private school, and the department states that approval of a nonpublic school is mandatory. Two pathways exist: attendance approval under Ed 403, renewed every three years on minimum standards the department evaluates, and attendance and program approval under Ed 404 for a school operating under a recognized accrediting agency. The recognized agencies include the Association of Christian Schools International, the American Association of Christian Schools, and the Accrediting Association of Seventh-day Adventist Schools. Approval required with a religious accreditor recognized by the state satisfying it is the anchor for 2. Tier B because the approval mechanics rest on the department's guidance and the Ed 400 rules, which were not opened.

autonomy.instrument: RSA 189:11; RSA 189:19; RSA 193-C:6; N.H. Code Admin. Rules Ed 401.03
autonomy.note: Courses in the history, government, and constitutions of the United States and New Hampshire are required by grade eight, instruction must be in English absent an approved bilingual program, and minimum instructional hours are set by rule. Certification is not required of private school teachers, and participation in statewide assessment under RSA 193-C:6 is at the school's election. Broad subject areas prescribed with content, texts, and staffing the school's own is the anchor for 3.

portability.instrument: RSA ch. 194-F (2021 N.H. Laws ch. 91, § 431), as amended by 2025 N.H. Laws ch. 75, §§ 1 to 6, and 2025 N.H. Laws ch. 141, §§ 17, 302
portability.note: As amended in 2025, RSA 194-F:1, VI defines an eligible student as a resident of the state who is eligible to enroll in a public elementary or secondary school, other than a student in the special school district within the department of corrections, and section 75:6 repealed the income definition that had limited eligibility. The commissioner transfers the per pupil adequate education grant plus differentiated aid to an approved scholarship organization for the family's use, including at a religious school. A universal program open to religious schools with no condition reaching religious character is the anchor for 4.

household.instrument: RSA ch. 193-A, as amended and in part repealed by 2026 N.H. Laws ch. 297 (H.B. 1268), § 297:10, I
household.note: Chapter 297 repeals and reenacts RSA 193-A:1 to 193-A:5 and provides that a declaration of home education is not required except to obtain access to public school programs under RSA 193:1-c or on withdrawal from a public school, and section 297:10, I repeals RSA 193-A:6, relative to the record keeping and evaluation of home education programs. The act took effect 1 July 2026. No notice and no assessment required is the anchor for 4.

security.instrument: N.H. Const. Pt. II, Art. 83; Duncan v. State, No. 2013-045 (N.H. Aug. 28, 2014)
security.note: Part II, article 83 forbids money raised by taxation ever being granted or applied for the use of the schools or institutions of any religious sect or denomination, and it remains in force. The one challenge to the education tax credit was resolved on standing without reaching the merits, so neither that credit nor the education freedom account program has been tested against the provision. A restrictive constitutional provision in force is the anchor for 1.

formation.instrument: N.J.S.A. 18A:38-25; New Jersey Department of Education, nonpublic school registration
formation.note: Compulsory attendance is discharged by a day school in which there is given instruction equivalent to that provided in the public schools, and the state requires no accreditation, licensing, or approval of that school. The department's registration requirement exists so that, in its words, only if the school is registered will the school's eligible students receive state funded services such as auxiliary and remedial services, nursing, textbooks, technology, and security aid; that is a condition on the money and is recorded under portability rather than here. The anchor for 4 is taken.

autonomy.note: The standard is instruction equivalent to that provided in the public schools for children of similar grades and attainments, with named courses in the Constitution of the United States from the seventh grade and in accident and fire prevention. No teacher certification policy and no testing policy exists for nonpublic schools. Broad subject areas prescribed with content, texts, and staffing the school's own is the anchor for 3; the equivalence standard is why 4 is not taken.

portability.instrument: N.J.S.A. 18A:58-37.3 (textbook loan); N.J.S.A. 18A:39-1 (transportation); N.J.S.A. 18A:40-23 (nursing); N.J.S.A. 18A:46A-3 (auxiliary services)
portability.note: The federal compilation records that there are no programs at this time providing financial assistance for private school attendance. What state money reaches a nonpublic school student does so as services in kind, textbooks, transportation, nursing, technology, security, and remedial and auxiliary services, none of which is a fund that follows a child to tuition. No program is the anchor for 0.

household.instrument: N.J.S.A. 18A:38-25; New Jersey Department of Education, homeschooling frequently asked questions
household.note: The statute permits a child to receive equivalent instruction elsewhere than at school, and the department states that the law does not require or authorize the local board of education to review and approve the curriculum or program of a child educated elsewhere than at school, nor to test that child. Notice is asked only on withdrawal from high school or where a district refuses enrollment. No notice and no assessment required is the anchor for 4.

security.instrument: N.J.S.A. 18A:38-25; N.J. Const. art. VIII, § 4, para. 3
security.note: The federal compilation records that the New Jersey Constitution has no provision relating to public aid for private education, and the constitution affirmatively authorizes the legislature to provide student transportation to any school. The statutory position on private schools is minimal, has not moved in five years, and nothing material is pending. Statutory and stable with no restrictive constitutional provision is the anchor for 3; the anchor for 4 is not taken because the protections are statutory rather than constitutional.

formation.note: No registration, licensing, or approval is required to operate, and accreditation is optional, with the recognized bodies including the Association of Christian Schools International, Christian Schools International, and the Adventist Accrediting Association. The department does require periodic attendance reports from private schools on forms it prescribes, and the school's governing authority must enforce compulsory attendance. Required reporting that the state records rather than evaluates is the anchor for 3.

autonomy.instrument: Santa Fe Community School v. State Board of Education, 518 P.2d 272 (N.M. 1974); NMSA 1978, § 22-12-2
autonomy.note: The court held that the department's authority does not extend to supervision, control, or management over private schools, and the state prescribes no curriculum, requires no teacher certification, and mandates no assessment of nonpublic school students. The anchor for 4 is taken; section 22-12-2, which requires attendance for at least the length of the school year established in the resident district, runs to the pupil's attendance duty rather than to the school's calendar, which is why it does not pull the score to 3.

portability.instrument: N.M. Const. art. XII, § 3
portability.note: Article XII, section 3 forbids the appropriation of state educational funds to support any sectarian, denominational, or private school, and bars appropriations for educational purposes not under the absolute control of the state. The compilation records that no programs for financial assistance to attend a private school currently exist, and the state declined the federal Education Freedom Tax Credit election. No program is the anchor for 0.

household.note: The operator of a home school must submit the department's registration form within thirty days of establishing the school and notify the department on or before 1 August of each subsequent year, maintain immunization records, and provide instruction by a person holding at least a high school diploma or its equivalent. The section imposes no assessment, the achievement test requirement having been deleted by amendment in 2001. Notice required with no assessment or portfolio review is the anchor for 3.

security.instrument: N.M. Const. art. XII, § 3; Moses v. Ruszkowski, No. S-1-SC-34974 (N.M. Dec. 13, 2018)
security.note: On remand after the United States Supreme Court vacated its 2015 decision, the New Mexico Supreme Court read article XII, section 3 not to reach the textbook loan program, reversing its own earlier holding. The provision itself was narrowed rather than removed and remains in force. A restrictive constitutional provision in force is the anchor for 1.

formation.instrument: N.Y. Educ. Law § 3204(2); 8 NYCRR Part 130; Matter of Parents for Educational and Religious Liberty in Schools v. Young, 2025 NY Slip Op 03689 (N.Y. June 18, 2025)
formation.note: A nonpublic school satisfies compulsory attendance only by falling within one of the section 3204(2) categories or by passing local substantial equivalency review, and the Court of Appeals upheld the rule that a final determination of failure means the school 'shall no longer be deemed a school that provides compulsory education.' The accreditation pathway runs only through bodies the commissioner approves and may revoke. Approval required with only state-designated approvers satisfying it is the anchor for 1; whether any commissioner-approved accreditation body is religious could not be established, because the department's list could not be opened.

autonomy.note: Instruction must be 'at least substantially equivalent' to the local public schools, section 3204(3) names the required courses for each span of grades, and section 801 adds patriotism, citizenship, and human rights content. This reaches quality and content and not merely subject headings, which rules out 3; it is not 1 because section 3204(5) excuses a pupil from health and hygiene instruction on the parent's religious grounds and no teacher certification or state assessment is imposed on nonpublic schools generally. The anchor for 2.

portability.instrument: N.Y. Const. art. XI, § 3
portability.note: Neither the state nor any subdivision may use public money 'in aid or maintenance, other than for examination or inspection, of any school or institution of learning wholly or in part under the control or direction of any religious denomination.' No scholarship, account, or tax credit program for private school attendance is in force. The anchor for no program.

household.note: The family must file an individualized home instruction plan, the district must notify the parent whether the plan complies and must give written notice of any deficiency for the parent to correct, quarterly reports follow, and a superintendent with reasonable grounds may make a home visit. Approval of a plan by a school official is the anchor for 1. Tier B because the regulation was read through the federal compilation that names it.

security.instrument: N.Y. Const. art. XI, § 3
security.note: A restrictive constitutional provision, amended into its present form in 1938 and renumbered in 1962, is in force, which is the anchor for 1. The substantial equivalency challenge was resolved against the schools in June 2025, so nothing on that front is now pending.

formation.note: A new private church school or school of religious charter sends the Division of Nonpublic Education a notice of intent to operate with the school's name, address, owner, and chief administrator, keeps attendance and immunization records, and submits to ordinary fire, health, and safety inspection. No approval or accreditation exists to be withheld. Registration that is ministerial is the anchor for 3.

autonomy.note: There is no curriculum requirement and no teacher certification requirement; the only mandates are a nine calendar month term and an annual nationally standardized test 'selected by the chief administrative officer of such school' in grades three, six, nine, and eleven, with records held for inspection. This is not 4, because testing and calendar are not left to the school; it is not 2, because no state assessment is imposed and the school picks the instrument. The anchor for 3.

portability.note: The household income definitions were repealed effective July 1, 2023, and an eligible student is now any student residing in North Carolina who has not received a high school diploma, is eligible to attend a public school, and is not enrolled full time in a postsecondary institution. Universal eligibility in force is the anchor for 4.

household.note: A home school files a notice of intent to operate, the person giving instruction must hold at least a high school diploma, and testing under section 115C-549 applies annually, using a nationally standardized instrument the school itself selects. Notice plus an assessment the family chooses is the anchor for 2.

security.instrument: Hart v. State, No. 372A14 (N.C. July 23, 2015); N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 115C-562.1 to 115C-562.8
security.note: The state supreme court held in 2015 that no constitutional prohibition prevents the General Assembly from funding private school attendance, so no restrictive constitutional provision is in force and nothing is pending against the program. Statutory with nothing pending is the anchor for 3; it is not 4 because the position rests on statutes amended as recently as the 2024 veto override rather than on anything constitutional.

formation.note: The superintendent of public instruction must approve a nonpublic school offering elementary or secondary education, on an annual compliance report, due 1 October and approved by the school's governing board, certifying that each classroom teacher is licensed by the education standards and practices board, that the required subjects are taught, that the physical plant has passed fire marshal inspection, and that background checks have been made. No accreditor of the school's choosing satisfies the requirement. Approval required and only the state satisfying it is the anchor for 1. Correction: the federal compilation attributes this requirement to section 15.1-06-06, which governs the approval of public school districts and does not reach nonpublic schools; the nonpublic provision is section 15.1-06-06.1, as the department's own compliance guidance states. Tier B because the text of section 15.1-06-06.1 was not opened.

autonomy.note: Teacher licensure with a matching major is mandatory at the elementary, middle, and high school levels, the curriculum is prescribed unit by unit for graduation, and every grade eleven student must take the ACT with writing or three WorkKeys assessments. Teacher credentials required and a state assessment mandated, without the religious content of instruction being reached, is the anchor for 2; the anchor for 1 is not taken because no prescribed content engages the school's religious teaching and hiring is not constrained on religious criteria.

portability.instrument: N.D. Const. art. VIII, § 5; 2025 N.D. H.B. 1540 (vetoed 23 April 2025); 2023 N.D. S.B. 2237 (failed 17 March 2023)
portability.note: No money raised for the support of the public schools may be appropriated to or used for the support of any sectarian school, and the compilation records that no financial assistance programs currently exist. The two most recent attempts, Senate Bill 2237 in 2023 and House Bill 1540 in 2025, failed and were vetoed respectively. No program is the anchor for 0.

household.note: The parent files an annual statement at least fourteen days before starting, stating the parent's own qualifications; a parent without a diploma or its equivalent must be monitored by a licensed teacher; standardized tests are required in grades four, six, eight, and ten and must be administered by a licensed educator; scores are filed with the district superintendent, and a composite below the thirtieth percentile triggers a multidisciplinary learning assessment. Review by a public official is the anchor for 1.

security.instrument: N.D. Const. art. VIII, § 5
security.note: A restrictive constitutional provision is in force, which is the anchor for 1 whatever the statutory position. The 2025 veto of House Bill 1540 removed nothing that existed, so the anchor for 0 is not taken.

formation.instrument: Ohio Rev. Code § 3301.0732(A); Ohio Admin. Code 3301-35-08
formation.note: A nonchartered nonpublic school that is not seeking a charter 'because of truly held religious beliefs' certifies annually to its own parents that it meets the minimum education standards and files a copy with the department by September 30. There is no state approval to be granted or withheld on that route. Annual reporting that is ministerial is the anchor for 3.

autonomy.note: The statute prescribes instructional hours and a list of subjects, and division (D) requires that 'teachers and administrators at nonchartered nonpublic schools shall hold at least a bachelor's degree, or the equivalent, from a recognized college or university,' with no religious waiver. A staffing credential is required while no state assessment is imposed and religious content is untouched, which is the anchor for 2 rather than 3.

portability.instrument: Ohio Rev. Code § 3310.032(A) (H.B. 33, 135th General Assembly)
portability.note: An eligible student is any student entering kindergarten through grade twelve whose resident district is not a Cleveland pilot district; income certification affects the award and not eligibility. Universal eligibility in force is the anchor for 4. The trial court ruling of June 24, 2025 was stayed, so the program is operating; that risk is scored under security, not here.

household.note: Since H.B. 33 took effect on October 3, 2023 the parent transmits a notice naming the child and assuring instruction in the listed subjects, 'the child's exemption under this section is effective immediately upon receipt of notice,' and the section 'shall not be subject to any rules adopted by' the department. No assessment or portfolio review survives. Notice with no assessment is the anchor for 3.

security.instrument: Columbus City School Dist. v. State of Ohio, Franklin C.P. No. 22CV000067 (June 24, 2025), on appeal, 10th Dist. No. 25-AP-000603
security.note: A live case could remove an existing protection: the Court of Common Pleas granted the districts summary judgment against the EdChoice program on June 24, 2025 and the appeal is pending in the Tenth District. That is the anchor for 1. It is not 0, because the judge stayed her own ruling and the program has continued in force throughout.

formation.instrument: Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 3-104; Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 10-105(A)
formation.note: Private and parochial schools may be accredited by the State Board of Education, or through an accrediting association the board approves, only if application is made for it, and no registration, licensing, or approval is required to operate. The anchor for 4 is taken. The requirement that a school be accredited to receive Parental Choice Tax Credit money is a condition on the money, recorded under portability and excluded here. Tier B because section 3-104 rests on the federal compilation, though section 10-105 was opened.

autonomy.note: The staffing, school day, course, and health services requirements the compilation lists attach to a school that has sought state accreditation, which is optional under section 3-104, so they are excluded. For an unaccredited private school the state mandates no testing, prescribes no curriculum, and sets no staffing standard, leaving only observances such as flag display and Oklahoma Heritage Week. Curriculum, texts, calendar, testing, and staffing being the school's own is the anchor for 4.

portability.instrument: Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 28-101 (2023 Okla. Sess. Laws, H.B. 1934; amended by H.B. 3388 (2024) and H.B. 3705 (2026))
portability.note: An eligible student is a resident of the state who is eligible to enroll in a public school in the state, with no income ceiling on eligibility; the refundable credit runs from $7,500 where combined adjusted gross income is below $75,000 down to $5,000 above $250,000, so income graduates the amount rather than the entitlement. The annual cap rises to $275,000,000 from fiscal year 2027. A universal program open to religious schools with no condition reaching religious character is the anchor for 4; the annual cap and the priority for lower incomes are rationing devices, not eligibility limits, and the accreditation condition reaches the school's organization rather than its religious character.

household.instrument: Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 10-105(A); Okla. Stat. tit. 70, § 10-109
household.note: The compulsory attendance duty does not apply where other means of education are provided for the full term the schools of the district are in session, and the state prescribes no application, notice, curriculum, or assessment for a home-educating family. No notice and no assessment required is the anchor for 4.

security.instrument: Okla. Const. art. II, § 5; Drummond ex rel. State v. Oklahoma Statewide Virtual Charter School Board, 2024 OK 53; Oliver v. Hofmeister, 2016 OK 15
security.note: Article II, section 5 forbids the appropriation of public money or property for the benefit of any sectarian institution, and the court applied it in 2024 to void a charter contract with a religious virtual school. Oliver v. Hofmeister had earlier sustained the disability scholarship against the same clause. A restrictive constitutional provision in force is the anchor for 1; the 2024 ruling concerned a charter contract rather than the removal of a protection private religious schools held, and it falls outside the two-year window, so the anchor for 0 is not taken.

formation.instrument: Or. Rev. Stat. § 339.030(1)(a); Or. Rev. Stat. § 336.615; Or. Rev. Stat. § 418.327
formation.note: Compulsory attendance is excused for a child taught in a private or parochial school in the courses of study usually taught in kindergarten through grade twelve, and the state requires no accreditation, registration, licensing, or approval of that school. Registration with the department under section 336.615 and rule 581-021-0072 reaches only a private alternative school seeking public funds, which is a condition on the money and is recorded under portability, and licensure under section 418.327 reaches residential programs rather than day schools. The anchor for 4 is taken.

autonomy.note: The school must offer the courses of study usually taught in the public schools and must instruct primarily in English, and nothing further: no teacher certification, no prescribed content, no prescribed texts, and no assessment. The statewide assessment under section 336.637(2) and the licensure procedures under rule 584-036-0015 reach only private alternative schools registered to receive public funds and are excluded as conditions on the money. Broad subject areas prescribed with content, texts, and staffing the school's own is the anchor for 3.

portability.instrument: Or. Const. art. I, § 5; Dickman v. School District 62C, 366 P.2d 533 (Or. 1961), cert. denied, 371 U.S. 823 (1962)
portability.note: The free textbook statute was struck down under article I, section 5, and the compilation records that no state financial assistance programs for private school attendance currently exist. The state declined the federal Education Freedom Tax Credit election. No program is the anchor for 0.

household.note: The parent notifies the education service district in writing once, and annual notification is not required. Comprehensive examinations approved by the State Board are required at grades three, five, eight, and ten, the parent chooses the examination from the approved list, and a qualified neutral person administers it, scores it, and reports the result to the parent, with the result going to the district only on request. Notice plus an assessment with the reviewer of the family's choosing is the anchor for 2; the anchor for 1 is not taken, though the district superintendent may require instruction by a licensed teacher or order attendance after three consecutive years below the fifteenth percentile.

security.instrument: Or. Const. art. I, § 5
security.note: Article I, section 5 bars drawing money from the treasury for the benefit of a religious or theological institution, and it has been applied to strike down aid to nonpublic school pupils. A restrictive constitutional provision in force is the anchor for 1.

formation.note: A day school operated by a bona fide religious institution registers by the notarized affidavit of its principal filed with the Department of Education certifying that the prescribed subjects are taught in English and that the school complies with the law. The licensing regime under the Private Academic Schools Act reaches K-12 private academic schools except those owned or operated by or under the authority of bona fide religious institutions, so it does not reach a Christian school. A filing the state records rather than evaluates is the anchor for 3.

autonomy.note: The section names the subjects required at the elementary and secondary levels and sets 180 days or 900 and 990 hours, but it also provides that nothing in the act shall empower the Commonwealth, any of its officers, agencies, or subdivisions to approve the course content, faculty, staff, or disciplinary requirements of any religious school without the consent of that school. No testing of nonpublic school students is required, and the Commonwealth imposes no faculty approval on religious schools. Broad subject areas prescribed with content, texts, and staffing the school's own is the anchor for 3.

portability.instrument: 24 P.S. §§ 20-2001-B to 20-2013-B (Educational Improvement Tax Credit, 2001; Opportunity Scholarship Tax Credit, 2012)
portability.note: The department records the Educational Improvement Tax Credit household income limit at $122,322 plus $21,531 for each dependent member, which is an income ceiling that reaches well into the middle of the distribution, and the Opportunity Scholarship Tax Credit serves students residing in the attendance boundary of a low-achieving school with awards to $8,500, or $15,000 for a student with a disability. Both are open to religious schools on the same terms as others. A broad program, income- or category-limited, is the anchor for 3; the anchor for 2 describes a narrow program, which two credits of this eligibility and award size are not, though both are rationed by annual credit caps and carry waiting lists. Tier B because the income figures rest on the department's page rather than on the statutory escalator.

household.note: The supervisor files a notarized affidavit with the superintendent of the district of residence before commencement and annually on 1 August, maintains a contemporaneous log and a portfolio of samples, obtains results of nationally normed or statewide tests in grades three, five, and eight, and obtains an annual written evaluation by a certified teacher or a licensed psychologist, whose certification is provided to the superintendent by 30 June each year. Review by a public official is the anchor for 1, notwithstanding that the family chooses the evaluator from a defined class.

security.instrument: Pa. Const. art. III, § 15; Pa. Const. art. III, § 30
security.note: Article III, section 15 forbids any appropriation of money raised for the public schools to a sectarian school, and section 30 bars appropriations to educational institutions not under the absolute control of the Commonwealth absent a two-thirds vote of each House. Both remain in force, which is the anchor for 1 whatever the statutory position; the tax credits, being funded by credits against corporate liability rather than by appropriation, have not been tested against either, and the PASS and Lifeline scholarship proposals have not been enacted.

formation.note: Section 16-19-1 satisfies compulsory attendance only through "a private day school approved by the commissioner of elementary and secondary education pursuant to § 16-60-6(10)," section 16-60-6(10) gives the commissioner the power to approve and accredit elementary and secondary schools, and section 16-19-2 provides that a private school "shall be approved only when it complies with" an attendance period substantially equal to the public schools, register keeping, and a list of subjects taught in English. Approval that only the state itself can grant is the anchor for 1. It is not 0: the grounds named in the statute are attendance, registers, and subjects, and none of them reaches the school's religious character. Registration and the annual July return under section 16-40-11 sit on top of the approval requirement rather than in place of it.

autonomy.note: The statute prescribes reading, writing, geography, arithmetic, United States history, Rhode Island history, and the principles of American government, taught in English substantially to the same extent as in the public schools, and expressly preserves the right to teach any other subject in any other language in addition. Broad subject areas prescribed with texts and staffing left to the school is the anchor for 3. Teacher certification is not required and participation in state testing is voluntary, both of which rest on the federal compilation rather than on a statute opened here. The approval requirement is scored under formation and is deliberately not counted a second time here.

portability.note: The one program is a credit against business taxes for cash contributions to a qualified scholarship organization, capped at $100,000 a year per business entity, nonrefundable, nonassignable, and usable only in the year the contribution was made. A narrow tax credit is the anchor for 2. The statute carries no condition reaching the religious character of a recipient school.

household.note: At-home instruction "shall be approved only when it complies with" the statutory requirements, and the statute provides an appeal to the department for any person "aggrieved by the action of the school committee of the city or town either in approving or refusing to approve at-home instruction," which shows on the face of the instrument that approval may be withheld. Approval that may be withheld is the anchor for 0. The approving body is the local school committee acting under state law rather than a state officer, which is recorded here as the one qualification on the score.

security.instrument: R.I. Const. art. I, § 3; R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 44-62-1 to 44-62-7
security.note: Article I, section 3 is a compelled support and religious liberty clause providing that no person shall be compelled to frequent or support any religious worship, place, or ministry, and it contains no bar on appropriations to sectarian schools, so no restrictive constitutional provision is in force. The tax credit has stood unamended in substance since 2006 and nothing is pending on the register, which is the anchor for 3. It is not 4 because the position rests entirely on a statute the General Assembly can revisit in any session.

formation.instrument: S.C. Code Ann. § 59-65-10(A); S.C. Code Ann. § 59-13-130
formation.note: Section 59-65-10(A) satisfies compulsory attendance through "a parochial, denominational, or church-related school" as a category standing on its own, alongside membership in the South Carolina Independent Schools' Association, the South Carolina Association of Christian Schools, or a similar organization, with no state approval, registration, or licensure attached to the church-related route. No requirement to operate is the anchor for 4. The only continuing duty located is the report to the county superintendent under section 59-13-130, which is owed on request and is ministerial. The State Board approval condition in the scholarship statute is a condition on the money and is scored under portability.

autonomy.instrument: S.C. Code Ann. § 59-65-10(A); S.C. Code Ann. § 59-13-130
autonomy.note: Chapter 65 attaches no curriculum, calendar, teacher credential, or assessment requirement to a parochial, denominational, or church-related school, and the only obligation in chapter 13 is a statistical report on request. Curriculum, texts, calendar, testing, and staffing left to the school is the anchor for 4. The federal compilation records "no state policy" on teacher certification, curriculum, length of school year, and testing, which agrees with the two chapters opened here.

portability.instrument: S.C. Code Ann. §§ 59-8-110 to 59-8-140 (Education Scholarship Trust Fund, as re-enacted by 2025 Act No. 11 (S. 62), eff. May 7, 2025); S.C. Code Ann. § 12-6-3790
portability.note: The Education Scholarship Trust Fund was re-enacted in 2025 with tuition and fees restored as a qualifying expense, eligibility set at 300 percent of the federal poverty guidelines for 2025-2026 and 500 percent thereafter, and capacity of 10,000 students rising to at least 15,000. A broad program that is income and capacity limited and open to nonprofit independent schools on the same terms as others is the anchor for 3. The conditions on a participating school under section 59-8-140(A)(2), namely in-state location, a curriculum covering the state diploma courses, and satisfaction of the State Board approval requirement in section 59-65-10, are conditions on the money and are excluded from formation and autonomy, where South Carolina imposes nothing.

household.note: Three routes exist. The district route under section 59-65-40 requires approval by the board of trustees and participation in the statewide testing program, but the two association routes under sections 59-65-45 and 59-65-47 require no district approval and no state test, only a 180-day year, the listed subjects, and a plan book, diary, or other written record with a portfolio of the student's work. Notice plus a portfolio held to a reviewer of the family's choosing is the anchor for 2, since a family may take an association route as of right.

security.instrument: S.C. Const. art. XI, § 4; Eidson v. South Carolina Department of Education, Op. No. 28235 (S.C. Sept. 11, 2024)
security.note: Article XI, section 4 provides that no money shall be paid from public funds nor the credit of the State be used "for the direct benefit of any religious or other private educational institution," and the Supreme Court used it on 11 September 2024 to strike the tuition provisions of the Education Scholarship Trust Fund Act and to enjoin disbursement for private school tuition. A protection struck down inside the two-year window is the anchor for 0. The General Assembly re-enacted the program on 7 May 2025 and the redesigned statute has not been tested against article XI, section 4 in any retrieved decision, so the restrictive provision stands unadjudicated as to the current program.

formation.instrument: S.D. Codified Laws § 13-27-1; S.D. Codified Laws § 13-3-47
formation.note: Section 13-27-1 satisfies compulsory attendance through "a public or nonpublic school" with no approval, registration, or accreditation condition attached, and section 13-3-47 places classification and accreditation with the secretary of the Department of Education without making either compulsory for a nonpublic school. No requirement to operate is the anchor for 4. The federal compilation reports no registration, licensing, or approval requirement, which agrees with the two sections opened here.

autonomy.instrument: S.D. Codified Laws § 13-33-4; S.D. Codified Laws § 13-33-6.1
autonomy.note: Section 13-33-4 requires regular courses on the United States and South Dakota constitutions in all nonpublic schools from the eighth grade through high school, and section 13-33-6.1 requires character development instruction in all nonpublic elementary and secondary schools unless the governing body resolves otherwise, which is an opt-out the school itself controls. Broad subject areas prescribed with content, texts, and staffing left to the school is the anchor for 3. No teacher certification and no state assessment applies to a nonpublic school.

portability.note: The Partners in Education program is a credit against the insurance company premium and annuity tax for contributions to a scholarship granting organization, and eligibility is capped at 200 percent of the free or reduced-price lunch income standard on entry, with foster children qualifying without regard to income. A narrow, income-limited credit funded from one line of tax is the anchor for 2. Section 13-65-4(4) requires the scholarship granting organization to verify annually that each receiving school is accredited by the Department of Education, which is a condition on the money and is excluded from formation, where accreditation is voluntary.

household.instrument: S.D. Codified Laws § 13-27-3; S.D. Codified Laws § 13-27-7
household.note: The current text of section 13-27-3 requires only a filed notification, instruction in the basic skills of language arts and mathematics, instruction leading to mastery of English, and no more than twenty-two children per instructor, and it states that the person providing instruction need not be certified; section 13-27-7 makes the notification a one-time standard form renewed only on a change of school or district. Notice with no assessment or review is the anchor for 3. CORRECTION TO THE FEDERAL COMPILATION: the compilation reports that children receiving alternative instruction in grades two, four, eight, and eleven must take a nationally standardized achievement test, and it reports an equivalent-time requirement and an application to a school official. The codified text carries none of these. The testing paragraph and the investigation and revocation provisions were removed by 2021 S.D. Sess. Laws ch. 76 (S.B. 177), which is why the section is now captioned "Alternative instruction--Notification--Requirements" rather than including "Testing." The statute governs.

security.instrument: S.D. Const. art. VI, § 3; S.D. Const. art. VIII, § 16
security.note: Article VI, section 3 provides that no money or property of the state shall be given or appropriated for the benefit of any sectarian or religious society or institution, and article VIII, section 16 provides that no appropriation of lands, money, or other property or credits to aid any sectarian school shall ever be made. Two restrictive constitutional provisions in force is the anchor for 1 whatever the statutory position, and the tax credit's routing through private scholarship organizations has not been tested against either. Nothing is pending on the register, which is why it is not lower.

formation.note: A Christian school has two routes. As a Category IV church-related school it must meet the accreditation standards of the Tennessee Association of Christian Schools, the Association of Christian Schools International, the Tennessee Association of Independent Schools, or a comparable body, or be recognized as a 501(c)(3) religious organization, which is anchor 2 on its own terms. As a Category V school it registers with the Department by furnishing name, address, telephone number, principal credentials, and enrollment by 15 October each year, with no accreditation mandate, which is ministerial registration and is anchor 3. The lighter route that is available as of right sets the score, so this is 3.

autonomy.note: Subsection (b) provides that "the state board of education and local boards of education are prohibited from regulating the selection of faculty or textbooks or the establishment of a curriculum in church-related schools," and no state assessment is imposed on a Category IV school. Subsection (d) requires that a church-related school be conducted for the same length of term as the public schools, so the calendar is not the school's own and 4 is not available. Content, texts, and staffing left to the school with the term prescribed is the anchor for 3.

portability.instrument: Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 49-6-3501 to 49-6-3512 (Education Freedom Scholarship Act); State Board of Education Rule 0520-01-24
portability.note: The Department of Education records the Education Freedom Scholarship as open to students who are Tennessee residents entitled to attend a public school in grades kindergarten through twelve, with no income limit and an award of $7,295 for 2025-2026. A universal program open to religious providers is the anchor for 4. Participation is limited to registered Category I, II, or III nonpublic schools, which is a condition on the money and is excluded from formation and autonomy; a Christian school reaches Category II through an approved accrediting agency, so the condition does not reach religious character. Scored at tier B: the department's own page was opened, the enacting act is behind a robots exclusion, and the codified sections were not opened.

household.note: An independent home school files annual notice with the director of schools naming the children, the location, the proposed curriculum, and the parent-teacher's qualifications, the parent-teacher must hold a high school diploma or its equivalent, and students take the state board's secure standardized tests in grades five, seven, and nine, with the director able to require enrollment elsewhere after two consecutive years more than one year below level. That route alone would sit at 1. The statute also exempts from the section a family teaching under the supervision of a church-related school, which substitutes a reviewer of the family's choosing, and that route is available as of right, which is the anchor for 2. Scored at tier B: the statute text was read from a reproduction and from the federal compilation rather than from an official code source.

security.instrument: Metropolitan Government of Nashville and Davidson County v. Tennessee Department of Education, No. M2020-00683-SC-R11-CV (Tenn. May 18, 2022); remanded claims against Tenn. Code Ann. § 49-6-2601
security.note: Tennessee has no constitutional bar on aid to religious schools, and the Supreme Court removed the Home Rule objection to the Education Savings Account Pilot Program in 2022. The equal protection and education claims left on remand were revived by the Court of Appeals in January 2024 and are outstanding, and a statewide program was enacted in 2025 that has not been tested at all. Live litigation that could move the position in either direction is the anchor for 2. Scored at tier C: the 2022 opinion is tier A, but the pending status of the remanded claims rests on a dated secondary account and no final judgment has been verified against a primary source.

formation.note: The federal compilation records no accreditation, registration, licensing, or approval requirement of any kind for a Texas private school; a student is exempt from compulsory attendance by attending a private or parochial school whose course includes a study of good citizenship. Nothing is filed and nothing is approved, which is the anchor for 4.

autonomy.note: Teacher certification is not required, no state assessment is imposed, and no calendar or textbook requirement applies; the sole statutory condition is that the course of study include good citizenship. Curriculum, texts, calendar, testing, and staffing left to the school is the anchor for 4, and the single named topic is too narrow to be the prescribed subject areas of 3.

portability.instrument: Tex. Educ. Code § 29.355(a) (S.B. 2, 89th Leg., R.S. (2025))
portability.note: A child is eligible if a citizen or lawfully admitted and eligible to attend a school district or open-enrollment charter school, with no income or category limit, and no condition of the program reaches a school's religious character. Universal eligibility in force is the anchor for 4; enrollment is 'subject to available funding,' which rations access without narrowing eligibility.

household.instrument: Tex. Educ. Code § 25.086(a)(1); Leeper v. Arlington Independent School District
household.note: The compilation records that the state 'does not regulate, monitor, approve, register, or accredit' home education, and that no notice or assessment requirement exists; a home school is treated as a private school, so hybrid and part-time arrangements are equally unregulated. No notice and no assessment is the anchor for 4.

security.instrument: Tex. Const. art. I, § 7
security.note: The constitution provides that no money shall be appropriated, or drawn from the treasury, for the benefit of any sect or religious society, theological or religious seminary, and that no state property shall be appropriated for such purposes. The provision was adopted in 1876 and is unrepealed. A restrictive constitutional provision in force is the anchor for 1 whatever the statutory position, and the savings account program is in any case only one session old.

formation.instrument: Utah Code § 53G-6-202; Utah Admin. Code R277-410-3(A)
formation.note: Section 53G-6-202 requires a parent to "enroll and send the school-age child to a public or regularly established private school" and imposes no approval, registration, or licensure condition on the private school, and rule R277-410-3(A) states that the Board "is not responsible for the accreditation of nonpublic schools, including private, parochial, or other independent schools." No requirement to operate is the anchor for 4.

autonomy.instrument: Utah Code § 53G-6-202; Utah Admin. Code R277-410-3(A)
autonomy.note: No curriculum, calendar, teacher credential, or assessment requirement attaches to a private school; the federal compilation records requirements only for immunization records, age certificates, and voter registration documentation, and the assessment provisions it names are permissive participation in the state system at the school's option. Curriculum, texts, calendar, testing, and staffing left to the school is the anchor for 4. Scored at tier B because the score rests on an absence confirmed by the compilation rather than on a prohibitory statute, and the compilation cites the repealed title 53A numbering throughout.

portability.instrument: Utah Code §§ 53F-6-401 to 53F-6-414, particularly § 53F-6-402(6)
portability.note: The Utah Fits All Scholarship is open to eligible school-age children generally, with income used only to order priority when applications exceed available scholarships: returning recipients first, then new applicants at or below 300 percent of the federal poverty level, then siblings, then a lottery. The statute refers throughout to a "qualifying provider" with no exclusion of religious schools or providers. A universal program with no condition reaching religious character is the anchor for 4. The 2025 declaratory judgment against the program is scored under security; no injunction is in force and the program continues to operate.

household.note: A parent gives a one-time initial notification to the local school board, and the board "may not" require records of instruction or attendance, require credentials of the person instructing, inspect the home school facility, or require standardized or other testing; selection of materials, the time, place, and method of instruction, and evaluation are the parent's alone. Notice with no assessment or review is the anchor for 3. CORRECTION TO THE FEDERAL COMPILATION: the compilation reports a yearly signed affidavit and cites the repealed section 53A-11-102. The current section requires one initial notification only, and expressly excuses even that where a notification or affidavit was filed on or before 7 May 2025.

security.instrument: Utah Const. art. X, § 9
security.note: Article X, section 9 provides that neither the state nor its political subdivisions "may make any appropriation for the direct support of any school or educational institution controlled by any religious organization." A restrictive constitutional provision in force is the anchor for 1. A live case points the same way: the Third District Court held the Utah Fits All Scholarship Program unconstitutional in April 2025 under articles X and XIII and the appeal was still pending in the Utah Supreme Court as of July 2026. It is not 0: the trial judge entered no injunction and the program has operated throughout, so nothing has been enjoined, repealed, or reversed.

formation.note: Coder A scored 3 and coder B scored 1. The statute settles it for 3, and the disagreement was a scoping error rather than a reading error. Section 166(c) provides that 'upon filing an enrollment notice, a recognized independent school may provide elementary or secondary education in Vermont' - operation begins on the filing, with no grant required, which is the anchor for 3. The evaluative approval in s. 166(b), where the State Board must find a minimum course of study, substantial compliance with its rules, and adequate finances, faculty, and facilities, is the condition for receiving public tuition. That is a condition on money following a child, and it is scored under portability. Formation asks how hard it is to open and keep open a school, and in Vermont that is a filing.

autonomy.instrument: 16 V.S.A. §§ 166(b), (c), 906; State Board Manual of Rules and Practices 2226.5.1
autonomy.note: Section 906 prescribes the minimum course of study, the recognition filing must carry assurances of annual student assessment and adequate staff, and the State Board rule requires teachers at approved schools to hold a bachelor's degree in their field of instruction or equivalent training. An assessment assurance plus a staffing credential is the anchor for 2.

portability.instrument: 16 V.S.A. §§ 821, 822, 828(a)(2) (2025 Vt. Acts and Resolves No. 73, Sec. 21)
portability.note: Town tuitioning reaches only pupils whose district does not maintain a school of their grade, and since 2025 an approved independent school qualifies only if it satisfies five cumulative conditions, including having had at least 25 percent district-funded enrollment in 2023-2024 and approval on or before July 1, 2025. A program limited to particular students is the anchor for 2; the new conditions are facially neutral, so they are not coded as reaching religious character.

household.note: The parent sends the Secretary a notice of intent at least ten business days before beginning, the Secretary's written acknowledgment of receipt 'shall constitute sufficient enrollment verification,' and an annual assessment is attested, with the options including a parent portfolio report or review by a Vermont-certified teacher. Notice plus an assessment the family chooses is the anchor for 2.

security.instrument: 2025 Vt. Acts and Resolves No. 73, Sec. 21, codified at 16 V.S.A. § 828(a)(2)(D); Chittenden Town School District v. Department of Education, 169 Vt. 310 (1999)
security.note: Access to town tuitioning for approved independent schools was cut back by statute effective July 1, 2025, which removes an existing protection inside the two-year window and is the anchor for 0. Chittenden's reading of Chapter I, Article 3 of the Vermont Constitution against sectarian tuition also remains on the books, displaced federally but not overruled at home.

formation.note: Section 22.1-254(A) satisfies compulsory attendance through "a private, denominational, or parochial school" with no approval, registration, or licensure attached, and section 22.1-19 has the Board recognize accreditation by the Virginia Council for Private Education rather than accredit schools itself, which is voluntary. No requirement to operate is the anchor for 4. Licensure under sections 22.1-320 and 22.1-323 reaches schools serving students with disabilities, and section 63.2-1717 reaches preschools, neither of which is a condition on operating an elementary or secondary Christian school.

autonomy.note: Virginia prescribes no curriculum, requires no teacher credential, and does not require private school students to sit state tests, but section 22.1-254(A) requires attendance "during the period of each year the public schools are in session and for the same number of days and hours per day as the public schools," which section 22.1-98 sets at 180 days or 990 teaching hours. The calendar is therefore not the school's own, which is what keeps this off 4; content, texts, and staffing are the school's own, which is the anchor for 3.

portability.instrument: Va. Code §§ 58.1-439.25 to 58.1-439.28 (Education Improvement Scholarships Tax Credits Program)
portability.note: The single program is a tax credit for donations to scholarship foundations, administered by the Department of Education since 2012. A narrow tax credit is the anchor for 2. Scored at tier C: the enacting sections were not opened and the entry rests on the dated national inventory carried in the register.

household.note: A parent notifies the division superintendent by 15 August with a list of subjects and evidence of meeting one of four qualifying criteria, and by the following 1 August files either a composite score in or above the fourth stanine on any nationally normed test or an evaluation letter from a person licensed to teach in any state or holding a master's degree in an academic discipline. Notice plus an assessment held by a reviewer of the family's choosing is the anchor for 2, since the test route is satisfied by a score and requires no official's judgment. Virginia also has the religious exemption under section 22.1-254(B)(1), which lifts compulsory attendance entirely and is a further latitude not reflected in the anchor.

security.instrument: Va. Const. art. VIII, § 10
security.note: Article VIII, section 10 provides that no appropriation of public funds shall be made to any school not owned or exclusively controlled by the State, and its first proviso permits appropriations for education "in public and nonsectarian private schools," so the exception on its face excludes sectarian schools. A restrictive constitutional provision in force is the anchor for 1 whatever the statutory position. Nothing is pending on the register, which is why it is not lower.

formation.note: Compulsory attendance is satisfied only at "an approved private school," approval is granted by the state board of education on minimum requirements covering instructional time, teacher certification, records, health and fire safety, curriculum, and a policy statement, and each principal files a yearly statement certifying compliance. Approval that only the state board can grant is the anchor for 1. It is not 0: the only ground of denial named in RCW 28A.195.040 is a policy of racial segregation or discrimination, and nothing in the chapter reaches a school's religious character.

autonomy.note: All classroom teachers must hold Washington state certification, with an exception for those teaching religious courses or courses having no public school counterpart, and the curriculum must include the listed basic skills. Required teacher credentials with the religious content of instruction untouched is the anchor for 2, and the statute reinforces the second half by leaving decisions on curriculum outside subsection (7), materials, and school rules to the private administration. No state assessment is imposed: the board may not require private school students to meet the learning goals or obtain a certificate of academic achievement.

portability.instrument: Wash. Const. art. I, § 11; Wash. Const. art. IX, § 4
portability.note: No voucher, education savings account, tax credit scholarship, or deduction reaching kindergarten through grade twelve is on the register for Washington, and the constitution forbids public money being appropriated for or applied to any religious instruction and requires schools supported by public funds to be free from sectarian control or influence. No program at all is the anchor for 0. The only entry on the register is the 2019 repeal of a sectarian employer exclusion in the State Work Study Program, which is a postsecondary employment program and not portability.

household.note: A parent files an annual signed declaration of intent by 15 September and must have a standardized achievement test approved by the state board administered annually by a qualified individual, or an annual assessment of academic progress written by a certificated person. Notice plus an assessment where the family picks the tester or the certificated reviewer is the anchor for 2. The parent qualification routes in RCW 28A.225.010(4) include one that turns on the superintendent deeming the parent qualified, but the alternatives of supervision by a certificated person or forty-five college credit hours are available as of right, so this is not 1.

security.instrument: Wash. Const. art. I, § 11; Wash. Const. art. IX, § 4
security.note: Article I, section 11 provides that no public money or property shall be appropriated for or applied to any religious worship, exercise, or instruction, or the support of any religious establishment, and article IX, section 4 provides that all schools maintained or supported wholly or in part by public funds shall be forever free from sectarian control or influence. Two restrictive constitutional provisions in force is the anchor for 1. Nothing is pending on the register, which is why it is not lower.

formation.note: Section 18-8-1(b) makes county board approval one route, but section 18-8-1(k) exempts from compulsory attendance any child at a private, parochial, or church school that elects to comply with article 28, and under that article the school owes only a notice of intent to operate to the State Superintendent on opening, a notice on termination, a 900-hour term, attendance and immunization records, a list of enrolled children on the superintendent's request, and fire, health, and safety inspection. Ministerial notice that the state records is the anchor for 3. Section 18-28-6 makes those requirements exclusive, so the election is a genuine alternative to approval.

autonomy.note: A school electing article 28 "shall administer during each school year a nationally normed standardized achievement test" at the same grade levels and in the same subject areas as the statewide summative assessment, with a participation rate matching the public schools, and composite results furnished to the State Superintendent on request. A mandated assessment with the religious content of instruction untouched is the anchor for 2. The school selects the test, sets its own curriculum objectives under section 18-28-3(e), and employs uncertified teachers, which is why it is not 1.

portability.instrument: W. Va. Code §§ 18-31-1 et seq. (Hope Scholarship Program), particularly § 18-31-2(5)
portability.note: The definition of eligible recipient carries a trigger that, the participation threshold not having been met, makes a child eligible from 1 July 2026 if he or she is "enrolled, eligible to be enrolled, or required to be enrolled" in a kindergarten or public elementary or secondary program, which removes the prior public school attendance condition. As of this coding the program is universal, and a participating school is any private school that notifies the board of its intention to participate, with no condition reaching religious character. A universal program open to religious schools is the anchor for 4.

household.note: A parent files a notice of intent naming the child and assuring instruction in the listed subjects, submits evidence of a high school diploma or equivalent, and obtains an annual academic assessment by one of four routes: a nationally normed test, the state testing program, a portfolio reviewed by a certified teacher, or an assessment mutually agreed with the superintendent. Notice plus an assessment where the family may pick the test or the reviewing teacher is the anchor for 2. Results are filed with the county superintendent at grades three, five, eight, and eleven, and a second consecutive year without acceptable progress requires additional evidence rather than surrender of the program.

security.instrument: State v. Beaver, No. 22-616 (W. Va. Nov. 17, 2022); W. Va. Code § 18-31-2(5)
security.note: West Virginia has no constitutional bar on aid to religious schools, the Supreme Court of Appeals held in November 2022 by four to one that the constitution does not prohibit the Legislature from enacting the Hope Scholarship Act, and nothing is pending on the register. Statutory with nothing pending is the anchor for 3. The 2022 injunction sits outside the two-year window, so 0 is not available; it is not 4 because the program has changed materially inside five years, becoming universal by the operation of its own trigger in 2026, and article 28 itself was amended in 2025.

formation.note: An institution "is a private school" if its program meets the six criteria in section 118.165(1), which the school satisfies of itself, and section 118.165(2) provides only that an institution "may request" the state superintendent to approve its program, with approval based solely on those criteria. The one continuing duty is the enrollment statement filed by 15 October under section 115.30(3). Registration and annual reporting that the state records is the anchor for 3. The preaccreditation and accreditation requirements in sections 118.60(2)(a)7 and 119.23(2)(a)7 apply only to schools in the choice programs; those are conditions on the money, are scored under portability, and are excluded here.

autonomy.note: The program must provide at least 875 hours of instruction and "a sequentially progressive curriculum of fundamental instruction in reading, language arts, mathematics, social studies, science and health," and the same paragraph provides that this "does not require the program to include in its curriculum any concept, topic or practice in conflict with the program's religious doctrines or to exclude from its curriculum any concept, topic or practice consistent with the program's religious doctrines." Broad subject areas prescribed with an express religious proviso, and content, texts, and staffing left to the school, is the anchor for 3. Teacher licensure is not required and no assessment is imposed outside the choice programs.

portability.instrument: Wis. Stat. § 118.60; Wis. Stat. § 119.23; Wis. Stat. § 115.7915
portability.note: The statewide parental choice program admits a pupil whose total family income does not exceed 3.0 times the federal poverty level, with the Milwaukee and Racine programs and the special needs scholarship alongside it. A broad, income-limited program is the anchor for 3. The conditions on participating schools, namely accreditation or preaccreditation, bachelor's degrees for teachers and administrators, higher instructional hours, and the state examination, are conditions on the money and are excluded from formation and autonomy. They do not reach religious character: the preaccrediting entities named in section 118.60(1)(cm) include the Wisconsin Association of Christian Schools, Christian Schools International, the Association of Christian Schools International, Lutheran synod accreditors, and the diocese or archdiocese in which the school sits.

household.note: Instruction in a home-based private educational program meeting the section 118.165(1) criteria may be substituted for attendance at a public or private school, and the only filing is the enrollment statement due by 15 October under section 115.30(3), in which the administrator indicates whether the program meets those criteria. Notice with no assessment or portfolio review is the anchor for 3; testing is not required of home-based programs. Section 118.145(4) also admits a home-based student to up to two public high school courses a semester, so hybrid arrangements are not restricted.

security.instrument: Wis. Const. art. I, § 18; Jackson v. Benson, No. 97-0270 (Wis. June 10, 1998)
security.note: Article I, section 18 provides that no money shall be drawn from the treasury for the benefit of religious societies or religious or theological seminaries, but the Supreme Court construed it in 1998 to permit the amended Milwaukee program including religious schools, and the court declined in December 2023 to take the original action challenging the statewide and special needs programs. A provision authoritatively construed to permit the programs, with nothing pending, is the anchor for 3. It is not 4 because the clause has never been repealed and the per pupil payments were rewritten as recently as 2023 Wisconsin Act 11.

formation.note: Private school licensing under Wyo. Stat. §§ 21-2-401 and 21-2-406 does not reach "any parochial, church or religious school" maintained by a church or religious organization that offers elementary and secondary education programs only, and no registration or approval requirement applies. No requirement to operate is the anchor for 4 for a Christian school. The $200 annual license application and the department's chapter 18 rules on certification, curriculum, and reporting bind only nonreligious licensed private schools.

autonomy.note: A basic academic educational program is one providing "a sequentially progressive curriculum of fundamental instruction in reading, writing, mathematics, civics, history, literature and science," and the same paragraph provides that the requirements do not require any private school to include any concept, topic, or practice in conflict with its religious doctrines or to exclude any consistent with them. Broad subject areas prescribed with an express religious proviso is the anchor for 3, and the compulsory attendance sections tie the term to the public school session. Teacher certification and the department's curriculum and reporting rules do not reach a religious school.

portability.instrument: Wyo. Stat. §§ 21-2-901 to 21-2-909 (Steamboat Legacy Scholarship Act, as amended by 2025 Wyo. H.B. 199, Enrolled Act No. 52)
portability.note: The Department of Education records the program as open to Wyoming residents in prekindergarten through grade twelve who are not enrolled in a public school, with an income test of 250 percent of the federal poverty guidelines applying only to prekindergarten, and an award of $7,000. A universal program at the compulsory school ages, usable for tuition at a participating school with no condition reaching religious character, is the anchor for 4. The enrolled 2025 act was opened for the award amounts, but the eligibility subsection at Wyo. Stat. § 21-2-904(a) was not, so this is tier B. The 2025 injunction is scored under security; the Supreme Court lifted it and the program is operating.

household.instrument: Wyo. Stat. § 21-4-102(b), as amended by 2025 Wyo. H.B. 46
household.note: Subsection (b) now reads that "it shall be the responsibility of every person administering a home-based educational program to ensure a curriculum is administered to pupils in the program that complies with the requirements of this subsection," with no filing, no submission, and no assessment. No notice and no assessment is the anchor for 4. CORRECTION TO THE FEDERAL COMPILATION: the compilation reports that administrators "must submit annual curricula to local school boards demonstrating compliance" and cites this subsection. The Department of Education states that per House Bill 46, effective 1 July 2025, the homeschooling entity is no longer required to submit the curriculum to the local district, and the codified text carries no submission duty. The statute governs. The in-person meeting in subsection (c) is a condition of withdrawing a child already enrolled in a public school, not a continuing requirement.

security.instrument: Wyoming Education Association v. Degenfelder, No. 2025-CV-0203366 (Wyo. Dist. Ct., 1st Jud. Dist., July 15, 2025); Degenfelder v. Wyoming Education Association, 2026 WY 54, Nos. S-25-0203 and S-25-0204; Wyo. Const. art. 1, § 19; art. 3, § 36; art. 7, § 8
security.note: The district court enjoined the State, the Superintendent, and the Treasurer from distributing any funds to education service providers under the Steamboat Legacy Scholarship Act on 15 July 2025, and the program stood halted until the Supreme Court reversed on 14 May 2026 for failure to show irreparable personal injury. A protection enjoined inside the two-year window is the anchor for 0. Three restrictive constitutional provisions also stand: article 1, section 19 forbids state money ever being given to any sectarian or religious society or institution, article 3, section 36 forbids appropriations for educational purposes to anything not under the absolute control of the state or to any denominational or sectarian institution, and article 7, section 8 forbids any public school fund being used to assist a school controlled by any church or sectarian organization. The merits were expressly left undecided on remand.

events.instrument: One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Pub. L. 119-21, sec. 70411; 26 U.S.C. sec. 25F
events.summary: Education Freedom Tax Credit: a $1,700, nonrefundable, dollar for dollar federal tax credit for donations to scholarship granting organizations, for families at or below 300% of area median gross income, effective 2027-01-01. The state elects to participate by filing IRS Form 15714 and a list of qualified scholarship granting organizations with the Treasury.

The Governor's office has said it is awaiting further federal guidance.

events.instrument: Hile v. State of Michigan, No. 22-1986 (6th Cir.)
events.summary: The Sixth Circuit upheld Michigan's constitutional ban on public money for nonpublic schools against an equal protection challenge brought by families who wished to use Michigan Education Savings Program accounts for religious school tuition. Governor Gretchen Whitmer and the State Treasurer were named in their official capacities.
A school voucher program that gives aid to parents, who then choose among religious and secular schools, does not violate the Establishment Clause.

events.instrument: Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia v. Comer, 582 U.S. 449

events.instrument: Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue, 591 U.S. 464
events.summary: A state that funds private school scholarships may not exclude religious schools from the program because of their religious character.
A state tuition assistance program may not exclude schools because the education they provide is religious.

events.summary: An evenly divided Court affirmed the Oklahoma Supreme Court, which had held that public funds may not go to a religious charter school. An equally divided affirmance sets no nationwide precedent.
A school district burdens parents' religious exercise when it requires their children to take part in instruction that conflicts with their religious beliefs, so an opt-out must be permitted.

Alabama's anti-aid provision, Section 263 of the Constitution of 1901, states that no money raised for the support of the public schools shall be appropriated to or used for the support of any sectarian or denominational school. The provision restricts only money raised for the public schools rather than all public funds, and it carried forward without change of text into the recompiled Constitution of Alabama of 2022.

The Alabama Accountability Act of 2013 was approved by the Governor on 14 March 2013 at 10:53 a.m. and received by the Secretary of State the same day. The act established Alabama's first two private school choice mechanisms: a refundable individual income tax credit for parents transferring a child out of a school designated as failing, and an income tax credit for contributions to scholarship granting organizations that award scholarships usable at nonpublic schools, including church and parochial schools. The act is codified at Ala. Code §§ 16-6D-1 through 16-6D-9.

Act 2013-265 amended sections 4, 5, 8, and 9 of the Alabama Accountability Act of 2013 within weeks of the original enactment. It revised the definitions of eligible student and failing school, set the parent tax credit at 80 percent of the average annual state cost of attendance for a public K-12 student or the actual cost of attendance at a nonfailing public or nonpublic school, whichever is less, and set the credit for corporate donors to scholarship granting organizations at a stated percentage of contributions. The act also provides that a nonpublic school may not be compelled to enroll a student and that any enrollment terms may not discriminate on the basis of race, gender, religion, color, disability status, or ethnicity.

The Supreme Court of Alabama held the Alabama Accountability Act of 2013 constitutional as to the challenges presented, reversing a circuit court judgment that had struck the act down. The court affirmed the trial court's disposition of counts one through eight, reversed the determination that counts nine and ten were moot, and remanded for further proceedings on those two counts. The decision left the tax credit scholarship program and the parent refundable credit in operation.

Act 2015-434, signed by the Governor on 9 June 2015, amended sections of the Alabama Accountability Act of 2013. The Secretary of State's record describes the act as amending sections relating to the Alabama Accountability Act of 2013; the act is recorded in the code history of Ala. Code § 16-6D-9, the section governing tax credit claims and administrative accountability for the scholarship program.

Act 2022-390, signed by the Governor on 13 April 2022, amended the law relating to scholarship granting organizations under the Alabama Accountability Act of 2013. The act appears in the code history of Ala. Code § 16-6D-9.

Act 2023-418, signed by the Governor on 8 June 2023, amended sections relating to the Alabama Accountability Act of 2013. It is the most recent act recorded in the code history of Ala. Code § 16-6D-9 governing the tax credit scholarship program.

events.instrument: Act 2024-21 (H.B. 129), Creating Hope and Opportunity for Our Students' Education Act of 2024 (CHOOSE Act)
events.summary: The CHOOSE Act creates a refundable income tax credit funding education savings accounts administered by the Department of Revenue. Accounts carry $7,000 per participating student enrolled at a participating school, or the actual cost if lower, and $2,000 per student not enrolled at a participating school, capped at $4,000 per family. Eligible students are Alabama residents aged 5 through 19, or through 21 with a disability, who have not graduated from high school. Participating schools expressly include church, parochial, and religious schools that meet department approval and accreditation requirements, and the act states that it does not expand state regulatory authority over a participating school's instructional content, curriculum, admissions policies, or hiring policies. Awards begin with the 2025-2026 academic year.

Alaska's anti-aid provision directs the legislature to establish and maintain a system of public schools open to all children of the State, requires that schools and institutions so established be free from sectarian control, and states that no money shall be paid from public funds for the direct benefit of any religious or other private educational institution. The provision has not been amended and is the clause at issue in the correspondence allotment litigation.

Senate Bill 134 of the 20th Legislature, titled an act relating to home schooling for elementary and secondary students, was signed into law on 4 June 1997 as chapter 68, Session Laws of Alaska 1997.
