The measure established the statutory basis on which Alaska families may educate children at home without prior approval by a school district.

House Bill 278 of the 28th Legislature was signed into law on 13 May 2014 as chapter 15, Session Laws of Alaska 2014. Among many education provisions, the act addressed correspondence programs, funding, and student allotments, creating the individual learning plan requirement and the statutory student allotment that districts pay to parents of correspondence students. AS 14.03.310 permits allotments to purchase nonsectarian services and materials from a public, private, or religious organization when required by the student's individual learning plan and approved by the district.

events.instrument: Alexander v. State, No. 3AN-23-04309 CI (Alaska Super. Ct., 3d Jud. Dist., Apr. 12, 2024)
events.summary: The Anchorage superior court held AS 14.03.300 and AS 14.03.310, enacted by section 15 of chapter 15, Session Laws of Alaska 2014, unconstitutional under article VII, section 1 of the Alaska Constitution. A memorandum of the Legislative Affairs Agency's Legal Services Division records that the ruling invalidated only the student allotment provisions, leaving the remaining correspondence study statutes and regulations intact.

events.instrument: State, Dep't of Educ. & Early Dev. v. Alexander, No. S-19083 (Alaska, order of June 28, 2024)
events.summary: The Alaska Supreme Court announced on 28 June 2024 that it was reversing the superior court's ruling striking down the correspondence study statutes, with a full opinion to follow. The Department of Law's published statement records that the reversal restored the statutory framework under which approximately 22,000 correspondence students received allotments, and that the court's reasoning rested on the presumption of constitutionality and the availability of an as-applied challenge to particular spending.

events.instrument: State of Alaska, Dep't of Educ. & Early Dev. v. Alexander, No. S-19083, Op. No. 7759 (Alaska Mar. 28, 2025)
events.summary: The Alaska Supreme Court reversed the superior court's judgment that AS 14.03.300 and AS 14.03.310 are facially unconstitutional, holding that the statutes have a substantial number of constitutional applications and therefore a plainly legitimate sweep. The court vacated the judgment and remanded, requiring that school districts alleged to have authorized unconstitutional spending be joined as parties before an as-applied challenge proceeds. The court expressly declined to decide whether using allotment funds for private school tuition violates article VII, section 1 of the Alaska Constitution, so that question remains open.

Arizona's aid clause provides that no tax shall be laid or appropriation of public money made in aid of any church, or private or sectarian school, or any public service corporation. This is the provision the Arizona Supreme Court applied in Cain v. Horne to invalidate the state's two 2006 voucher programs, and the provision the Court of Appeals applied in Niehaus v. Huppenthal to uphold the Empowerment Scholarship Account program.

Arizona's religion clause provides that no public money or property shall be appropriated for or applied to any religious worship, exercise, or instruction, or to the support of any religious establishment, and that no religious qualification shall be required for any public office or employment. The clause was one of the two provisions litigated in Kotterman v. Killian and in Cain v. Horne.

events.instrument: Laws 1997, ch. 48 (adding A.R.S. §§ 43-1087 and 43-1088, later renumbered § 43-1089)
events.summary: Approved by the Governor on 7 April 1997, chapter 48 created Arizona's original individual income tax credit for voluntary cash contributions to school tuition organizations, which award scholarships for attendance at private schools, together with a companion credit for contributions to public school extracurricular activities. The credit was capped at $500 per taxpayer per year with a five-year carryforward, and no credit was allowed where the taxpayer designated the donation for the direct benefit of the taxpayer's own dependent.

events.instrument: Kotterman v. Killian, 193 Ariz. 273, 972 P.2d 606 (1999) (No. CV-97-0412-SA)
events.summary: The Arizona Supreme Court upheld A.R.S. § 43-1089, the individual income tax credit for contributions to school tuition organizations enacted by Laws 1997, chapter 48, against challenges under the Arizona and federal constitutions. The opinion treated the credit as a reduction in tax liability rather than an appropriation of public money, and it surveyed the comparable anti-aid provisions of other state constitutions in the course of construing the Arizona clauses.

Chapter 14 of the 2006 session created a corporate income tax credit for contributions to school tuition organizations. The bill was not returned to the legislature within five days after presentation to the Governor and became law on 29 March 2006, being filed with the Secretary of State the same day. The stated purpose of the credit is to allow corporations to direct taxes to school tuition organizations to raise tuition scholarships for children in the state.

events.instrument: Laws 2006, ch. 340 (H.B. 2676), enacting A.R.S. § 15-891 (Arizona Scholarships for Pupils with Disabilities Program)
events.summary: Approved by the Governor on 21 June 2006, chapter 340 established the Arizona Scholarships for Pupils with Disabilities Program, under which the parent of a public school pupil with a disability who is dissatisfied with the pupil's progress could request and receive a state scholarship to attend a qualified nonpublic school of the parent's choice. The act made an appropriation for the program.

events.instrument: Laws 2006, ch. 358 (S.B. 1164), enacting A.R.S. §§ 15-817 to 15-817.02 (Displaced Pupils Choice Grant Program)
events.summary: Approved by the Governor on 21 June 2006, chapter 358 established the Displaced Pupils Choice Grant Program, providing grants for pupils who had been placed in foster care, so that a custodian could enroll the pupil in a qualified nonpublic school. The act made an appropriation and included a delayed repeal of the program and of the associated income tax provision.

The Arizona Supreme Court held that the Arizona Scholarships for Pupils with Disabilities Program and the Displaced Pupils Choice Grant Program violate article IX, section 10 of the Arizona Constitution, which forbids any appropriation of public money in aid of any church, or private or sectarian school. The court reasoned that state funds directed to private schools through parental choice still constitute aid to the schools. It reversed the superior court's judgment, vacated the Court of Appeals opinion, and remanded.

events.instrument: Laws 2009, 2d Spec. Sess., ch. 1 (H.B. 2001), adding A.R.S. §§ 20-224.06 and 43-1184 (Lexie's Law)
events.summary: Approved by the Governor on 29 May 2009 as an emergency measure, chapter 1 of the second special session created a corporate income tax credit and an insurance premium tax credit for contributions to school tuition organizations that award scholarships to displaced pupils and pupils with disabilities. The credits replaced the two direct-appropriation voucher programs the Arizona Supreme Court had invalidated ten weeks earlier in Cain v. Horne.

events.instrument: Laws 2011, ch. 75 (S.B. 1553), adding A.R.S. title 15, ch. 19 (Arizona Empowerment Scholarship Accounts)
events.summary: Approved by the Governor and filed with the Secretary of State on 12 April 2011, chapter 75 created the Arizona Empowerment Scholarship Accounts program, the first education savings account program in the United States. Eligibility at enactment was limited to students with disabilities. The chapter provides that a qualified school accepting a payment from a parent is not an agent of the state or federal government, that a qualified school shall not be required to alter its creed, practices, admissions policy, or curriculum in order to participate, and that in any legal proceeding challenging application of the chapter to a qualified school the state bears the burden of establishing that the law is necessary and imposes no undue burden.

Approved by the Governor on 29 February 2012, chapter 4 created a second individual income tax credit for contributions to school tuition organizations, available to taxpayers who have already claimed the maximum under the original credit. The act also amended the corporate credits at A.R.S. §§ 43-1183 and 43-1184 and the school tuition organization requirements at A.R.S. §§ 43-1501 through 43-1605.

Approved by the Governor on 14 May 2012, chapter 360 expanded eligibility for Arizona Empowerment Scholarship Accounts beyond students with disabilities to additional categories, including students attending or assigned to a school that received a letter grade of D or F, and children of members of the armed forces on active duty. The act also made an appropriation.

Approved by the Governor on 20 June 2013, chapter 250 further amended the definitions and account provisions of the Arizona Empowerment Scholarship Accounts program. Section 3 of this chapter was itself later amended by Laws 2017, chapter 139.

events.instrument: Niehaus v. Huppenthal, 233 Ariz. 195, 310 P.3d 983 (App. 2013) (No. 1 CA-CV 12-0242)
events.summary: The Arizona Court of Appeals, Division One, affirmed the superior court and held that the Empowerment Scholarship Account program does not violate the aid clause of article IX, section 10, reasoning that the specified object of the program is the beneficiary families rather than private or sectarian schools, because account funds may be applied to a range of educational options at the parent's discretion. The judgment was affirmed in its entirety.

Approved by the Governor on 19 May 2016, chapter 353 added further eligibility categories to the Arizona Empowerment Scholarship Accounts program, including siblings of current or previous account recipients, children residing within the boundaries of an Indian reservation in the state, and children of a parent who is legally blind or deaf or hard of hearing.

Approved by the Governor on 6 April 2017 and filed with the Secretary of State on 7 April 2017, chapter 139 would have phased in eligibility for Arizona Empowerment Scholarship Accounts to all students in kindergarten through grade twelve over four school years, subject to an annual cap on new accounts, and would have added a policy handbook requirement, an appeal right, and a spending disclosure requirement. The act never took effect: a veto referendum suspended it, and the voters rejected it as Proposition 305 on 6 November 2018.

events.instrument: Arizona Proposition 305 (veto referendum on S.B. 1431, 2018 general election)
events.summary: Arizona voters rejected Proposition 305 at the general election of 6 November 2018, with 790,608 votes in favor and 1,457,070 against, or 35.17 percent to 64.83 percent of 2,247,678 votes cast. A no vote repealed Senate Bill 1431 of 2017, so the phased expansion of Empowerment Scholarship Accounts to all students never took effect and the categorical eligibility rules remained in force. The referendum qualified after the Secretary of State announced on 8 September 2017 that sufficient signatures had been verified. The source states that the results are officially certified; the Arizona Secretary of State's own canvass was not reachable.

Approved by the Governor on 7 July 2022, chapter 388 extended eligibility for Arizona Empowerment Scholarship Accounts to every student who is eligible to enroll in a public school in the state, making Arizona the first state with a universally available education savings account program. The universal eligibility definition was placed in a new section, A.R.S. § 15-2401.01, alongside the categorical definitions retained at § 15-2401.

Approved by the Governor on 18 June 2024, chapter 218, the kindergarten through grade twelve budget reconciliation act for fiscal year 2024-2025, tightened administration of the Empowerment Scholarship Account program. It requires the Department of Education to conduct or contract for annual audits of accounts, to conduct random, quarterly, and annual audits as needed, to develop risk-based auditing procedures in consultation with the Auditor General, and to review annually a randomly selected sample of accounts for compliance with the contract and applicable law.

Arkansas has no Blaine amendment or express anti-aid clause barring public funds to sectarian schools. The nearest analogue is article 14, section 2, which provides that no money or property belonging to the public school fund, or to the State for the benefit of schools or universities, shall ever be used for any other than the respective purposes to which it belongs. This provision, together with article 16, section 11, is the basis of the pending illegal-exaction challenge to the Educational Freedom Account program.

events.instrument: Act 1178 of 2015 (H.B. 1552), Succeed Scholarship Program for Students with Disabilities
events.summary: Act 1178 of the 2015 regular session, with an act date of 7 April 2015, established the Succeed Scholarship Program for Students with Disabilities, Arkansas's first program placing state funds with private schools chosen by parents. The program provided scholarships for eligible students with disabilities to attend approved private schools.

events.instrument: Act 904 of 2021 (S.B. 680), Philanthropic Investment in Arkansas Kids Program Act
events.summary: Act 904 of 2021 created an income tax credit for eligible contributions to a sponsor granting organization under the Philanthropic Investment in Arkansas Kids Program, adding a new subchapter 22 to Arkansas Code title 6, chapter 18. The act established Arkansas's tax credit scholarship program, under which scholarships are awarded for attendance at private schools. The act date recorded by the General Assembly is 26 April 2021.

events.instrument: Act 237 of 2023 (S.B. 294), Arkansas LEARNS Act, § 42 (Arkansas Children's Educational Freedom Account Program)
events.summary: The LEARNS Act, an omnibus education measure, was signed by Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders on 8 March 2023 after Senate concurrence on 7 March 2023. Section 42 created the Arkansas Children's Educational Freedom Account Program, codified at Ark. Code Ann. §§ 6-18-2501 through 6-18-2511, which provides funds to defray expenses of parents who home-school a child or enroll a child in a private school. Eligibility was phased in from the 2023-2024 school year and reached all students in 2025-2026. Section 73 of the act contained an emergency clause that became the subject of litigation.

events.instrument: Arkansas Department of Education v. Jackson, 2023 Ark. 105 (No. CV-23-358)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of Arkansas reversed the Pulaski County Circuit Court's order granting a temporary restraining order against implementation of the LEARNS Act, vacated the restraining order, and remanded. The suit, brought by individual plaintiffs and the ballot question committee Citizens for Arkansas Public Education and Students, challenged the validity of the emergency clause in section 73 of Act 237 of 2023.

events.instrument: Arkansas Department of Education v. Jackson, 2023 Ark. 140 (No. CV-23-468)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of Arkansas reversed the circuit court's declaratory judgment that the emergency clause of the LEARNS Act had not received a separate roll-call vote as the Arkansas Constitution requires, and dismissed the case below. The LEARNS Act, including the Educational Freedom Account program, remained in effect.

events.instrument: Arkansas Department of Education v. Faulkenberry, 2025 Ark. 203 (No. CV-24-803)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of Arkansas dismissed the State's interlocutory appeal from the Pulaski County Circuit Court's denial of a motion to dismiss on sovereign immunity grounds. The underlying suit alleges that the Educational Freedom Account program is an illegal exaction that violates article 14, sections 1 through 3, and article 16, section 11 of the Arkansas Constitution, and seeks to stop payments for private school tuition and to recover funds already disbursed. The merits of that challenge remain pending in the circuit court.

The Supreme Court of Arkansas reversed and remanded the circuit court's denial of a motion by parents of children eligible for the Educational Freedom Account program to intervene as of right in the illegal-exaction challenge to that program. The court held the parents were entitled to intervention of right and did not reach permissive intervention. The underlying constitutional challenge remains pending.

California's education anti-aid provision, adopted in 1879, states that no public money shall ever be appropriated for the support of any sectarian or denominational school, or any school not under the exclusive control of the officers of the public schools, and that no sectarian or denominational doctrine shall be taught in the common schools. The provision has not been amended.

California's general anti-aid provision forbids the Legislature and local governments from making any appropriation, paying from any public fund, or granting anything to or in aid of any religious sect, church, creed, or sectarian purpose, or helping to support any school, college, university, hospital, or other institution controlled by any religious creed, church, or sectarian denomination. The section in its present form was added by Proposition 8 at the general election of 5 November 1974.

events.instrument: California Proposition 38 (2000), School Vouchers, State-Funded Private and Religious Education, Public School Funding, Initiative Constitutional Amendment
events.summary: California voters rejected Proposition 38 at the general election of 7 November 2000. The Secretary of State's Statement of Vote records 3,101,193 votes in favor, or 29.4 percent, and 7,422,037 against, or 70.6 percent, and lists the measure among the proposed laws defeated by the voters. The measure would have amended the California Constitution to create a state-funded scholarship usable at private and religious schools.

events.instrument: Jonathan L. v. Superior Court, 165 Cal. App. 4th 1074 (2008) (No. B192878)
events.summary: The California Court of Appeal, Second Appellate District, decided the question of home education under California's compulsory attendance law after vacating its earlier opinion in the same matter. The decision addressed whether parents may educate children at home under the private school exemption in Education Code section 48222 and the related tutorial exemption, and it is the controlling California appellate authority on the position of home-educating families.

events.instrument: Doe v. California Lutheran High School Ass'n, 170 Cal. App. 4th 828 (2009) (No. E044811)
events.summary: The California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Two, affirmed summary judgment for a private religious high school that had expelled two students for conduct the school found contrary to its Christian conduct rule. In the published portion of the opinion the court held that the school is not a business establishment within the meaning of the Unruh Civil Rights Act and therefore is not subject to that act. The decision remains the leading California authority on the reach of the Unruh Act to religious schools.

Senate Bill 277 was chaptered on 30 June 2015 as chapter 35 of the Statutes of 2015. The act amended Health and Safety Code sections 120325, 120335, 120370, and 120375, added section 120338, and repealed section 120365, eliminating the personal belief exemption from the immunization requirements that condition admission to schools. The requirement applies to private schools as well as public schools, so it is the most consequential California regulatory change of the period for religious schools.

Colorado's anti-aid provision, entitled aid to private schools, churches, sectarian purpose, forbidden, provides that neither the general assembly nor any county, city, town, township, school district, or other public corporation shall ever make any appropriation, or pay from any public fund or moneys whatever, anything in aid of any church or sectarian society, or for any sectarian purpose, or to help support or sustain any school, academy, seminary, college, university, or other literary or scientific institution controlled by any church or sectarian denomination. The Colorado Supreme Court quoted and applied the provision in 2015 to strike down the Douglas County scholarship program.

events.instrument: Colorado Opportunity Contract Pilot Program, §§ 22-56-101 to 22-56-110, C.R.S. (2003)
events.summary: The Colorado General Assembly enacted the Colorado Opportunity Contract Pilot Program in the 2003 session, codified at sections 22-56-101 to 22-56-110, C.R.S. The program required participating school districts to pay a portion of per-pupil funding to private schools, including religious schools, chosen by parents of eligible students. The exact date of approval was not established from a record retrieved; the program is described and cited in the Colorado Supreme Court opinion that struck it down the following year.

events.instrument: Owens v. Colorado Congress of Parents, Teachers & Students, 92 P.3d 933 (Colo. 2004) (No. 03SA364)
events.summary: The Colorado Supreme Court held the Colorado Opportunity Contract Pilot Program unconstitutional under the local control provisions of article IX, section 15 of the Colorado Constitution, affirming the trial court. The court found that the program interferes with local school districts' discretion to allocate their funding by directing locally raised revenue to schools outside district control. Colorado's only statewide private school choice program was thereby ended within a year of enactment.

events.instrument: Taxpayers for Public Education v. Douglas County School District, 2013 COA 20, 356 P.3d 833 (Nos. 11CA1856 and 11CA1857)
events.summary: The Colorado Court of Appeals reversed the district court's permanent injunction against the Douglas County School District Choice Scholarship Program, under which the district paid scholarships to parents who then remitted them to partnering private schools, some of them religious. The court held that the plaintiffs lacked standing under the Public School Finance Act of 1994 and that the program did not violate the state constitutional provisions at issue. The decision was later reversed in part by the Colorado Supreme Court.

events.instrument: Taxpayers for Public Education v. Douglas County School District, 2015 CO 50, 351 P.3d 461 (No. 13SC233)
events.summary: The Colorado Supreme Court held that the petitioners lacked standing to challenge the Douglas County Choice Scholarship Program under the Public School Finance Act of 1994, but that the program violates article IX, section 7 of the Colorado Constitution. The court reversed the court of appeals and remanded with instructions to return the case to the trial court so that the permanent injunction against the program could be reinstated. Fifteen of the sixteen private school partners were religious schools.

events.instrument: Colorado Amendment 80 (2024), Constitutional Right to School Choice Initiative
events.summary: Colorado voters rejected Amendment 80 at the general election of 5 November 2024. The measure would have placed in the Colorado Constitution a right to school choice covering neighborhood schools, charter schools, private schools, home schools, open enrollment options, and future innovations in education. The recorded result was 1,507,236 votes in favor, or 49.32 percent, against 50.68 percent opposed; an initiated constitutional amendment in Colorado requires 55 percent approval, so the measure failed on both counts. The Colorado Secretary of State's own abstract was not reachable.

Connecticut has no Blaine amendment or express anti-aid clause barring public funds to religious or private schools. Article Seventh of the Connecticut Constitution provides that no person shall by law be compelled to join or support, nor be classed or associated with, any congregation, church, or religious association, and that no preference shall be given by law to any religious society or denomination. Article Eighth, section 1 provides that there shall always be free public elementary and secondary schools in the state.

events.instrument: Conn. Public Act 21-6 (Substitute S.B. 568), amending Conn. Gen. Stat. § 10-204a
events.summary: Public Act 21-6, an act concerning immunizations, was signed by the Governor in original form on 28 April 2021. It eliminated the nonmedical exemption to the school immunization requirement for individuals attending public or private school from prekindergarten through grade twelve, for individuals in higher education, and for children in day care settings. The amended text of Conn. Gen. Stat. § 10-204a applies expressly to bodies governing nonpublic schools and preserves the exemption only for children enrolled in a preschool or other prekindergarten program who held it before 28 April 2021. The act is the period's principal Connecticut regulatory change affecting religious schools.

Delaware's anti-aid provision states that no portion of any fund appropriated for educational purposes shall be appropriated to any sectarian, church, or denominational school. Section 1 of the same article requires the General Assembly to provide for the establishment and maintenance of a general and efficient system of free public schools. The provision has not been amended or repealed during the period covered.

events.instrument: 74 Del. Laws, c. 79 (S.B. 103), adding 14 Del. C. § 2703A and amending 14 Del. C. § 2704
events.summary: Approved 30 June 2003, this act defined a homeschool as a nonpublic school for purposes of Delaware's school attendance chapter and established three categories: the multi-family homeschool, the single-family homeschool, and the single-family homeschool coordinated with the local school district. The act also amended the nonpublic school reporting statute at 14 Del. C. § 2704, under which all persons conducting nonpublic schools must report end-of-year attendance to the Department of Education by 31 July and a statement of pupil enrollment by 30 September.

events.instrument: 83 Del. Laws, c. 87 (S.B. 106), amending 14 Del. C. § 2703A
events.summary: Approved 29 July 2021, this act amended the definition of a homeschool so that, while a homeschool remains a nonpublic school for purposes of the attendance chapter, students enrolled in homeschools are deemed parentally-placed private school children for purposes of receiving equitable services from proportionate share funds under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act.

events.instrument: DC School Choice Incentive Act of 2003, Pub. L. 108-199, div. C, tit. III, 118 Stat. 126
events.summary: Approved 23 January 2004, title III of division C of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2004 created the District of Columbia's first publicly funded private school scholarship program, later known as the Opportunity Scholarship Program. The findings state that funds are needed to assist low-income parents to exercise choice among enhanced public opportunities and private educational environments, whether religious or nonreligious, and cite Zelman v. Simmons-Harris. The title created a five-year program and was codified at D.C. Official Code §§ 38-1851.01 through 38-1851.11.

events.instrument: Placement of Students with Disabilities in Nonpublic Schools Amendment Act of 2006, D.C. Law 16-269, 54 DCR 841, codified at D.C. Code §§ 38-2561.01 to 38-2561.16
events.summary: Effective 14 March 2007, this act required the District's state education agency to develop and administer a Certificate of Approval process by 1 January 2009 for nonpublic special education schools and programs that serve District students with disabilities using District government funds. Approval requires compliance with chapters 22, 25, 30, and 38 of title 5 of the District of Columbia Municipal Regulations, applicable fire safety, building code, health, and sanitation requirements, and a policy and practice prohibiting aversive intervention, and it depends on an onsite inspection. Certificates run for periods not exceeding three years. The regime applies to religiously affiliated nonpublic schools that accept District placements.

events.instrument: Omnibus Appropriations Act, 2009, Pub. L. 111-8, div. C, tit. III, 123 Stat. 653
events.summary: Approved 11 March 2009, the District of Columbia appropriations title restricted the Opportunity Scholarship Program. It barred use of scholarship funds at a participating school unless the school held a valid certificate of occupancy and its core subject matter teachers held four-year bachelor's degrees, and it provided that use of any funds for opportunity scholarships after school year 2009-2010 would be available only upon enactment of reauthorization by Congress and adoption of legislation by the District of Columbia approving the reauthorization. New admissions to the program ceased under this restriction.

events.instrument: Scholarships for Opportunity and Results Act, Pub. L. 112-10, div. C, 125 Stat. 199
events.summary: Approved 15 April 2011, the SOAR Act revived and restructured the District of Columbia scholarship program, stating in its findings that funds are needed to provide low-income parents with enhanced public opportunities and private educational environments, regardless of whether such environments are secular or nonsecular. Section 3012(a) of the act repealed the 2003 program codified at D.C. Official Code §§ 38-1851.01 and following, replacing it with the SOAR provisions now codified at D.C. Official Code §§ 38-1853.01 through 38-1853.14.

events.instrument: Scholarships for Opportunity and Results Reauthorization Act, Pub. L. 115-31, tit. IX, 131 Stat. 394
events.summary: Approved 5 May 2017, title IX of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2017 reauthorized the SOAR Act. Section 902 repealed section 817 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2016 and restored the provisions that section had amended or repealed. Later sections amended the purposes, priority, and school participation requirements of the program, including fire code provisions applicable to participating schools.

Article I, section 3 of the Florida Constitution states that no revenue of the state or any political subdivision or agency of the state shall ever be taken from the public treasury directly or indirectly in aid of any church, sect, or religious denomination or in aid of any sectarian institution. The provision was in force throughout the period covered by this chronology. The date recorded here is the start of that period; the cited page supplies the text and does not state the date of adoption.

events.instrument: 1999 Fla. Laws ch. 99-398, s. 3 (codified at Fla. Stat. s. 229.05371, later s. 1002.39)
events.summary: The John M. McKay Scholarships for Students with Disabilities Program was created by chapter 99-398, section 3, Laws of Florida. The program provided scholarships allowing students with disabilities to attend a participating private school. The statute was later recodified within the K-20 Education Code as section 1002.39.

The Florida Tax Credit Scholarship Program was created by section 5 of chapter 2001-225, Laws of Florida. The program grants tax credits to taxpayers that contribute to eligible nonprofit scholarship-funding organizations, which award scholarships for attendance at participating private schools. The history note to section 1002.395 records amendment in most subsequent legislative sessions.

The Florida Supreme Court held that the Opportunity Scholarship Program, which funded private school attendance for students assigned to low-performing public schools, violated article IX, section 1(a) of the Florida Constitution. The court reasoned that the constitutional command to make adequate provision for education through a uniform system of free public schools restricts the legislature from funding a parallel private school system with public money. The opinion was filed January 5, 2006.

Section 16 of chapter 2014-184, Laws of Florida, created the Florida Personal Learning Scholarship Accounts Program, allowing parents of students with disabilities to draw on an account for instructional materials, curriculum, specialized services, private school enrollment, and postsecondary study. The program was later renamed the Gardiner Scholarship.

events.instrument: McCall v. Scott, 199 So. 3d 359 (Fla. Dist. Ct. App. 2016)
events.summary: A Florida appellate court held that the taxpayers challenging the Florida Tax Credit Scholarship Program lacked standing, so the merits of the constitutional challenge were not reached. The case is recorded from a national organization's litigation summary; the published opinion was not retrieved.

Section 16 of chapter 2018-6, Laws of Florida, created the Hope Scholarship Program. The program allows a parent of a public school student who reported an incident of battery, harassment, hazing, bullying, or violence to transfer the student to another public school or to obtain a scholarship for enrollment in a participating private school.

events.instrument: Citizens for Strong Schools, Inc. v. Florida State Board of Education, 262 So. 3d 127 (Fla. 2019)
events.summary: The Florida Supreme Court declined to address the claims directed at the state's scholarship programs on the merits. The case is recorded from a national organization's litigation summary; the published opinion was not retrieved.

Section 6 of chapter 2019-23, Laws of Florida, created the Family Empowerment Scholarship Program. As enacted, the program was limited to 18,000 students annually on a first-come, first-served basis, with the award calculated at 95 percent of the Florida Education Finance Program funding for the student's grade level and district, and with annual growth of 0.25 percent of total public school enrollment beginning in 2020-2021.

events.instrument: 2021 Fla. Laws ch. 2021-27 (amending Fla. Stat. s. 1002.394)
events.summary: Chapter 2021-27, Laws of Florida, amended the Family Empowerment Scholarship Program. The history note to section 1002.394 records this chapter among the amending session laws, alongside chapters 2021-52, 2022-23, 2022-30, and 2022-154.

House Bill 1 of the 2023 regular session was approved by the Governor on March 27, 2023, and became chapter 2023-16, Laws of Florida, effective July 1, 2023. The act revised the Family Empowerment Scholarship Program and the Florida Tax Credit Scholarship Program, along with provisions on part-time public school enrollment, student transportation, graduation requirements, the duties of the Commissioner of Education, and educator certification. The Senate bill record shows House passage 83-27 on March 17, 2023, and Senate passage 26-12 on March 23, 2023.

events.instrument: Fla. Admin. Code R. 6A-6.03315, Private School Scholarship Compliance
events.summary: Rule 6A-6.03315 sets the compliance requirements for private schools participating in Florida's scholarship programs. The rule was adopted on October 13, 2004, and was last amended on September 24, 2024. It implements sections 1002.39, 1002.395, 1002.40, 1002.42, 1002.421, 1003.22, and 1003.23 of the Florida Statutes.

events.instrument: Ga. Const. art. I, s. II, para. VII
events.summary: Article I, section II, paragraph VII of the Georgia Constitution provides that no money shall ever be taken from the public treasury, directly or indirectly, in aid of any church, sect, cult, or religious denomination or of any sectarian institution. The provision was in force throughout the period covered by this chronology. The date recorded here is the start of that period; the cited page supplies the text and does not state the date of adoption.

The Georgia Special Needs Scholarship Act was placed in the Code by 2007 Georgia Laws 117, section 1, effective May 18, 2007. The Act allows a student with a disability who was enrolled in a Georgia public school to receive a scholarship to attend a participating private school.

events.instrument: 2008 Ga. Laws 773, s. 1 (House Bill 1133; O.C.G.A. ss. 20-2A-1 to 20-2A-7)
events.summary: Chapter 2A of Title 20, governing student scholarship organizations, was added by 2008 Georgia Laws 773, section 1, effective May 14, 2008. The chapter, paired with the qualified education expense income tax credit, allows a charitable organization that obligates at least 90 percent of its annual revenue to scholarships or tuition grants to award those grants to eligible students who transfer to a qualified nonpublic school or program.

The definitions governing the student scholarship organization program, including the definitions of eligible student, qualified school or program, and student scholarship organization, were amended by 2011 Georgia Laws 170, section 1, effective July 1, 2011.
The definitions governing the student scholarship organization program were further amended by 2013 Georgia Laws 335, section 33A, effective May 7, 2013.

events.instrument: Gaddy v. Georgia Department of Revenue, No. S17A0177 (Ga. June 26, 2017)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of Georgia held that four taxpayers challenging the qualified education expense tax credit created by House Bill 1133 lacked standing, because a credit against income tax liability does not remove money from the state treasury and the asserted increase in the burden on remaining taxpayers was speculative. The court also rejected the mandamus claim against the Department of Revenue. The judgment was affirmed in Case No. S17A0177 and reversed in the cross-appeal, Case No. S17X0178.

events.instrument: 2024 Ga. Laws 457, s. 2-1 (Georgia Promise Scholarship Act; O.C.G.A. ss. 20-2B-20 to 20-2B-31)
events.summary: The Georgia Promise Scholarship Act was enacted by 2024 Georgia Laws 457, section 2-1. The Act creates promise scholarship accounts administered through the Georgia Education Savings Authority. Its operation was made conditional on full funding of the Quality Basic Education Act, and on that condition being met it applies to school years beginning on or after July 1, 2025. The Act is scheduled for repeal on June 30, 2035, or ten years after it becomes effective, whichever is later, with continued eligibility for students already qualified. The cited page does not give the date of approval.

events.instrument: Haw. Const. art. X, s. 1 (renumbered from art. IX by the 1978 Constitutional Convention)
events.summary: Article X, section 1 of the Hawaii Constitution provides for a statewide system of public schools free from sectarian control and states that no public funds shall be appropriated for the support or benefit of any sectarian or nonsectarian private educational institution. The provision was renumbered from article IX to article X by the 1978 Constitutional Convention, approved at the election of November 7, 1978.

events.instrument: Haw. Const. art. X, s. 1, as amended by 1994 Haw. Sess. Laws ch. 280, s. 4 (H.B. 2692-94)
events.summary: An amendment approved at the election of November 8, 1994, added an exception to the bar on appropriations for private educational institutions, permitting the proceeds of special purpose revenue bonds authorized under article VII, section 12 to finance or assist certain not-for-profit entities.

events.instrument: Haw. Const. art. X, s. 1, as amended by H.B. 2848 (2002)
events.summary: An amendment approved at the election of November 5, 2002, extended the special purpose revenue bond exception in article X, section 1 so that it reaches not-for-profit private nonsectarian and sectarian elementary schools, secondary schools, colleges, and universities, as well as not-for-profit corporations providing early childhood education and care facilities serving the general public.

Article IX, section 5 of the Idaho Constitution bars the legislature and any county, city, town, township, school district, or other public corporation from making any appropriation or paying from any public fund anything in aid of any church or sectarian or religious society, or for any sectarian or religious purpose, or to help support or sustain any school, academy, seminary, college, university, or other literary or scientific institution controlled by any church or sectarian or religious denomination, subject to an exception for a health facilities authority financing not-for-profit health facilities. The provision was in force throughout the period covered by this chronology. The date recorded here is the start of that period; the cited page supplies the text and does not state the date of adoption.

events.instrument: 2025 Idaho Sess. Laws ch. 9, s. 2 (Idaho Code s. 63-3029N, Idaho Parental Choice Tax Credit)
events.summary: Section 63-3029N of the Idaho Code was added by 2025 Idaho Session Laws chapter 9, section 2. The section creates a refundable income tax credit of up to $5,000 per eligible student, rising to $7,500 for a student aged 5 to 21 with a disability requiring ancillary personnel, for qualified expenses including nonpublic school tuition and fees, tutoring, standardized assessments, and transportation. The credit is capped statewide at $50 million a year, with priority for parents whose income does not exceed 300 percent of the federal poverty level, and with an advance payment election for qualifying parents. The cited page does not give the date of approval.

Article X, section 3 of the Illinois Constitution bars the General Assembly and any county, city, town, township, school district, or other public corporation from making any appropriation or paying from any public fund anything in aid of any church or sectarian purpose, or to help support or sustain any school, academy, seminary, college, university, or other literary or scientific institution controlled by any church or sectarian denomination, and bars any grant or donation of land, money, or other personal property to any church or for any sectarian purpose. The provision was in force throughout the period covered by this chronology. The date recorded here is the start of that period; the cited page supplies the text and does not state the date of adoption.

Illinois enacted an individual income tax credit for qualified education expenses in 1999, with the credit first available in 2000. The credit is codified at 35 ILCS 5/201(m). The record here rests on a national organization's program summary; the enacting public act was not located in a primary source.

events.instrument: Invest in Kids Act, P.A. 100-465 (35 ILCS 40)
events.summary: The Invest in Kids Act was created by Public Act 100-465, effective August 31, 2017. The Act allowed a taxpayer making a qualified contribution to a scholarship granting organization an income tax credit equal to 75 percent of the contribution, capped at $1,000,000 per taxpayer, to fund scholarships for students from low-income households attending qualified nonpublic schools.

events.instrument: 35 ILCS 5/201(m), income limitation on the credit for educational expenses
events.summary: Beginning in 2018, Illinois limited eligibility for the credit for educational expenses by federal adjusted gross income, excluding married filers above $500,000 and other filers above $250,000. The record here rests on a national organization's program summary; the amending public act was not located in a primary source.

events.instrument: Invest in Kids Act, 35 ILCS 40, as amended by P.A. 102-16
events.summary: The index of the Illinois Compiled Statutes records the Invest in Kids Act at 35 ILCS 40 as repealed by Public Act 102-16, the 2021 act that fixed the Act's termination. The cited index entry establishes the attribution of the repeal to that public act.

Section 65 of the Invest in Kids Act allowed the credit only for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2018, and ending before January 1, 2024, and provided that the Act is repealed on January 1, 2025. The last tax year for which credits were available under the program was therefore 2023, and no legislation extending the program was located.

Article 1, section 4 of the Indiana Constitution provides that no preference shall be given by law to any creed, religious society, or mode of worship, and that no person shall be compelled to attend, erect, or support any place of worship, or to maintain any ministry, against that person's consent. Article 1, section 6 provides that no money shall be drawn from the treasury for the benefit of any religious or theological institution. Both provisions were in force throughout the period covered by this chronology. The date recorded here is the start of that period; the cited page supplies the text and does not state the date of adoption.

events.instrument: P.L. 182-2009(ss), SEC. 205 (Ind. Code ch. 6-3.1-30.5, school scholarship tax credit)
events.summary: Public Law 182-2009, enacted in the special session, added Indiana Code chapter 6-3.1-30.5. The chapter entitles a taxpayer that contributes to a scholarship granting organization for use in a school scholarship program to a credit against state tax liability in the year of the contribution.

events.instrument: P.L. 92-2011, SEC. 10 (Ind. Code s. 20-51-4-2, Choice Scholarship Program)
events.summary: Public Law 92-2011 added Indiana Code section 20-51-4-2, which entitles an eligible choice scholarship student to a choice scholarship for each school year in which the student enrolls in an eligible school. This provision is the operative entitlement of the Choice Scholarship Program.

events.instrument: Ind. Code s. 6-3-2-22, private school and home school deduction
events.summary: Indiana enacted an income tax deduction of $1,000 per dependent child for parents whose children attend a private school or are educated at home, codified at Indiana Code section 6-3-2-22. A family may claim the deduction for more than one child. The record here rests on a national organization's program summary; the enacting public law was not located in a primary source.

The definition of an eligible choice scholarship student at Indiana Code section 20-51-1-4.3 was added by Public Law 211-2013 and amended by Public Law 205-2013, the session in which the Choice Scholarship Program was broadened beyond its original entry pathways.

The Indiana Supreme Court affirmed summary judgment for the state and upheld the Choice Scholarship Program. The court held that the program falls within the legislature's power under article 8, section 1 and does not conflict with the duty to maintain a general and uniform system of common schools; that it does not compel support of a place of worship or ministry under article 1, section 4; and that any benefit to religious schools is ancillary rather than a drawing of money from the treasury for the benefit of a religious or theological institution under article 1, section 6.

events.instrument: P.L. 165-2021, SEC. 180 (Ind. Code s. 20-51.4-4-1, Education Scholarship Account Program)
events.summary: Public Law 165-2021 added Indiana Code section 20-51.4-4-1, allowing a parent of an eligible student to establish an Indiana education scholarship account by written agreement with the state treasurer. Account funds may be used only for qualified educational expenses, including instruction in core subjects and special education services. A student may not participate in the account program and the choice scholarship program at the same time, and participants must demonstrate academic progress through state assessments.

Public Law 201-2023 amended both the definition of an eligible choice scholarship student and the annual cap on school scholarship tax credits. The cap provision records a ceiling of $18,500,000 in total credits for state fiscal years beginning July 1, 2022, and after, following a series of increases from $9,500,000 recorded for 2016 and 2017.

Public Law 213-2025 amended the definition of an eligible choice scholarship student. The version of section 20-51-1-4.3 shown as taking effect on June 29, 2026, defines an eligible choice scholarship student solely by legal settlement in Indiana and by age of at least five and less than twenty-two on October 1 of the school year, and contains no household income limit.

Article I, section 3 of the Iowa Constitution provides that the general assembly shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion or prohibiting the free exercise of religion, and that no person shall be compelled to attend any place of worship or to pay tithes, taxes, or other rates for building or repairing places of worship or for the maintenance of any minister or ministry. Iowa's provision is framed as a compelled support clause rather than as a general bar on aid to sectarian schools. The provision was in force throughout the period covered by this chronology. The date recorded here is the start of that period; the cited page supplies the text and does not state the date of adoption.

events.instrument: 2006 Iowa Acts ch. 1163, ss. 1-2 (Iowa Code s. 422.11S, school tuition organization tax credit)
events.summary: Sections 1 and 2 of chapter 1163 of the 2006 Iowa Acts created the school tuition organization tax credit at Iowa Code section 422.11S. The credit is available to a taxpayer making a voluntary cash or noncash contribution to a qualifying school tuition organization.

events.instrument: Iowa Code s. 422.11S, as amended by 2021 Iowa Acts chs. 76, 139, and 177
events.summary: As the section now stands, the school tuition organization tax credit equals 75 percent of the contribution and the aggregate statewide cap is $20,000,000 a year for calendar year 2022 and after. The history note records amendment in the 2021 session, following earlier amendments in 2007, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2018, 2019, and 2020.

events.instrument: Iowa Code s. 422.12, tuition and textbook credit, as amended by 2021 Iowa Acts chs. 80, 139, and 177
events.summary: Iowa's tuition and textbook credit now equals 25 percent of the first $2,000 paid each year for each dependent receiving private instruction or attending an accredited nonprofit Iowa elementary or secondary school that complies with federal civil rights law. Textbooks are defined to exclude materials used to teach religious doctrine. The history note records amendment in the 2021 session, following a long series of earlier amendments.

events.instrument: 2023 Iowa Acts ch. 1, ss. 7 and 10 (Students First Act; Iowa Code s. 257.11B)
events.summary: Chapter 1 of the 2023 Iowa Acts created the education savings account program at Iowa Code section 257.11B. Each account is funded at the regular program state cost per pupil and may be used for tuition, fees, textbooks, tutoring, curriculum materials, online education programs, vocational training, and standardized test fees. Eligibility was phased in: for the year beginning July 1, 2023, kindergarten-eligible residents, residents in grades one through twelve not previously enrolled in a nonpublic school, and previously enrolled nonpublic school students in households at or below 300 percent of the federal poverty guidelines; for the year beginning July 1, 2024, households at or below 400 percent and prior-year recipients; and for the year beginning July 1, 2025 and after, all residents eligible for kindergarten through grade twelve.

events.instrument: 2023 Iowa Acts ch. 111, ss. 23, 25, and 26 (amending Iowa Code s. 257.11B)
events.summary: Chapter 111 of the 2023 Iowa Acts amended the education savings account program in the same session in which it was created. The history note to section 257.11B records the amendment; the cited page does not describe the substance of the changes.

Article 6, section 6 of the Kansas Constitution directs the legislature to make suitable provision for the finance of the educational interests of the state and provides that no religious sect or sects shall control any part of the public educational funds. The provision was in force throughout the period covered by this chronology. The date recorded here is the start of that period; the cited page does not state the date of adoption, although section 7 of the same article refers to a July 1, 1969 compliance deadline following adoption of the amendment.

events.instrument: L. 2014, ch. 93, ss. 56, 57, and 61 (K.S.A. 72-4351 to 72-4357, Tax Credit for Low Income Students Scholarship Program)
events.summary: Chapter 93 of the 2014 Kansas Session Laws created the tax credit for low income students scholarship program, codified at K.S.A. 72-4351 through 72-4357. The program provides eligible students an opportunity to attend schools of their parents' choice, funded by scholarship granting organizations that receive contributions carrying an income tax credit. No more than $8,000 in educational scholarships may be awarded for an eligible student in a school year.

The 2015 session amended both the definitions section and the program section of the tax credit for low income students scholarship program. The history notes to K.S.A. 72-4352 and 72-4353 record chapter 4, section 67 and chapter 99, sections 20 and 21 of the 2015 Session Laws.

Chapter 95 of the 2017 Kansas Session Laws amended the definitions section and the credit section of the tax credit for low income students scholarship program. The credit remained at 70 percent of the amount contributed for tax years 2017 through 2021, and the total credits allowed in any one tax year remained capped at $10,000,000.

The definition of an eligible student for the tax credit for low income students scholarship program was amended in the 2019, 2021, and 2022 sessions. The cited history note records these session laws; the page does not describe the substance of each change.

Chapter 98 of the 2023 Kansas Session Laws raised the credit to 75 percent of the amount contributed for tax years beginning in 2023 and amended the definition of an eligible student. As the definitions section now stands, an eligible student is a child who resides in Kansas and whose annual family income is at or below 250 percent of the federal poverty guidelines, subject to the prior attendance and age conditions in the section. The total credits allowed in any one tax year remain capped at $10,000,000.

Section 189 of the Kentucky Constitution provides that no portion of any fund or tax raised or levied for educational purposes shall be appropriated to, used by, or used in aid of any church, sectarian, or denominational school. The cited page states that the provision was ratified on August 3, 1891, revised on September 28, 1891, and has not been amended since its adoption.

events.instrument: 2021 Ky. Acts ch. 167, s. 5 (KRS 141.500 to 141.528, Education Opportunity Account Act)
events.summary: The Education Opportunity Account Program was created by chapter 167, section 5 of the 2021 Kentucky Acts, effective June 29, 2021. The stated purpose of the program was to provide flexibility and choice in education to Kentucky residents and to address disparities in the educational options available to students. The program operated through income tax credits for contributions to account granting organizations.

events.instrument: Commonwealth ex rel. Cameron v. Johnson, Nos. 2021-SC-0518-TG, 2021-SC-0519-TG, 2021-SC-0520-TG, and 2021-SC-0522-TG (Ky. Dec. 15, 2022)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of Kentucky affirmed the circuit court and held that the Education Opportunity Account Act, KRS 141.500 to 141.528, violates section 184 of the Kentucky Constitution, which bars the raising or collection of funds for education other than in common schools without voter approval. The court reasoned that the tax credit structure redirected taxpayer income tax liability to nonpublic schools. The circuit court's alternative holding under section 59 was treated as moot. The Act was held unenforceable.

events.instrument: La. Rev. Stat. §§ 47:293(9)(a)(xiv), 47:297.10, and 47:297.11, elementary and secondary school tuition deduction
events.summary: Louisiana enacted an individual income tax deduction for elementary and secondary school tuition and related expenses, available for any K-12 child enrolled in a private school in the state. The summary relied on reports 63,355 participating taxpayers in 2024 and an average deduction of 5,922 dollars for 2022-2023, and states that no legal challenge has been filed against the program.

events.instrument: La. Rev. Stat. § 47:6301, Tuition Donation Credit Program
events.summary: Louisiana created a tax-credit scholarship program under which donations to school tuition organizations generate a state tax credit and the organizations award scholarships to eligible students. Students must reside in Louisiana and have a household income under 250 percent of the federal poverty level, and must meet one of the program's entry conditions. The summary relied on reports 3,606 participating students and an average award of 4,318 dollars for 2023-2024.

events.instrument: 2012 La. Acts 2 (House Bill 976), Student Scholarships for Educational Excellence Program
events.summary: House Bill 976 of the 2012 Regular Session was signed by the Governor on April 18, 2012 and became Act No. 2, with an effective date of August 1, 2012. The act provided relative to the Student Scholarships for Educational Excellence Program, parent petitions for the transfer of certain schools to the Recovery School District, charter school authorizers, and course providers, and it expanded the scholarship program beyond its earlier pilot footprint.

events.instrument: Louisiana Federation of Teachers v. State, 118 So. 3d 1033 (La. 2013) (Nos. 2013-CA-0120, 2013-CA-0232, 2013-CA-0350)
events.summary: The Louisiana Supreme Court held that by their express terms Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 99 and 2012 La. Acts 2 unconstitutionally divert Minimum Foundation Program funds to nonpublic entities in violation of La. Const. art. VIII, § 13(B), which requires state Minimum Foundation Program funds to be allocated equitably to parish and city school systems. The court further held that SCR 99 was a matter intended to have the effect of law, that it was not timely introduced or considered in the session and did not receive the vote required to enact such a matter, and it rendered judgment declaring SCR 99 void from the outset, reversing the district court's contrary holding on that point. Once the unconstitutional provisions of Act 2 were severed, the court held that the legislature did not violate the one-object rule of La. Const. art. III, § 15(A) and affirmed that portion of the district court's judgment. The decree was affirmed in part, reversed in part, and rendered. Justice Victory concurred and Justice Guidry dissented.

events.instrument: La. Rev. Stat. § 17:236(A) and Louisiana Department of Education nonpublic school registration and approval requirements
events.summary: This federal compilation of Louisiana requirements states that nonpublic schools must be registered or approved, that a nonpublic school not seeking state approval must periodically register, and that the Louisiana Department of Education must be notified within thirty days of the start of the session with information on the school year, the name of the school, contact information, and the number of students enrolled. It further records that instructional staff at a nonpublic school receiving local, state, or federal funds or support, directly or indirectly, must be certified in accordance with rules established by the State Board of Elementary and Secondary Education, while instructional staff at a nonpublic school receiving no such funds or support must meet requirements prescribed by the school or the church. Accreditation is not required.

events.instrument: 2024 La. Acts 1 (Senate Bill 313), Louisiana Giving All True Opportunity to Rise (LA GATOR) Scholarship Program
events.summary: Senate Bill 313 of the 2024 Regular Session created the Louisiana Giving All True Opportunity to Rise Scholarship Program to provide education savings accounts for parental choice in K-12 education. The bill was signed by the Governor on June 19, 2024 and became Act No. 1.

events.instrument: LA GATOR Scholarship Program, Louisiana Department of Education program page
events.summary: The Louisiana Department of Education describes the LA GATOR Scholarship Program as created by Act 1 of the 2024 Louisiana Legislature and signed into law by Governor Jeff Landry, providing eligible families with education scholarship accounts that may be used for approved education expenses including nonpublic school tuition and fees, tutoring, educational therapies, textbooks, curricula, and dual enrollment.

events.instrument: LA GATOR Scholarship Program appropriation for the 2025-2026 school year
events.summary: The summary relied on reports that the legislature approved 43.5 million dollars for the LA GATOR Scholarship Program for 2025-2026 and that unused funds roll over annually. It records approximately 6,000 participating students and an average account value of 7,250 dollars for 2025-2026, describes a three-phase eligibility rollout with no stated timeline, and notes that former participants in the Student Scholarships for Educational Excellence Program, which ended with the conclusion of the 2024-2025 school year, receive priority.

events.instrument: Louisiana Scholarship Program (Student Scholarships for Educational Excellence Program), sunset June 30, 2025
events.summary: The Louisiana Department of Education states that the Louisiana Scholarship Program continued to be administered through the end of the 2024-2025 school year and sunset on June 30, 2025, and that Louisiana Scholarship Program students and nonpublic schools receive priority access to the LA GATOR Scholarship Program. The department reported contacting participating families and schools about the transition for the 2025-2026 school year.

events.instrument: 20-A M.R.S. § 5204 (PL 1981, c. 693, §§ 5, 8), secondary students' right to attend school in another administrative unit
events.summary: Maine's town tuitioning statute governs the right of secondary students to attend school in a school administrative unit other than the one in which they reside. A secondary student may attend an approved private school or a public secondary school in another unit with the consent of the receiving school's board, with the parent paying tuition and transportation in that instance, and separate subsections govern students whose parents live remote from a public school in their unit and students in contract school arrangements, where the resident unit pays tuition. The section was enacted by PL 1981, c. 693.

events.instrument: Bagley v. Raymond School Department, 1999 ME 60, 728 A.2d 127 (Me. 1999)
events.summary: The Maine Supreme Judicial Court considered whether Maine's education tuition program, which excluded religious schools from receipt of state funds under 20-A M.R.S.A. § 2951(2), violated any section of the United States or Maine Constitution. The court concluded that it did not and affirmed the judgment of the Superior Court. On the free exercise claim the court held that the parents failed to generate a material fact from which a factfinder could conclude that section 2951(2) places a substantial burden on the free exercise of their religion, and it therefore held that the exclusion of religious schools from the tuition program does not violate the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment. Justice Clifford dissented.

events.instrument: Anderson v. Town of Durham, 2006 ME 39, 895 A.2d 944 (Me. 2006)
events.summary: The Maine Supreme Judicial Court affirmed the summary judgment of the Superior Court holding that 20-A M.R.S. § 2951(2) is constitutional, stating that more recent federal court decisions and its review of the current state of the law confirmed that the legislative choice made in enacting the section continued to be a valid enactment. The court described its earlier holding in Bagley, in which it upheld the section on equal protection grounds on the view that the then-current Establishment Clause jurisprudence required Maine to continue to exclude religious schools from approval for state paid tuition, and it noted that the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit had reached substantially the same conclusion. Justice Levy concurred and Justice Clifford dissented.

events.instrument: Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 20-A, §§ 2906 and 5001-A, private school approval for attendance purposes
events.summary: This federal compilation of Maine requirements states that registration is not required and accreditation is not required, but that approval or recognition is mandatory, because attendance at a private school satisfies the compulsory attendance requirement only if the school is approved for attendance purposes or is recognized by the state department of education as providing equivalent instruction. A private school may operate as an approved private school for attendance purposes if it meets hygiene, health, and safety standards and is either accredited by the New England Association of Colleges and Secondary Schools or meets applicable state requirements. Schools using the accreditation route must report to the commissioner of education on a timely basis and notify the commissioner of any determination that the school is not accredited or is on probation.

events.instrument: 20-A M.R.S. § 2951(6), as amended by PL 2021, c. 386, §§ 1 and 2
events.summary: The Legislature amended the conditions on which a private school may be approved for the receipt of public funds for tuition purposes. As amended, subsection 6 requires that the school participate in the statewide assessment program, meet the applicable requirements of and maintain a curriculum aligned with the system of learning results established in section 6209, and meet health and safety requirements applicable to public schools. It further provides that where public funding supports more than 85 percent of the school's students, determined by the previous year's October and April average enrollment, and the municipality where the school is located does not exercise school choice, the school must enroll all students from that municipality, including those with disabilities, who must be served in accordance with applicable state and federal law. Except for that enrollment obligation, the subsection applies only to a school that enrolls 60 percent or more publicly funded students.

events.instrument: 5 M.R.S. § 4602, as amended by PL 2021, c. 366, § 19 (Maine Human Rights Act, unlawful educational discrimination)
events.summary: The Legislature restructured the educational discrimination provisions of the Maine Human Rights Act. As amended, subsection 1 makes it unlawful educational discrimination, on the basis of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, physical or mental disability, ancestry, national origin, race, color, or religion, to exclude a person from participation in, deny a person the benefits of, or subject a person to discrimination in any academic, extracurricular, research, occupational training, or other program or activity, to deny equal opportunity in athletic programs, to apply rules concerning familial or marital status or to exclude a person because of pregnancy or related conditions or because of sex or sexual orientation or gender identity, to deny admission or equal access to and information about an institution or program through recruitment, or to deny financial assistance availability and opportunity. The prior separate subsections addressing disability, national origin or race, and sexual orientation were repealed.

The summary relied on states that on June 21, 2022 the United States Supreme Court held in Carson v. Makin that it violates the United States Constitution for a state to prohibit a parent using school choice program funding from choosing a religious private school, whether the prohibition rests on the status of the school as a religious school or on the school's use of the funding. The decision reversed the judgment of the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit reported at 979 F.3d 21 (1st Cir. 2020), which had upheld the Maine exclusion, and it displaced the sectarian exclusion in 20-A M.R.S. § 2951(2) as applied to the town tuitioning program.

The subsection of the private school approval statute headed Nonsectarian, which had conditioned approval for the receipt of public funds for tuition purposes on the school being nonsectarian, was repealed by PL 2025, c. 112, § 5. The section as published carries the repeal note for subsection 2 and lists PL 2025, c. 112, § 5 in its section history. The enactment date of chapter 112 and the legislative document number were not established from this source and remain outstanding.

events.instrument: St. Dominic Academy v. Makin, No. 24-1739 (1st Cir. July 2, 2026)
events.summary: The United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit ruled on an appeal from an order denying the plaintiffs' motion for a preliminary injunction against antidiscrimination rules codified in the Maine Human Rights Act as applied to schools seeking approval for the receipt of town tuitioning funds. The court affirmed the order in part, reversed it in part, stated that the religious expression rule burdens St. Dominic's religious exercise and is not neutral and subjected the rule to heightened review, and reversed the portion of the order concerning the gender identity nondiscrimination rule. The court remanded one claim brought only on behalf of individual plaintiffs and ordered its dismissal without prejudice. Proceedings on remand remain outstanding.

events.instrument: Crosspoint Church v. Makin, No. 24-1590 (1st Cir. July 2, 2026)
events.summary: The United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit ruled the same day on a companion appeal from an order denying a preliminary injunction against the Maine Human Rights Act rules applied to schools seeking approval for the receipt of town tuitioning funds. The court reversed the order insofar as it rejected Crosspoint's challenge concerning the gender identity nondiscrimination rule. Proceedings on remand remain outstanding.

events.instrument: Broadening Options and Opportunities for Students Today (BOOST) Program, Senate Bill 190 § R00A03.05
events.summary: Maryland created the BOOST program in 2016 as a scholarship program funded by legislative appropriation through the annual budget bill rather than by permanent authorizing statute. Students are eligible if family income is at or below 100 percent of the federal free and reduced-price lunch limit, and renewing students whose family remains under the income limit are entitled to awards, with priority for siblings of participants. Awards may cover up to the statewide average per-pupil expenditure or private school tuition, whichever is lower, larger awards for students with special needs must be approved by the BOOST Advisory Board, awards are made from a ranked and certified applicant list, and unused funds are carried forward. The summary relied on reports 2,403 participating students in 2024-2025 and an average award of 3,535 dollars.

events.instrument: Md. Code Ann., Educ. § 2-206(e)(4) and Code of Maryland Regulations governing nonpublic school approval
events.summary: This federal compilation of Maryland requirements states that registration is mandatory and that accreditation has no requirements. Institutions operated by a bona fide church organization are exempt from holding a certificate of approval from the Maryland State Board of Education if the legal authority of the organization so chooses; the head of the organization must register the school by giving its name and address, submitting acceptable evidence of the organization's legal authority status, and providing the Nonpublic School Approval Branch of the Maryland State Department of Education with certification of the legal authority's assumption of responsibility for governing and operating the school. Schools in this category are described as church-exempt schools. Registered bona fide church organizations and other entities operating nonpublic nursery schools must hold valid child care center licenses or letters of compliance issued by the department's Office of Child Care.

events.instrument: Bethel Ministries, Inc. v. Salmon, Civil Case No. SAG-19-01853 (D. Md. Dec. 10, 2021)
events.summary: The summary relied on states that the United States District Court for the District of Maryland held that the state board administering the BOOST program violated the First Amendment free speech rights of Bethel Christian Academy when it removed and excluded the school from the program, reasoning that the state conditioned government funding on a viewpoint-based restriction of speech and violated the unconstitutional conditions doctrine. Participating schools are barred from discriminating against students in admissions on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the school was found not to have violated that requirement; it had been disqualified over statements in its parent and student handbook concerning marriage and gender. The court declined to rule on whether the BOOST program itself is constitutional, and the state did not appeal.

events.instrument: Mass. Const. amend. art. XVIII, as amended by amend. art. XLVI (ratified and adopted November 6, 1917) and by amend. art. CIII
events.summary: Article XVIII of the Articles of Amendment, in place of the article of amendment ratified and adopted April 9, 1821, was submitted by the constitutional convention and ratified and adopted November 6, 1917 as Article XLVI. Section 1 provides that no law shall be passed prohibiting the free exercise of religion, and Section 2 provides that all moneys raised by taxation in the towns and cities for the support of public schools and all moneys appropriated by the Commonwealth for the support of common schools shall be applied and expended in no other schools than those conducted according to law under the order and superintendence of the local authorities, and that no grant, appropriation, or use of public money or property or loan of public credit shall be made or authorized for the purpose of founding, maintaining, or aiding a nonpublic institution. Article CIII later struck Section 2 of Article XLVI and inserted a revised Section 2 extending the bar to any infirmary, hospital, institution, primary or secondary school, or charitable or religious undertaking that is not publicly owned and under the exclusive control, order, and supervision of public officers or public agents, with exceptions for the Soldiers' Home in Massachusetts, free public libraries, and legal obligations already in existence. The date of ratification of Article CIII was not established from this source.

events.instrument: Mass. Gen. Laws c. 76, § 1, approval of private schools by the local school committee
events.summary: This federal compilation of Massachusetts requirements states that accreditation has no requirements and that approval is mandatory, because attendance at a private school satisfies the compulsory attendance requirement if the school is approved by the school committee, which is the local educational agency in Massachusetts. School committees approve a private school when satisfied that its instruction equals that of the public schools in the same town in thoroughness and efficiency and that private students are making the same progress as public school students, and a school committee may not withhold approval on the basis of the school's religious teaching. The compilation notes an advisory of the Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education on approval of private schools under the section, and records that state law does not specify a required length of school year for private schools and does not mandate particular courses.

events.instrument: Caplan v. Town of Acton, 479 Mass. 69, 92 N.E.3d 691 (2018) (SJC-12274)
events.summary: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court addressed whether two grants of public funds to renovate an active church identified as a historic resource under the Community Preservation Act, G. L. c. 44B, are categorically barred by the anti-aid amendment, Article XVIII of the Articles of Amendment as amended by Articles XLVI and CIII, which prohibits in Section 2, clause 2, the grant, appropriation, or use of public money for the purpose of founding, maintaining, or aiding any church, religious denomination, or society. The court held that such grants are not categorically barred and are instead evaluated under the three-factor test applied under Commonwealth v. School Committee of Springfield, 382 Mass. 665 (1981), which asks whether the purpose of the grant is to aid a private charity, whether the grant does in fact substantially aid a private charity, and whether the grant avoids the political and economic abuses that prompted the passage of the anti-aid amendment. The court directed that grants of community preservation funds to active religious institutions warrant careful scrutiny. Justice Cypher dissented in part.

events.instrument: MCL 388.551 and MCL 388.555 (Private, Denominational, and Parochial Schools Act, 1921 PA 302, §§ 1 and 5)
events.summary: The 1921 act places the private, denominational, and parochial schools of Michigan under the supervision of the superintendent of public instruction in the matters and manner the act provides. The act states the intent that the sanitary conditions of the schools subject to it, the courses of study in those schools, and the qualifications of the teachers in those schools be of the same standard as provided by the general school laws of the state. Section 5 authorizes the superintendent, assistants, or an authorized agent to investigate and examine the condition of any school operating under the act, and requires the school to submit for examination its sanitary condition, its records of enrollment of pupils, its courses of study, and the qualifications of its teachers. Refusal to comply is cause to suspend the operation of the school after the proceedings stated in section 4.

events.instrument: MCL 388.553 (Private, Denominational, and Parochial Schools Act, 1921 PA 302, § 3), teacher certification
events.summary: Section 3 of the 1921 act provides that no person shall teach or give instruction in any of the regular or elementary grade studies in a private, denominational, or parochial school in Michigan who does not hold a certificate that would qualify that person to teach in like grades of the public schools of the state. The section includes provisos for persons who had taught in a qualifying elementary school for ten years or more before the act's passage, treats teaching in such schools as equivalent to public school teaching for purposes of obtaining a certificate, and authorizes the superintendent of public instruction to direct examinations. The section remains on the books in this form.

events.instrument: Mich. Const. 1963, art. VIII, § 2, ¶ 2 (Proposal C of 1970, initiated constitutional amendment)
events.summary: Michigan voters approved Proposal C, an initiated constitutional amendment adding a second paragraph to Article VIII, Section 2 of the 1963 Constitution.
