The amendment provides that no public monies or property shall be appropriated or paid, and no public credit utilized, by the legislature or any other political subdivision or agency of the state, directly or indirectly, to aid or maintain any private, denominational, or other nonpublic elementary or secondary school, and it further barred public payments to support the attendance of students or the employment of persons at nonpublic schools, with an exception for transportation. The reported result was 56.77 percent in favor and 43.23 percent opposed. This paragraph is the anti-aid provision that governs every later Michigan question about public support to nonpublic schools.

events.instrument: Traverse City School District v. Attorney General, 384 Mich. 390, 185 N.W.2d 9 (1971)
events.summary: The Michigan Supreme Court construed the paragraph added to Article VIII, Section 2 by Proposal C. The court held that shared time instruction may continue at public schools and at premises leased and controlled by public school authorities, and it struck as contrary to the federal Free Exercise and Equal Protection guarantees the clause barring public funds at any location or institution where instruction is offered in whole or in part to nonpublic school students. The court held that auxiliary services may be provided at nonpublic schools as general health and safety measures with only an incidental educational connection, that federal grant funds are not state public monies within the meaning of the provision, and that direct public payment of nonpublic school teacher salaries is prohibited. This decision remains the controlling construction of the provision.

events.instrument: Citizens Research Council of Michigan, State Ballot Issues: Proposal 00-1, School Choice (June 13, 2000)
events.summary: A pre-election analysis of Proposal 00-1 described the voucher mechanism the amendment would have created. Students in qualified districts, defined by a graduation rate below the stated threshold, and in districts that adopted vouchers by board action or a public vote would have received a voucher worth the lesser of half the average per-pupil state and local revenue, estimated at 3,318 dollars, or actual tuition. The analysis identified seven districts as initially qualified, the largest being Detroit with 173,557 students, and noted the amendment would have required regular testing of the academic subject knowledge of teachers in public schools and in nonpublic schools redeeming vouchers. The measure was rejected at the November 7, 2000 election.

events.instrument: Michigan Proposal 1 of 2000 (Proposal 00-1), initiated constitutional amendment
events.summary: Michigan voters rejected Proposal 1, an initiated constitutional amendment that would have eliminated the constitutional ban on indirect support of students attending nonpublic schools through tuition vouchers, credits, tax benefits, exemptions or deductions, subsidies, grants, or loans of public monies or property. The measure would have allowed tuition vouchers in districts with a graduation rate below the stated threshold and in districts adopting vouchers by school board action or a public vote, capped each voucher at half of the state average per-pupil public school revenue, and required testing of teachers in public schools and in nonpublic schools redeeming vouchers. The reported result was 30.87 percent in favor and 69.13 percent opposed.

events.instrument: 2012 PA 131, 2012 PA 132, 2012 PA 133, and 2012 PA 134 (Senate Bills 622, 623, 709, and 710), nonpublic school dual enrollment
events.summary: Four public acts allow postsecondary institutions to bill the state for reimbursement of eligible charges for dually enrolled students attending a state approved nonpublic school. The program permits a student enrolled in a nonpublic school to take postsecondary coursework while remaining enrolled at the nonpublic school, with the postsecondary institution submitting eligible costs to the Michigan Department of Education for reimbursement. The department issued correspondence to nonpublic schools and postsecondary institutions on September 12, 2012 setting out the eligible costs and the form and manner of submission.

events.instrument: MCL 380.1561 (Revised School Code, 1976 PA 451), as amended by 1995 PA 289, 1996 PA 339, 2009 PA 204, and 2016 PA 532
events.summary: Michigan's compulsory attendance statute excuses a child from public school attendance where the child is attending regularly and is being taught in a state approved nonpublic school that teaches subjects comparable to those taught in the public schools. The section also excuses a child taught at home in an organized educational program, permits a child regularly enrolled in a public school to attend religious instruction classes for not more than two class hours per week, and provides exemptions for distance from school, for confirmation classes for children aged twelve and thirteen, and for high school graduates. The 2009 amendment extended compulsory attendance to age eighteen for children turning eleven on or after December 1, 2009. State approval of the nonpublic school under this section is the hinge on which Michigan's regulation of nonpublic schools turns.

events.instrument: 2016 PA 249, § 152b (MCL 388.1752b), reimbursement of nonpublic schools for health, safety, and welfare mandates
events.summary: Section 152b of 2016 PA 249, signed into law on June 27, 2016, appropriated 2.5 million dollars to reimburse nonpublic schools for the actual costs of complying with state health, safety, and welfare statutes and regulations. The appropriation was challenged as an appropriation to aid or maintain nonpublic schools contrary to Article VIII, Section 2 of the 1963 Constitution, and it became the subject of litigation that reached the Michigan Supreme Court.

events.instrument: U.S. Department of Education, Michigan State Regulation of Private and Home Schools (page updated November 24, 2016)
events.summary: This federal compilation of Michigan requirements states that registration of a private school is not required, but that state approval is required for a nonpublic school to satisfy the compulsory attendance statute under MCL 380.1561(3)(a), and that the Michigan Department of Education annually requests information including enrollment by grade, teacher qualifications, courses offered, and criminal history check compliance under MCL 388.555. It states that certification is optional for nonpublic school teachers, who may qualify by holding a Michigan teaching certificate under MCL 388.553, by holding a nonpublic school teaching permit under Michigan Administrative Code R 390.1142, R 390.1143, and R 390.1145, or by holding a bachelor's degree, and that where a school asserts an objection to teacher certification based on sincerely held religious beliefs the minimum education requirements are waived, citing People v. DeJonge, 442 Mich. 266. It further records curriculum requirements under MCL 380.1561(3)(a), MCL 380.1166, and MCL 380.1151, immunization and vision screening requirements with religious exemptions, and criminal history and unprofessional conduct checks under MCL 380.1230, MCL 380.1230a, and MCL 380.1230b.

events.instrument: Council of Organizations and Others for Education About Parochiaid v. State, 321 Mich. App. 456, 909 N.W.2d 449 (2017) (Docket Nos. 338258, 338259)
events.summary: The Michigan Court of Appeals affirmed the Court of Claims decision denying motions to intervene as defendants filed by a group of nonpublic schools and parents, the Michigan Catholic Conference, and the Michigan Association of Non-Public Schools, holding that the Court of Claims lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over claims against those parties. The underlying complaint, filed on March 21, 2017, asserted that Section 152b of 2016 PA 249 appropriated public funds to aid nonpublic schools contrary to Article VIII, Section 2, paragraph 2 of the 1963 Constitution.

events.instrument: Council of Organizations and Others for Education About Parochiaid v. State, 326 Mich. App. 124, 931 N.W.2d 65 (2018) (Docket No. 343801)
events.summary: The Michigan Court of Appeals held that, without offending Article VIII, Section 2 of the 1963 Constitution, the legislature may allocate public funds to reimburse nonpublic schools for actual costs incurred in complying with state health, safety, and welfare laws, resting on the Michigan Supreme Court's construction of the provision in Traverse City School District v. Attorney General and in Advisory Opinion re Constitutionality of 1974 PA 242. Reimbursement is permitted only where the action required to comply with the mandate is at most merely incidental to teaching and providing educational services and is noninstructional in nature, together with the further criteria the court set out. The Court of Claims had ruled that MCL 388.1752b is unconstitutional on its face. The Court of Appeals reversed that ruling and remanded for examination of each actual cost for which a nonpublic school may be reimbursed, and it noted that the Court of Claims had not reached the plaintiffs' claim under Article IV, Section 30. Judge Gleicher concurred in part and dissented in part.

events.instrument: Council of Organizations and Others for Education About Parochiaid v. State, No. 158751 (Mich. Dec. 28, 2020)
events.summary: The Michigan Supreme Court divided evenly and issued no majority opinion on the constitutionality of MCL 388.1752b. The opinion for affirmance concluded that the section does not violate Article VIII, Section 2 of the 1963 Constitution because it appropriates funds only to provide for nonpublic school students' health, safety, and welfare rather than for educational services, and would affirm the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remand to the Court of Claims for further proceedings. The dissenting opinion concluded that the section violates the provision under the common understanding of its language because direct payments to nonpublic schools aid or maintain those schools. The even division left the Court of Appeals judgment standing without a majority holding of the Supreme Court.

events.instrument: Michigan Senate Bills 687 and 688 and House Bills 5404 and 5405 of 2021, Student Opportunity Scholarship Program
events.summary: The legislature passed identical measures in October 2021 to establish student opportunity scholarship accounts funded by charitable donations to state-regulated qualified nonprofit organizations, with donors receiving a dollar-for-dollar credit against state taxes owed and an annual statewide credit limit of 500 million dollars. Most Michigan students would have qualified, with priority for families with household income below 200 percent of the federal free and reduced-price lunch threshold, children with disabilities, and students in foster care. Governor Gretchen Whitmer vetoed the legislation on November 5, 2021.

events.instrument: Let MI Kids Learn initiative petitions (Student Opportunity Scholarship Program and associated tax credit), withdrawn from the Board of State Canvassers
events.summary: Following the November 2021 vetoes, the Let MI Kids Learn campaign circulated two initiative petitions, the first to establish a Student Opportunity Scholarship Program providing funds for tuition and fees at K-12 public or private schools, home schooling materials, and online learning programs for students with financial need, and the second to make contributions to the program tax deductible. The campaign missed the June 1, 2022 deadline to submit signatures for the November 2022 ballot and then sought legislative adoption. On December 28, 2022 the campaign withdrew both petitions from the Board of State Canvassers. The reported reason was the change in control of both chambers of the legislature.

events.instrument: Hile v. State of Michigan, No. 22-1986 (6th Cir. Nov. 6, 2023)
events.summary: The United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed dismissal of an equal protection challenge to the paragraph of Article VIII, Section 2 of the Michigan Constitution barring appropriation or payment of public monies or property to aid or maintain any private, denominational, or other nonpublic school. The plaintiffs sought to use Michigan Education Savings Program funds for religious school tuition and argued that the facially neutral amendment creates an unequal political process for religious persons. The court rejected that argument, treating the provision as a policy choice to fund only public education notwithstanding its historical origins, and further held that the claim was not redressable because Michigan statutory law independently barred the use the plaintiffs sought.

events.instrument: MCL 388.1766b (State School Aid Act of 1979, 1979 PA 94, § 166b)
events.summary: Section 166b of the State School Aid Act provides that the act does not prohibit a parent or legal guardian of a minor enrolled in a nonpublic school, or being home-schooled, from also enrolling the minor in a district, public school academy, or intermediate district in a curricular offering provided at a public school site and available to pupils in the minor's grade level or age group, subject to the requirements that apply to a full-time pupil. State school aid is provided for such an enrollment only for a curricular offering restricted to nonessential elective courses. The section also addresses enrollment in a nonessential elective curricular offering provided by a district at a nonpublic school site, subject to conditions including the location of the nonpublic school site or the education of the nonpublic students within the district's geographic boundaries. This is the statutory basis for Michigan's shared time arrangements. The text retrieved is stated to be current as of 2024; the enacting session law was not established from this source.

events.instrument: Hile v. State of Michigan, petition for writ of certiorari denied (U.S. Oct. 2024)
events.summary: The United States Supreme Court denied the petition for a writ of certiorari in Hile v. State of Michigan, leaving the lower court rulings upholding the Michigan constitutional provision in place. The source, published on October 15, 2024, places the denial in the preceding week but does not state the exact date or the docket number, which remain to be established.

events.instrument: Minn. Const. art. XIII, § 2, prohibition as to aiding sectarian school
events.summary: The Minnesota Constitution provides in Article XIII, Section 2 that in no case shall any public money or property be appropriated or used for the support of schools wherein the distinctive doctrines, creeds, or tenets of any particular Christian or other religious sect are promulgated or taught. The published constitution records adoption on October 13, 1857 and a general revision on November 5, 1974, and the provision stands in the revised text in this form.

events.instrument: Minn. Stat. § 290.0674, Minnesota education credit (1Sp1997 c 4 art 13 s 3)
events.summary: Minnesota enacted a refundable individual income tax credit equal to 75 percent of the amount paid for education-related expenses for a qualifying child in kindergarten through grade 12. Qualifying expenses include instructional fees or tuition, a maximum of 200 dollars per family for personal computer hardware and educational software used in the home, and instruction by persons meeting the statutory instructor definitions. The published section history records the credit as enacted by 1Sp1997 c 4 art 13 s 3.

events.instrument: Minn. Stat. §§ 120A.22, 120A.24, and 123B.445, nonpublic school reporting, accreditation recognition, and instructor qualifications
events.summary: This federal compilation of Minnesota requirements states that registration has no requirements and approval has no requirements, and that accreditation is optional, with the Nonpublic Education Council able to recognize educational accrediting agencies under Minn. Stat. § 123B.445. Nonpublic schools directly accredited by an organization recognized by the council or by the commissioner of education are eligible for reduced reporting to the superintendents of the districts where their students reside under Minn. Stat. § 120A.24. Teacher certification is optional; an instructor must hold a valid Minnesota teaching license for the grade level taught, be directly supervised by a license holder, pass a teacher competency examination, teach in a school accredited by a recognized agency, hold a baccalaureate degree, or be a parent of a child whose performance is assessed annually under Minn. Stat. § 120A.22.

events.instrument: Minn. Stat. § 290.0674, as amended by 2023 Minn. Laws ch. 64, art. 1, § 37
events.summary: The Legislature amended the Minnesota education credit in the 2023 tax act. The published section history records amendments in 1998, 1999, 2001, 2005, 2016, 2017, 2019, and 2023, the last by 2023 Minn. Laws ch. 64, art. 1, § 37, and the section text refers to taxable year 2023 as the first year for the amended treatment. The credit remains in operation alongside the separate tuition deduction.

events.instrument: Minn. Stat. § 290.0132, subd. 4, as amended by 2023 Minn. Laws ch. 64, art. 1, § 22 (education expense subtraction)
events.summary: The Minnesota income tax subtraction for education expenses, the successor to the tuition deduction sustained against an Establishment Clause challenge in Mueller v. Allen, remains in the code at Minn. Stat. § 290.0132, subd. 4. The published legislative history for the section records that subdivision 4 was amended by 2023 Minn. Laws ch. 64, art. 1, § 22, and records further amendments to other subdivisions of the section in 2024, 2025, and 2026. The deduction and the education credit continue to operate together as Minnesota's household-level supports for nonpublic school expenses.

events.instrument: Mississippi Dyslexia Therapy Scholarship for Students with Dyslexia Program, Miss. Code Ann. § 37-173-1 et seq.
events.summary: This federal compilation records that Mississippi enacted in 2012 a scholarship program for children with dyslexia to attend state accredited special purpose nonpublic schools in order to receive comprehensive multisensory dyslexia therapy delivered by holders of an appropriate license in dyslexia therapy issued by the department. Eligibility is restricted to students in grades one through six with a diagnosis of dyslexia who attended a public school or another state approved nonpublic school emphasizing instruction in dyslexia intervention in the previous school year, and the maximum scholarship is based on the state's base funding per pupil. The compilation states that the statute's nonpublic school option was to be repealed effective July 1, 2016; whether that repealer took effect was not established from this source.

events.instrument: Equal Opportunity for Students with Special Needs Program, Miss. Code Ann. §§ 37-181-1 through 37-181-21
events.summary: Mississippi created an education savings account program for students with special needs, enacted and launched in 2015 and governed by Miss. Code Ann. §§ 37-181-1 through 37-181-21. Participating students must reside in Mississippi and have had an active individualized education program within the past three years, and a student in this program may not also receive a Dyslexia Therapy or Nate Rogers scholarship. Enrolled students are automatically approved for continued participation if they remain outside the public school system. The summary relied on reports an annual appropriation of 5 million dollars, an award amount based on the Mississippi Student Funding Formula, 454 participating students, and an average account value of 8,007 dollars.

events.instrument: Miss. Code Ann. §§ 37-17-7 and 37-17-9 and Mississippi Nonpublic Schools Accountability Standards (2004)
events.summary: This federal compilation of Mississippi requirements states that registration has no requirements, that accreditation is optional, and that approval is optional. Nonpublic schools may be accredited by independent nonpublic school accrediting agencies under Miss. Code Ann. § 37-17-9, and nonpublic schools serving school age students may request accreditation or approval by the State Board of Education under Miss. Code Ann. § 37-17-7, with the standards for nonpublic school approval barred from being more rigorous than the accreditation standards for public schools. Standards for state approval or accreditation are set out in the Nonpublic Schools Accountability Standards, and private schools must reapply for accreditation no later than October 1 each year. The compilation also records that the Mississippi Constitution prohibits the appropriation of state education funds for the support of sectarian schools or private schools at Article 8, Section 208.

events.instrument: Midsouth Association of Independent Schools v. Parents for Public Schools, No. 2022-SA-01129-SCT (Miss. May 2, 2024)
events.summary: The Mississippi Supreme Court reviewed a Hinds County Chancery Court judgment in litigation brought by Parents for Public Schools challenging a state grant program for independent schools under Section 208 of the Mississippi Constitution, which prohibits the appropriation of state education funds for the support of sectarian or private schools. The court held that Parents for Public Schools failed to demonstrate an adverse impact sufficient to confer standing, rejecting the asserted competitive disadvantage and taxpayer standing theories, and declined to reach the additional issues on appeal. The court vacated the judgment of the Hinds County Chancery Court. The judgment under review was entered October 13, 2022 before Chancellor Crystal Wise Martin.

The Missouri Constitution provides that no money shall ever be taken from the public treasury, directly or indirectly, in aid of any church, sect, or denomination of religion, or in aid of any priest, preacher, minister, or teacher thereof as such, and that no preference shall be given to nor any discrimination made against any church, sect, or creed of religion, or any form of religious faith or worship. The published section carries an effective date of February 27, 1945.

The Missouri Constitution provides that neither the general assembly nor any county, city, town, township, school district, or other municipal corporation shall ever make an appropriation or pay from any public fund anything in aid of any religious creed, church, or sectarian purpose, or to help support or sustain any private or public school, academy, seminary, college, university, or other institution of learning controlled by a religious creed, church, or sectarian denomination. The published section carries an effective date of February 27, 1945. This is the provision that constrains direct Missouri appropriations to religious schools and that shaped the design of the state's tax-credit funded scholarship program.

events.instrument: Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 167.031 and 168.071, nonpublic school registration, curriculum, and teacher certification
events.summary: This federal compilation of Missouri requirements states that accreditation has no requirements, that registration is mandatory, and that approval has no requirements. Teacher certification is not required by statute for teachers in nonpublic schools, although a nonpublic school teacher who holds state certification is subject to discipline by the Missouri State Board of Education for misconduct, and the board may refuse to issue or may revoke a nonpublic school teacher's certificate upon conviction of a felony or a crime involving moral turpitude under Mo. Rev. Stat. § 168.071. The compilation records that Mo. Rev. Stat. § 167.031 may not require a private, parochial, or parish school to include in its curriculum any concept, topic, or practice in conflict with the school's religious doctrines, and that state law does not specify a required length of school year for private schools.

events.instrument: 2021 Mo. H.B. 349, Missouri Empowerment Scholarship Accounts Program, Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 135.712 to 135.719 and 166.700 to 166.720
events.summary: House Bill 349 of 2021 established the Missouri Empowerment Scholarship Accounts Program, known as MOScholars, through Mo. Rev. Stat. §§ 135.712 to 135.719 and 166.700 to 166.720. The statute defines an educational assistance organization as a charitable organization registered in Missouri, exempt from federal taxation under section 501(c)(3), certified by the state treasurer, and allocating its annual revenue for educational assistance derived from contributions for which a credit is claimed, and it defines a qualifying contribution and a scholarship account. The published section carries an effective date of August 28, 2021.

events.instrument: 2024 Mo. S.B. 727, amending Mo. Rev. Stat. § 166.700 and related sections of the Missouri Empowerment Scholarship Accounts Program
events.summary: Senate Bill 727 of 2024 amended the Missouri Empowerment Scholarship Accounts Program. The amended definition of a qualified student covers an elementary or secondary school student who is a resident of Missouri, is not an illegal alien, and who meets one of the stated conditions, including a child eligible to begin kindergarten or first grade under §§ 160.051 to 160.055 and a sibling of a qualified student who received a scholarship grant in the previous school year and will receive one in the current school year. The published section records the source as 2021 H.B. 349 as amended by 2024 S.B. 727 and carries an effective date of August 28, 2024. The revisor also records a renumbering of a statutory reference in § 135.712 made in accordance with § 3.060 on the basis of the 2024 act.

events.instrument: Mont. Const. art. X, § 6 (1972), aid prohibited to sectarian schools
events.summary: Article X, Section 6 of the Montana Constitution provides that the legislature, counties, cities, towns, school districts, and public corporations shall not make any direct or indirect appropriation or payment from any public fund or monies for any sectarian purpose or to aid any school controlled in whole or in part by a church, sect, or denomination, and that the section does not apply to funds from federal sources provided to the state for the express purpose of distribution to nonpublic education. The Montana Supreme Court recorded that the 1972 constitutional convention delegates carried the provision forward from the 1889 Constitution's no-aid provision at Article XI, Section 8, which the delegates described as already among the most stringent in the nation, and the court held that the provision draws a more stringent line than its federal counterpart.

events.instrument: 2015 Mont. Laws ch. 457 (Senate Bill 410), Tax Credit for Qualified Education Contributions, Mont. Code Ann. tit. 15, ch. 30, pt. 31
events.summary: Montana enacted a tax credit for donations to student scholarship organizations, codified at Mont. Code Ann. §§ 15-30-3101 through 15-30-3114. The credit is allowed against the tax imposed by chapter 30 or chapter 31 for donations made to a student scholarship organization, the donor may not direct or designate donations to a parent, legal guardian, or specific qualified education provider, and the credit equals the amount of the donation subject to the per-donor cap. Unused credit may be carried forward three years, and a student scholarship organization must seek preapproval from the department that the credit sought is available under the aggregate limit and must issue a receipt on preapproval. The published section history records enactment by section 14 of chapter 457, Laws of 2015.

events.instrument: Mont. Code Ann. §§ 20-7-101 and 20-7-102 and Administrative Rules of Montana 10.55.605 and 10.55.712, nonpublic school accreditation
events.summary: This federal compilation of Montana requirements states that registration has no requirements and approval has no requirements, and that accreditation is optional, with nonpublic schools able to be accredited upon request to the superintendent of public instruction in the same manner as public schools under Mont. Code Ann. § 20-7-102. The three categories are regular accreditation, accreditation with advice, and deficiency accreditation, and nonaccredited status applies to a school on deficiency status that fails to meet the requirements of intensive assistance and is out of compliance with the Board of Public Education standards. A Montana educator license is required for all teachers working in an accredited Montana school, and accredited schools must comply with class size requirements and other board standards.

events.instrument: Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue, 2018 MT 306, 393 Mont. 446, 435 P.3d 603 (DA 17-0492)
events.summary: The Montana Supreme Court concluded that the Tax Credit Program enacted by Senate Bill 410 in 2015 violates Article X, Section 6 of the Montana Constitution, and it reversed the District Court's order granting the plaintiffs summary judgment. The court held that Montana's constitution more broadly prohibits any state aid to sectarian schools and draws a more stringent line than its federal counterpart, and it therefore confined the issue to whether the program runs afoul of the state no-aid provision, concluding that the program aids sectarian schools in violation of it. The result invalidated the program as a whole rather than only the Department of Revenue rule that had excluded religious schools. Justices Gustafson and Sandefur concurred and Justices Baker and Rice dissented.

events.instrument: Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue, 591 U.S. 464 (2020)
events.summary: The summary relied on states that on June 30, 2020 the United States Supreme Court ruled in favor of parents seeking to choose religious schools for their children under Montana's tax-credit scholarship program, overturning the prior decision of the Montana Supreme Court that had struck down the program, and holding that the Montana court erred in applying the state constitution's no-aid provision to the program. The source records that the program was the subject of three lawsuits that ultimately left it standing as written by the legislature.

events.instrument: 2021 Mont. Laws ch. 480, amending Mont. Code Ann. §§ 15-30-3111 and related sections
events.summary: The Legislature amended the qualified education tax credit in 2021. The published section history for Mont. Code Ann. § 15-30-3111 records amendment by sections 12 through 17 of chapter 480, Laws of 2021. The section as it now stands allows a credit equal to the amount of the donation not to exceed 200,000 dollars per donor, attributes the credit to shareholders, owners, or partners of a pass-through entity in the proportion used to report income or loss, permits a donation by an estate or trust to qualify with attribution to beneficiaries, and caps the credit at the taxpayer's income tax liability with a three-year carryforward.

events.instrument: 2023 Mont. Laws ch. 558, § 4, amending Mont. Code Ann. § 15-30-3111
events.summary: The Legislature further amended the qualified education tax credit in 2023. The published section history for Mont. Code Ann. § 15-30-3111 records amendment by section 4 of chapter 558, Laws of 2023, and the section is published as temporary. The bill number for chapter 558 was not established from this source.

events.instrument: 2023 Mont. Laws ch. 616, Students With Special Needs Equal Opportunity Act, Mont. Code Ann. §§ 20-7-1701 through 20-7-1710
events.summary: Montana created the Montana special needs equal opportunity education savings account program, codified at Mont. Code Ann. §§ 20-7-1701 through 20-7-1710. The statute states that the program is provided by the legislature as an educational program under Article X, section 1(3) of the Montana Constitution, which authorizes the legislature to provide educational programs and institutions in addition to a basic system of public schools, and it states the legislative finding that expanding special needs educational opportunities is a valid public purpose. The part sets out definitions, allowable educational resources, parent responsibilities, the responsibilities of the superintendent of public instruction including rulemaking, the responsibilities of public school districts as to student records, regulation of qualified schools, funding and administration, and the trust. The published section history records enactment by section 2 of chapter 616, Laws of 2023.

events.instrument: Litigation challenging the Montana special needs equal opportunity education savings account program, preliminary injunction denied July 2024
events.summary: The summary relied on states that opponents sued in January 2024 to stop the special needs education savings account program before its launch, arguing that the program violates the Montana Constitution by giving parents reimbursements from tax dollars, by allowing special needs students to access programs outside public school special education, by not capping the number of participants, and by sending local tax dollars to the accounts. The opponents sought a preliminary injunction in April 2024, and the trial court denied it in July 2024. Families used accounts for the 2024-2025 school year while the case remained pending in the trial court. The case name, docket number, and the current posture as of September 2026 remain outstanding.

events.instrument: Neb. Const. art. VII, § 11 (as amended by Laws 1976, LB 666, § 1)
events.summary: Nebraska's anti-aid provision states that appropriation of public funds shall not be made to any school or institution of learning not owned or exclusively controlled by the state or a political subdivision, subject to a proviso permitting contracts for nonsectarian educational or other services for children under twenty-one who are handicapped. It further provides that all public schools shall be free of sectarian instruction, that the state shall not accept money or property to be used for sectarian purposes, and that no religious test may be required of a teacher or student in any school supported in whole or in part by public funds. The official source note records the provision's origin as art. VIII, sec. 11 (1875), transfer to art. VII, sec. 11 by the 1919-1920 Constitutional Convention, and amendments in 1920, 1972, and 1976.

events.instrument: Nebraska Legislative Bill 753 (2023), Opportunity Scholarships Act
events.summary: The slip law records that LB 753 was approved by the Governor on May 30, 2023. The act adopted the Opportunity Scholarships Act and created income tax credits for contributions to certified scholarship granting organizations that award scholarships to students attending privately operated elementary and secondary schools in Nebraska. Section 17 provides that the act becomes operative for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2024.

The slip law records that LB 1402 was approved by the Governor on April 24, 2024. The act provided for education scholarships, defined as financial grants-in-aid to pay all or part of the cost of educating eligible students at nongovernmental, privately operated elementary and secondary schools, funded by direct appropriation rather than by tax credit.

events.instrument: Nebraska Legislative Bill 1402 (2024), §§ 5 and 7 (repealing Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 77-7101 to 77-7113)
events.summary: Section 7 of LB 1402 outright repealed sections 77-7101 through 77-7113, the sections comprising the Opportunity Scholarships Act enacted the previous year, and section 5 made that repeal operative on October 31, 2024. The tax-credit scholarship program created in 2023 was therefore replaced by the appropriation-funded education scholarship program before the tax credits had operated for a full taxable year.

The official canvass of the November 5, 2024 general election records Referendum Measure 435, which asked whether Section 1 of Legislative Bill 1402 should be repealed. Section 1 provided ten million dollars annually to fund education scholarships for eligible students attending nongovernmental, privately operated elementary and secondary schools. The statewide result was 508,140 votes to repeal and 382,921 votes to retain, so the section was repealed.

Article 11, Section 10 of the Nevada Constitution provides that no public funds of any kind or character whatever, State, County or Municipal, shall be used for sectarian purpose. The official annotation records that the section was added in 1880, having been proposed and passed by the 1877 Legislature, agreed to and passed by the 1879 Legislature, and approved and ratified by the people at the 1880 general election. Article 11, Section 9 separately prohibits sectarian instruction in any school or university established under the constitution.

events.instrument: Assembly Bill 165, ch. 22, Statutes of Nevada 2015
events.summary: Chapter 22 of the Statutes of Nevada 2015, approved April 13, 2015, established a credit against the modified business tax for taxpayers who donate money to a scholarship organization, set requirements for scholarship organizations and for schools receiving grants, and required each scholarship organization to submit an annual report to the Department of Education. The program is codified at NRS 363A.139, NRS 363B.119, and NRS 388D.250 through 388D.280.

events.instrument: Senate Bill 302, ch. 332, Statutes of Nevada 2015
events.summary: Chapter 332 of the Statutes of Nevada 2015, approved June 2, 2015, established a program under which a child receiving instruction from a participating entity rather than from a public school could receive a grant of money equal to the statewide average basic support per pupil, with the amount deducted from the apportionment to the child's school district. The act became effective July 1, 2015 for adopting regulations and performing preparatory administrative tasks and January 1, 2016 for all other purposes. The program was codified at NRS 353B.700 through 353B.930.

events.instrument: Schwartz v. Lopez, 132 Nev. Adv. Op. 73 (Nev. Sept. 29, 2016) (Nos. 69611, 70648)
events.summary: The Nevada Supreme Court decided consolidated appeals concerning the education savings account program created by Senate Bill 302. The court held that the program does not violate Article 11, Section 2, which requires a uniform system of common schools, and does not violate Article 11, Section 10, reasoning that the funds become private once deposited in the accounts. The court held that using money appropriated by Senate Bill 515 for K-12 public education in the State Distributive School Account to fund the education savings accounts violates Article 11, Sections 2 and 6, because Senate Bill 302 contained no independent appropriation. In No. 70648 the district court's dismissal was reversed and the matter remanded for entry of a permanent injunction; in No. 69611 the preliminary injunction was affirmed and the matter remanded for final declaratory judgment and permanent injunction.

events.instrument: Senate Bill 551, ch. 537, § 39.5, Statutes of Nevada 2019
events.summary: Chapter 537 of the Statutes of Nevada 2019, approved June 12, 2019, repealed NRS 353B.700, 353B.710, 353B.720, 353B.730, 353B.740, 353B.750, 353B.760, 353B.770, 353B.820, 353B.850, 353B.860, 353B.870, 353B.880, 353B.900, 353B.910, 353B.920, and 353B.930, together with NRS 388D.100 through 388D.140, effective July 1, 2019. Those sections comprised the education savings account program established by Senate Bill 302 of 2015, which the Legislature had never separately funded following the 2016 injunction.

events.instrument: N.H. Laws 2012, ch. 287, § 4 (RSA ch. 77-G, Education Tax Credit)
events.summary: The source notes to RSA chapter 77-G record that the education tax credit was enacted by 2012, 287:4, effective June 27, 2012. The chapter allows business taxpayers a credit against the business profits tax and the business enterprise tax for donations to scholarship organizations that award scholarships to students, including students attending nonpublic schools. The chapter was later amended in 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2021.

events.instrument: Bill Duncan v. State of New Hampshire, No. 2013-045 (N.H. Aug. 28, 2014)
events.summary: The New Hampshire Supreme Court considered a challenge to the education tax credit program under RSA chapter 77-G, including its use for scholarships to religious schools. The court did not reach the merits. It held that the 2012 amendment to RSA 491:22, I, which allowed taxpayers to sue without showing personal injury, violated Part II, Article 74 of the state constitution, and that without that amendment the petitioners lacked standing because the fiscal harm they alleged was the generalized wrong suffered by the public at large. The court vacated the trial court's ruling and remanded with instructions to dismiss the petition.

events.instrument: N.H. Laws 2021, ch. 91, § 431 (RSA ch. 194-F, Education Freedom Accounts)
events.summary: The source notes to RSA chapter 194-F record that the education freedom account program was enacted by 2021, 91:431, effective August 24, 2021. The commissioner of the department of education transfers to an approved scholarship organization the per pupil adequate education grant amount plus any differentiated aid that would have been provided to a public school for the student, and parents may use the account for enumerated qualifying expenses including tuition and fees at a private school, tutoring, instructional materials, and educational therapies. A signed agreement between the parent and the scholarship organization satisfies the compulsory attendance requirement of RSA 193:1.
The source notes to RSA 194-F:1 record an amendment by 2023, 110:1, effective August 26, 2023, altering the definitions that govern eligibility for the education freedom account program.

events.instrument: N.H. Laws 2025, ch. 75, §§ 1 to 6 (amending RSA 194-F:1 and 194-F:3)
events.summary: The source notes record amendments by 2025, 75:1, 2 to RSA 194-F:1 and by 2025, 75:3-5 to RSA 194-F:3, effective June 10, 2025. As amended, RSA 194-F:1, VI defines an eligible student as a resident of the state who is eligible to enroll in a public elementary or secondary school, other than a student in the special school district within the department of corrections. Section 75:6 repeals the definitions of priority guidelines and enrollment cap in RSA 194-F:1, XIII and XIV and the enrollment cap provisions in RSA 194-F:3, I-a and I-b, with those repeals effective on a contingency stated in 2025, 75:7. The statute as published shows both the pre-contingency and post-contingency versions of RSA 194-F:3, I.

events.instrument: N.H. Laws 2025, ch. 141, §§ 17 and 302 (amending RSA 194-F:2 and 194-F:3)
events.summary: The source notes to RSA 194-F record further amendments in the 2025 session by 2025, 141:17, effective June 27, 2025, and by 2025, 141:302, effective July 1, 2025, which amended the application provisions of RSA 194-F:3 and the program and qualifying expense provisions of RSA 194-F:2.

events.instrument: Secure Schools for All Children Act, P.L. 2016, c. 49 (N.J.S.A. 18A:58-37.8 to -37.14)
events.summary: The New Jersey Department of Education identifies the Secure Schools for All Children Act, P.L. 2016, c. 49, codified at N.J.S.A. 18A:58-37.8 through 37.14, as the statute governing the Nonpublic School Security Program, under which state security aid is provided for students enrolled in nonpublic schools and administered through the public school district in which the nonpublic school is located.

The New Mexico Supreme Court held that the plain meaning and history of Article XII, Section 3 of the New Mexico Constitution forbid the provision of books for use by students attending private schools, and that the Instructional Material Law violated that provision by supplying indirect financial support to private schools whether secular or sectarian. The court read Article XII, Section 3 as barring both direct and indirect support to private schools from funds appropriated, levied, or collected for educational purposes, and as more restrictive than the federal Establishment Clause.

events.instrument: Moses v. Ruszkowski, No. S-1-SC-34974 (N.M. Dec. 13, 2018)
events.summary: On remand after the United States Supreme Court vacated the 2015 decision and directed reconsideration in light of Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia, Inc. v. Comer, the New Mexico Supreme Court reversed its earlier position and held that the textbook loan program does not result in the use of public funds in support of private schools as prohibited by Article XII, Section 3. The majority reasoned that the program benefits students rather than schools, that any benefit to the institutions is incidental, and that reading Article XII, Section 3 to prohibit the lending raised Free Exercise Clause concerns. The court reinstated the provisions allowing private school participation in the Instructional Material Law. Two justices dissented.

events.instrument: 8 NYCRR Part 130, Substantially Equivalent Instruction for Nonpublic School Students
events.summary: The State Education Department submitted to the P-12 Education Committee, in an item dated September 1, 2022, the proposed addition of a new Part 130 of the Regulations of the Commissioner of Education relating to nonpublic schools and substantially equivalent instruction, recommending adoption as a permanent rule at the September 2022 meeting of the Board of Regents. The item records that a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking was published in the State Register on March 30, 2022 for a sixty-day comment period, that the Department received approximately 350,000 comments, that non-substantial revisions were made in response, and that if adopted at the September 2022 meeting the rule would become effective on September 28, 2022.

events.instrument: N.Y. Educ. Law § 3204(2), as amended effective May 16, 2025
events.summary: The published text of Education Law § 3204 shows a revision effective May 16, 2025. As revised, the section provides that instruction given to a minor elsewhere than at a public school shall be at least substantially equivalent to the instruction given at the public schools of the city or district where the minor resides, and sets out categories under which a nonpublic school satisfies that requirement, including a registered high school or a nonpublic school serving grades one through eight that has a registered high school, a state-approved private special education school or a school established under article eighty-five, eighty-seven, or eighty-eight, and a nonpublic school accredited or awarded provisional status by an accreditation body approved by the commissioner, with provisional status limited to the first five years. The section also allows a nonpublic school to satisfy the requirement by meeting stated assessment criteria, permits a school to elect different criteria at any time, and provides that satisfaction in one school year is not automatically satisfaction in later years. The section's published revision history records earlier revisions effective April 27, 2018, April 15, 2022, and July 8, 2022.

The General Assembly's bill record shows that Senate Bill 402 was signed by the Governor on July 26, 2013 and chaptered as Session Law 2013-360. Section 8.29(a) of that act created the Opportunity Scholarship Program at N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 115C-562.1 through 115C-562.8, under which the State Education Assistance Authority awards scholarship grants to eligible students to attend nonpublic schools.

The North Carolina Supreme Court reversed the trial court and upheld the Opportunity Scholarship Program, holding that no constitutional prohibition prevented the General Assembly from enacting legislation providing state funds for eligible lower-income students to attend private schools. The majority held that the program does not violate Article IX, Sections 2(1), 5, or 6, Article V, Sections 2(1) or 2(7), or Article I, Sections 15 or 19 of the North Carolina Constitution, and dissolved the injunction that had blocked implementation. Three justices dissented on the public purpose requirement, arguing that participating schools faced no substantive educational standards.

The North Carolina Supreme Court reversed the decision of the trial court in this case decided the same day as Hart v. State. The published case record establishes the docket number, the disposition reversing the trial court, and the decision date; the reasoning was not established from the record located.

The General Assembly's bill record shows that Senate Bill 257 was chaptered as Session Law 2017-57 on June 28, 2017 following a veto override. Section 10A.4(a) of that act created the personal education student account program at N.C. Gen. Stat. § 115C-595, under which the State Education Assistance Authority awards funds that parents of eligible students with disabilities may use for tuition, educational technology, therapies, and other enumerated expenses.

The General Assembly's bill record shows that Senate Bill 105 was signed by the Governor on November 18, 2021 and chaptered as Session Law 2021-180. Section 8A.3 of that act amended the scholarship grant statutes in Part 2A of Article 39 of Chapter 115C and the personal education student account statutes, including N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 115C-562.1 and 115C-595, restructuring the state's disability-related and income-based scholarship programs.

The enacted text of N.C. Gen. Stat. § 115C-562.1 records that subdivisions (3), (3c), and (5c), which had carried the income-based eligibility definitions, were repealed by Session Laws 2023-134, s. 8A.6(a), effective July 1, 2023, and that subdivision (3a) now defines an eligible student without reference to household income. The section's credit line records its enactment by Session Laws 2013-360, s. 8.29(a) and subsequent amendments in 2016, 2018, 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023.

events.instrument: N.C. Sess. Law 2023-134 (H.B. 259), § 8A.6(a) (amending N.C. Gen. Stat. § 115C-562.1)
events.summary: The General Assembly's bill record shows that House Bill 259 became law without the Governor's signature and was chaptered as Session Law 2023-134 on October 3, 2023. Section 8A.6(a) rewrote the eligibility definitions in N.C. Gen. Stat. § 115C-562.1 effective July 1, 2023, repealing the household income limits and defining an eligible student as any student residing in North Carolina who has not yet received a high school diploma, is eligible to attend a North Carolina public school, has not enrolled full time in a postsecondary institution, and has not been placed in a nonpublic school at public expense.

The General Assembly's bill record shows that House Bill 10 was ratified on September 11, 2024, vetoed by the Governor on September 20, 2024, and enacted over that veto, with the chapter action Ch. SL 2024-55 recorded on November 20, 2024. The act amended the scholarship grant statutes, including N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 115C-562.2, 115C-562.7, and 115C-562.8, and contained appropriations directed in part to the Opportunity Scholarship Grant Fund Reserve.

events.instrument: North Dakota Senate Bill 2237 (68th Legislative Assembly, 2023)
events.summary: The Legislative Assembly's official action record shows that Senate Bill 2237, which was reported out of the Senate Finance and Taxation Committee with a do-not-pass recommendation, passed the Senate and was then reported back in the House with a do-not-pass recommendation and failed to pass on second reading in the House on March 17, 2023 by 14 yeas to 78 nays. The measure is recorded as Failed.

events.instrument: North Dakota House Bill 1540 (69th Legislative Assembly, 2025)
events.summary: The Legislative Assembly's official action record shows that House Bill 1540 passed the House on February 13, 2025 by 49 yeas to 38 nays, passed the Senate as amended on April 17, 2025 by 27 yeas to 20 nays, and passed the House again on concurrence on April 21, 2025 by 49 yeas to 43 nays. The bill was sent to the Governor on April 23, 2025 and vetoed by the Governor the same day. On April 25, 2025 the House considered the veto and the veto was sustained by 45 yeas to 48 nays. The measure is recorded as Failed.

Article VI, Section 2 of the Ohio Constitution, effective September 1, 1851, directs the General Assembly to make provisions by taxation or otherwise that, with the income from the school trust fund, will secure a thorough and efficient system of common schools throughout the state, and provides that no religious or other sect or sects shall ever have any exclusive right to, or control of, any part of the school funds of this state. No amendment to this section is recorded on the official text.

events.instrument: Am.Sub.H.B. No. 117, 146 Ohio Laws, Part I, 898 (1995)
events.summary: The Ohio Supreme Court's opinion in Simmons-Harris v. Goff records that on June 28, 1995 the General Assembly adopted Am.Sub.H.B. No. 117, the biennial operating appropriations bill for fiscal years 1996 and 1997, reported at 146 Ohio Laws, Part I, 898. That act contained the Pilot Project Scholarship Program, which provided scholarships for students in the Cleveland City School District to attend participating private schools.

events.instrument: Simmons-Harris v. Goff, 86 Ohio St.3d 1, 1999-Ohio-77 (Ohio May 27, 1999)
events.summary: The Ohio Supreme Court held that the School Voucher Program violated the one-subject rule of Section 15(D), Article II of the Ohio Constitution because a substantive educational program was included in a general appropriations bill. The court rejected the challenges brought under the federal Establishment Clause, Section 7, Article I of the Ohio Constitution, the school funds clause of Section 2, Article VI, the thorough and efficient education clause, and the uniformity clause of Section 26, Article II, reasoning that funds reached religious schools through the choices of parents. The court held R.C. 3313.977(A)(1)(d), which allowed enrollment priority based on parental religious affiliation, unconstitutional and severable.

events.instrument: Ohio Autism Scholarship Program, Ohio Rev. Code §§ 3310.41 to 3310.43
events.summary: A national association's program page records that the Ohio Autism Scholarship Program was enacted in 2003 and launched in 2004, and that it is governed by Ohio Revised Code sections 3310.41 through 3310.43. The program provides scholarships for children with autism to receive special education and related services from an approved provider, including a chartered nonpublic school. The enacting session law was not located in a primary source.

The official code shows that the earliest published version of Ohio Revised Code section 3310.51, which establishes the Jon Peterson special needs scholarship program, took effect September 29, 2011 under House Bill 153 of the 129th General Assembly. The section was later amended by House Bill 110 of the 134th General Assembly effective September 30, 2021, by House Bill 33 of the 135th General Assembly effective October 3, 2023, and by House Bill 96 of the 136th General Assembly effective September 30, 2025.

The official code shows that the earliest published version of Ohio Revised Code section 3310.032, which establishes the expansion of the educational choice scholarship pilot program on income-based eligibility, took effect September 29, 2013 under House Bill 59 of the 130th General Assembly. Under division (C) the expansion began with students entering kindergarten in the 2013-2014 school year and added a grade level in each subsequent year through the 2019-2020 school year, and from the 2020-2021 school year applied to eligible students entering any of grades kindergarten through twelve for the first time.

events.instrument: Ohio Rev. Code §§ 5747.72, 5747.73, and 5747.75 (H.B. 110, 134th General Assembly)
events.summary: The official code shows that Ohio Revised Code sections 5747.72, 5747.73, and 5747.75 were each enacted by House Bill 110 of the 134th General Assembly effective September 30, 2021. Section 5747.72 provides an income tax credit for home education expenses, section 5747.73 provides a credit for donations to scholarship granting organizations, and section 5747.75 provides a credit for tuition paid to a nonchartered nonpublic school. Sections 5747.72 and 5747.75 were amended by House Bill 33 of the 135th General Assembly effective October 3, 2023, and section 5747.72 was further amended by House Bill 96 of the 136th General Assembly effective September 30, 2025.

events.instrument: Ohio Rev. Code § 3310.032, as amended by H.B. 33, 135th General Assembly
events.summary: The version of Ohio Revised Code section 3310.032 effective October 3, 2023 under House Bill 33 of the 135th General Assembly defines an eligible student for the expansion of the educational choice scholarship pilot program as a student whose resident district is not a district in which the Cleveland pilot project scholarship program operates and who is entering any of grades kindergarten through twelve, without a stated household income ceiling in the eligibility definition. Scholarships are paid to attend chartered nonpublic schools in accordance with section 3317.022, and the number awarded may not exceed the number that can be funded as authorized by the General Assembly. A student who receives a scholarship remains eligible in later years even if family income rises, provided the student remains enrolled in a chartered nonpublic school. The same act amended the Cleveland pilot program section, 3313.974, effective the same day.

The official code shows that Ohio Revised Code section 3301.0732 was enacted by House Bill 33 of the 135th General Assembly effective October 3, 2023. The section places in statute the minimum education standards applicable to nonchartered nonpublic schools, which had previously been prescribed only by rule.

The version of Ohio Administrative Code rule 3301-35-08 effective May 9, 2024 governs nonchartered, non-tax supported schools. It requires a nonchartered nonpublic school that is not seeking a charter because of truly held religious beliefs to certify annually to the parents of its pupils that the school meets the minimum education standards described in Ohio Revised Code section 3301.0732, and to file a copy of that report with the department of education and workforce on or before the thirtieth day of September each year. The rule also sets minimum hours of instruction by grade level.

events.instrument: Columbus City School District v. State, Franklin County Court of Common Pleas No. 2022-CV-000067
events.summary: An Ohio Senate publication records that on June 24, 2025 Franklin County Court of Common Pleas Judge Jaiza Page ruled that Ohio's school voucher program is unconstitutional, that the judge stayed her own ruling so that the program continues while the case is appealed, and that on July 25, 2025 the Attorney General and the Speaker of the House announced that the state would appeal. The publication states the expectation that the case will proceed to the Tenth District Court of Appeals and then to the Ohio Supreme Court.

events.instrument: Lindsey Nicole Henry Scholarships for Students with Disabilities Act, Okla. Stat. tit. 70 § 13-101.2
events.summary: Oklahoma created the Lindsey Nicole Henry Scholarships for Students with Disabilities, a voucher program codified at Okla. Stat. tit. 70 § 13-101.2. The program pays state funds to private schools, including religious schools, chosen by the parents of eligible students with disabilities. The enacting bill number is not given by the source consulted.

events.instrument: Oklahoma Equal Opportunity Education Scholarship Act, Okla. Stat. tit. 68 § 2357.206
events.summary: Oklahoma created a tax-credit scholarship program codified at Okla. Stat. tit. 68 § 2357.206. Private donors contribute to scholarship granting organizations and receive state income tax credits for their donations, subject to statutory limits, and the organizations award scholarships to eligible students attending participating private schools.

The Oklahoma Supreme Court held that the Lindsey Nicole Henry Scholarships for Students with Disabilities Act does not violate the no-aid clause at article II, section 5 of the Oklahoma Constitution when scholarship funds reach sectarian schools. The court reversed the trial court's contrary determination in part, reasoning that the program is religiously neutral, that participation is voluntary, and that parents rather than the state select the school. The court did not reach the defendants' second issue.

events.instrument: House Bill 1934 (2023), Oklahoma Parental Choice Tax Credit Act, Okla. Stat. tit. 70 §§ 28-100 to 28-103
events.summary: Governor Kevin Stitt signed House Bill 1934 into law on 25 May 2023, creating the Oklahoma Parental Choice Tax Credit Act. The act establishes a refundable income tax credit of $5,000 to $7,500 per student for private school tuition and fees, graduated by household adjusted gross income, and a credit of up to $1,000 per student for homeschool expenses. The credit first became available for tax year 2024, and the Oklahoma Tax Commission administers it.

The Oklahoma Legislature amended the Parental Choice Tax Credit Act during the 2024 session through House Bill 3388. The program operates under annual caps of $150 million for tax year 2024, $200 million for tax year 2025, and $250 million thereafter, with a separate $5 million annual cap on homeschool credits, and families with household incomes below $75,000 receive priority in the allocation of credits.

events.instrument: Drummond ex rel. State v. Oklahoma Statewide Virtual Charter School Board, 2024 OK 53 (No. 121694)
events.summary: The Oklahoma Supreme Court granted the Attorney General's request for a writ of mandamus and declaratory relief and directed the Statewide Virtual Charter School Board to rescind its charter contract with St. Isidore of Seville Catholic Virtual School. The court held that St. Isidore would be a governmental entity and a state actor, and that the contract violated article II, section 5 and article I, section 5 of the Oklahoma Constitution, the nonsectarian requirement of the Oklahoma Charter Schools Act at 70 O.S. § 3-132, and the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment.

events.instrument: Lindsey Nicole Henry Scholarships for Students with Disabilities Act, Okla. Stat. tit. 70 § 13-101.2, as amended in 2025
events.summary: Legislation enacted in Oklahoma in 2025 removed the requirement that a participant in the Lindsey Nicole Henry Scholarship program first attend a public school. The bill number and the date of enactment are not given by the source consulted.

The Oklahoma House of Representatives reported on 6 May 2026 that House Bill 3705 became law, raising the annual cap on the Parental Choice Tax Credit from $250 million to $275 million beginning in fiscal year 2027. Credits remain set at $5,000 to $7,500 per student for private school tuition according to household income, and at $1,000 per student for homeschool expenses.

events.instrument: Educational Improvement Tax Credit Program, 24 Pa. Stat. §§ 20-2001-B to 20-2013-B
events.summary: Pennsylvania created the Educational Improvement Tax Credit Program, codified at 24 Pa. Stat. sections 20-2001-B through 20-2013-B. Businesses receive state tax credits for contributions to scholarship organizations, educational improvement organizations, and pre-kindergarten scholarship organizations, and those organizations award scholarships that families may use at nonpublic schools, including religious schools. The Department of Community and Economic Development administers the program.

events.instrument: Opportunity Scholarship Tax Credit Program, 24 Pa. Stat. §§ 20-2001-B to 20-2013-B
events.summary: Pennsylvania created the Opportunity Scholarship Tax Credit Program, a second tax-credit scholarship codified within 24 Pa. Stat. sections 20-2001-B through 20-2013-B and directed at students residing in the attendance boundary of a low-achieving school. Donors receive credits equal to 75 percent of a contribution, or 90 percent for a two-year pledge, capped at $750,000 per business a year. Scholarship granting organizations may award up to $8,500 for a general education student, with higher limits for students with special needs and for students from economically disadvantaged school populations.

events.instrument: Tax Credits for Contributions to Scholarship Organizations, R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 44-62-1 to 44-62-7
events.summary: Rhode Island created a tax-credit scholarship program at R.I. Gen. Laws sections 44-62-1 through 44-62-7. Businesses receive a credit equal to 75 percent of a donation to a scholarship granting organization, or 90 percent where the business commits for two consecutive years and the second donation exceeds 80 percent of the first, subject to a $100,000 annual limit per business and a statewide cap of $1.6 million in credits. Students must come from households below 250 percent of the federal poverty level, and scholarship granting organizations must direct at least 90 percent of revenues to tuition assistance.

events.instrument: Educational Credit for Exceptional Needs Children Fund, S.C. Code Ann. § 12-6-3790
events.summary: South Carolina created a tax-credit scholarship program at S.C. Code Ann. § 12-6-3790 under which donors contribute to scholarship granting organizations in exchange for state tax credits. Scholarships go to students with disabilities or other qualifying conditions who attend eligible independent schools, capped at the lesser of $11,000 or tuition, and the program carries a $12 million annual cap on credits. The program launched in 2014.

events.instrument: Refundable Educational Credit for Exceptional Needs Children, S.C. Code Ann. § 12-6-3790(H)(2)
events.summary: South Carolina created a refundable tax credit at S.C. Code Ann. § 12-6-3790(H)(2) for families of children with exceptional needs who attend independent schools. The credit equals the lesser of $11,000 per student or the school's tuition and fees, and the program has no enrollment cap. Qualifying conditions include autism spectrum disorder, deaf-blindness, deafness or hearing impairment, and developmental delay.

events.instrument: Education Scholarship Trust Fund Act, 2023 S.C. Act No. 8 (S. 39), S.C. Code Ann. §§ 59-8-110 to 59-8-170
events.summary: South Carolina enacted the Education Scholarship Trust Fund Act as 2023 Act No. 8 (S. 39), codified at S.C. Code Ann. sections 59-8-110 through 59-8-170. The act established a fund providing scholarships to qualifying students for a defined list of educational expenses, which as enacted included tuition and fees at nonpublic educational institutions and at approved nonpublic online education service providers. The exact date of enactment is not established by the source consulted.

events.instrument: Eidson v. South Carolina Department of Education, Op. No. 28235 (S.C. 2024)
events.summary: The South Carolina Supreme Court held that parts of the Education Scholarship Trust Fund Act violate article XI, section 4 of the South Carolina Constitution, which forbids the use of public funds for the direct benefit of any religious or other private educational institution. The court declared unconstitutional and severed S.C. Code Ann. § 59-8-110(13)(e) and the portions of § 59-8-110(13)(a) and (l) that allowed scholarships to pay tuition and fees at nonpublic institutions, and it enjoined the Department of Education from disbursing scholarships for private school tuition and fees. The court upheld the provisions permitting scholarship funds to pay for tutoring, computer assistance, therapies for students with disabilities, and transportation.

events.instrument: 2025 South Carolina legislation redesigning the Education Scholarship Trust Fund program
events.summary: The South Carolina General Assembly enacted legislation in 2025 that restored the use of Education Scholarship Trust Fund awards for tuition at private schools and approved providers following the restriction imposed by the state supreme court in 2024. The bill number, the act number, and the date of enactment are not given by the source consulted, and the redesigned program has not been tested against article XI, section 4 in any retrieved decision.

events.instrument: Partners in Education Tax Credit Program, S.D. Codified Laws §§ 13-65-1 to 13-65-12
events.summary: South Dakota created the Partners in Education Tax Credit Program at S.D. Codified Laws sections 13-65-1 through 13-65-12. Insurance companies receive a tax credit equal to the full amount of donations made to scholarship granting organizations, subject to a $5 million annual cap on credits. Eligible students come from households below 150 percent of the free and reduced lunch threshold, continuing participants may remain if household income reaches 200 percent of that threshold at reapplication, and all foster children qualify without regard to income. Average scholarships may not exceed 82.5 percent of the state's per-pupil allocation share.

events.instrument: Individualized Education Account Program, Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 49-10-1401 to 49-10-1406
events.summary: Tennessee created the Individualized Education Account Program at Tenn. Code Ann. sections 49-10-1401 through 49-10-1406. The program provides education savings accounts to students with disabilities who hold an individualized education program and a qualifying diagnosis, subject to prior enrollment requirements, with account values capped at the state and local funding the student would have received in a district public school.

events.instrument: Tennessee Education Savings Account Pilot Program, Tenn. Code Ann. § 49-6-2601
events.summary: Tennessee created the Education Savings Account Pilot Program at Tenn. Code Ann. section 49-6-2601. The Tennessee Department of Education administers the program under State Board of Education Rule 0520-01-16, and it serves students zoned to schools in Memphis-Shelby County Schools, Metro Nashville Public Schools, Hamilton County Schools, and schools formerly in the Achievement School District as of 24 May 2019. Participants may direct state and local money toward tuition and fees at approved participating nonpublic schools.

events.instrument: Metropolitan Government of Nashville and Davidson County v. Tennessee Department of Education, No. M2020-00683-SC-R11-CV (Tenn. 2022)
events.summary: The Tennessee Supreme Court reversed the lower courts and held that the Education Savings Account Pilot Program does not trigger the Home Rule Amendment, reasoning that the statute governs local education agencies rather than the county and municipal governments themselves and that the act's effect on county funding does not make it applicable to those governments. The court affirmed that the plaintiffs had standing, vacated the trial court's judgment that the act was unconstitutional, and remanded with directions to dismiss the Home Rule claim and to take up the remaining constitutional claims concerning equal protection and the education provisions.

events.instrument: Remanded claims against the Tennessee Education Savings Account Pilot Program, Tenn. Code Ann. § 49-6-2601
events.summary: After the trial court dismissed the claims remaining on remand, the Tennessee Court of Appeals reversed that dismissal as to some claims in January 2024, and those claims returned to the trial court. The constitutional challenges to the Education Savings Account Pilot Program other than the Home Rule claim are outstanding, and no final judgment has been verified against a retrieved primary source.

events.instrument: Tennessee Education Freedom Scholarship Act, Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 49-6-3501 to 49-6-3512
events.summary: Tennessee enacted the Education Freedom Scholarship Act, codified at Tenn. Code Ann. sections 49-6-3501 through 49-6-3512, creating a statewide education savings account that began in the 2025-2026 school year. Half of the available accounts are reserved for families at or below 300 percent of the federal poverty level, families already eligible for other state choice programs, or families with a child who has a state-recognized disability, and the remaining half are open to all Tennessee families with eligible school-age children. The maximum account value for 2025-2026 is $7,296, funds must first be applied to private school tuition and fees, unused funds roll over, and the student cap rises by 5,000 each year in which more than 75 percent of scholarships are awarded. The enacting bill number and the date of enactment are not given by the source consulted.

events.instrument: Texas Education Savings Account Program, Tex. Educ. Code §§ 29.351 to 29.374
events.summary: Texas enacted an education savings account program codified at Texas Education Code sections 29.351 through 29.374, with conforming provisions at sections 22.092, 411.109, and 811.002. All Texas K-12 students are eligible, and a student need not have attended a public school in the state first. The program carries an initial appropriation of $1 billion and launches in the fall of 2026, most participants are to receive approximately $10,500 a year with larger amounts for students with special needs, accounts for homeschooled students are capped at $2,000, up to 90,000 accounts may be awarded in the first year under a multi-tiered priority system, and participants in grades three through twelve attending a private school must take a nationally norm-referenced examination each year. The enacting bill number and the date of enactment are not given by the source consulted.

The Supreme Court held that a federally funded program providing supplemental, remedial instruction to disadvantaged children on a neutral basis is not invalid under the Establishment Clause when public employees deliver the instruction on the premises of religious schools. The Court overruled Aguilar v. Felton, 473 U.S. 402, and the portion of School District of Grand Rapids v. Ball, 473 U.S. 373, addressing the Shared Time program. The decision restored the delivery of Title I services inside religious school buildings, which the 1985 decisions had ended.

The Supreme Court held that Chapter 2 of the Education Consolidation and Improvement Act, which lends educational materials and equipment to public and private schools on the basis of enrollment, does not violate the Establishment Clause. The plurality asked whether the program results in governmental indoctrination, defines its recipients by reference to religion, or creates excessive entanglement. The decision overruled Meek v. Pittenger and Wolman v. Walter, which had barred the lending of instructional materials and equipment to religious schools.

events.instrument: No Child Left Behind Act of 2001, Pub. L. 107-110, tit. I, sec. 101, 115 Stat. 1508 (ESEA sec. 1117, codified at 20 U.S.C. 6320)
events.summary: The No Child Left Behind Act restated and expanded the equitable services obligation of section 1117 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act. A local educational agency must, after timely and meaningful consultation with private school officials, provide eligible private school children with special educational, instructional, counseling, mentoring, tutoring, and other services on an equitable basis, and must ensure that their teachers and families participate on an equitable basis. Expenditures for those services must equal the proportion of funds allocated to participating school attendance areas based on the number of children from low-income families who attend private schools. The provision is the principal channel through which federal Title I money reaches students in religious schools.

The Supreme Court upheld the Cleveland Pilot Project Scholarship Program against an Establishment Clause challenge. The Court held that a program of true private choice, neutral toward religion, which provides aid to a broad class of citizens who then direct that aid to religious or secular schools by their own independent decisions, does not offend the Establishment Clause. The proportion of participating students enrolled in religious schools was held not to be constitutionally decisive. This decision is the constitutional foundation on which subsequent state voucher and scholarship programs were built.

events.instrument: DC School Choice Incentive Act of 2003, Pub. L. 108-199, div. C, tit. III, 118 Stat. 126
events.summary: Congress created the District of Columbia Opportunity Scholarship Program as Title III of Division C of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2004. The Act appropriated $14,000,000 to the Secretary of Education to provide opportunity scholarships for students in the District of Columbia, of which up to $1,000,000 could be used to administer and fund assessments. The appropriation formed one part of a three-part funding arrangement that also provided $13,000,000 for the District of Columbia public schools and $13,000,000 to expand public charter schools. This is the only federally funded private school voucher program for elementary and secondary students.

The Supreme Court held that Washington State may exclude students pursuing a devotional theology degree from its Promise Scholarship Program without violating the Free Exercise Clause. The Court described the exclusion as falling within the play in the joints between the Establishment Clause and the Free Exercise Clause: permitted by the first, but not required by the second. The Ninth Circuit judgment for the student was reversed. This is a loss for the religious claimant, and states relied on it for more than a decade to defend exclusions of religious institutions from public funding programs.

events.instrument: Individuals with Disabilities Education Improvement Act of 2004, Pub. L. 108-446, tit. I, sec. 101 (codified at 20 U.S.C. 1412(a)(10)(A))
events.summary: The 2004 reauthorization of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act set the terms on which children with disabilities enrolled by their parents in private schools participate in federally assisted special education. Local educational agencies must spend a proportionate amount of federal funds on such children, must conduct child find for children in private, including religious, schools, and must consult with private school representatives and parent representatives on the child find process, the proportionate share calculation, and how and where services will be delivered. Services may be provided on the premises of private, including religious, schools to the extent consistent with law, but must be secular, neutral, and nonideological, and control of the funds must remain with a public agency.

events.instrument: Arizona Christian School Tuition Organization v. Winn, 563 U.S. 125 (2011)
events.summary: The Supreme Court held that Arizona taxpayers lacked Article III standing under Flast v. Cohen to challenge the state's tax credit for contributions to school tuition organizations, because the challenge was directed at a tax credit rather than at a governmental expenditure. The Ninth Circuit judgment, which had found standing and a viable Establishment Clause claim, was reversed. The decision did not reach the merits of the Establishment Clause question, and it narrowed the route by which taxpayers may contest tax credit scholarship programs in federal court.
