events.instrument: Scholarships for Opportunity and Results Act, Pub. L. 112-10, div. C, 125 Stat. 199
events.summary: Congress reauthorized the District of Columbia Opportunity Scholarship Program as Division C of the Department of Defense and Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011. The findings state that the program was established in accordance with Zelman v. Simmons-Harris, 536 U.S. 639, that the program has consistently been oversubscribed, and that studies by the Institute of Education Sciences found improvements in parental satisfaction, in reading scores among students consistently using the scholarships, and in graduation rates. The stated purpose is to give low-income parents in the District of Columbia expanded opportunities to enroll their children in other schools.

events.instrument: Hosanna-Tabor Evangelical Lutheran Church and School v. EEOC, 565 U.S. 171 (2012)
events.summary: The Supreme Court recognized a ministerial exception, grounded in the Religion Clauses of the First Amendment, that bars employment discrimination claims brought by a minister against the religious group that employs her. The case arose from a called teacher at a Lutheran school who brought a claim under the Americans with Disabilities Act. The Court held that the exception applied to her and that the courts may not intrude on a religious group's decision about who will personify its beliefs and teach its faith.

events.instrument: Every Student Succeeds Act, Pub. L. 114-95, tit. I, secs. 1000(3), 1011, 129 Stat. 1814 (ESEA sec. 1117, codified at 20 U.S.C. 6320)
events.summary: The Every Student Succeeds Act amended the equitable services provisions of section 1117 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act. The amended text provides that the proportional share of funds is determined on the total amount received by the local educational agency under Title I, Part A before any allowable expenditures or transfers by the agency, and permits the agency to determine the equitable share annually or every two years. It expanded the list of subjects on which consultation with private school officials must occur, and required that the results of consultation be transmitted to a designated state ombudsman.

events.instrument: SOAR Reauthorization Act, Pub. L. 115-31, div. E, tit. IX, 131 Stat. 394
events.summary: Congress reauthorized and amended the Scholarships for Opportunity and Results Act in Title IX of Division E of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2017. Section 902 repealed section 817 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2016, and restored the provisions that section had amended or repealed. Section 903 redirected the program's stated purpose toward parents of students attending schools identified as lowest-performing under the District of Columbia accountability system. Section 904 added a provision prohibiting the Secretary from limiting the number of eligible students receiving scholarships.

events.instrument: Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia, Inc. v. Comer, 582 U.S. 449 (2017)
events.summary: The Supreme Court held that Missouri's categorical exclusion of a church-operated preschool from a generally available playground resurfacing grant program violated the Free Exercise Clause. Denying a generally available benefit solely on account of religious identity imposes a penalty on the free exercise of religion that must survive the most rigorous scrutiny. The preschool had ranked fifth among forty-four applicants and was denied on the basis of its church operation. The decision opened the line of cases governing religious institutions' access to public benefit programs.

events.instrument: CARES Act sec. 18005, Pub. L. 116-136, 134 Stat. 281
events.summary: Section 18005 of the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act required a local educational agency receiving funds under the Governor's Emergency Education Relief Fund or the Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief Fund to provide equitable services in the same manner as provided under section 1117 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act to students and teachers in non-public schools, as determined in consultation with representatives of non-public schools. Subsection (b) required that control of the funds, and title to materials, equipment, and property purchased with them, remain in a public agency. The meaning of the phrase in the same manner became the subject of rulemaking and litigation later in 2020.

events.instrument: SBA interim final rule, Business Loan Program Temporary Changes; Paycheck Protection Program, 85 FR 20817
events.summary: The Small Business Administration's first interim final rule implementing the Paycheck Protection Program exempted otherwise qualified faith-based organizations from the agency's affiliation rules, including those in 13 CFR part 121, where application of those rules would substantially burden the organizations' religious exercise. The rule stated that the exemption is required, or at a minimum authorized, by the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, and it reasoned that the organizational structure of faith-based entities may itself be a matter of religious concern. The exemption allowed churches, dioceses, and affiliated schools to apply without aggregating employees across affiliated entities.

events.instrument: SBA interim final rule, Business Loan Program Temporary Changes; Paycheck Protection Program - Nondiscrimination and Additional Eligibility Criteria, 85 FR 27287
events.summary: The Small Business Administration issued an interim final rule providing that, for purposes of the Paycheck Protection Program, nonprofit borrowers must meet their nondiscrimination obligations under existing federal laws and executive orders rather than under agency regulations that did not restate statutory limitations and exemptions. The rule addressed the single-sex admissions permission for preschools and non-vocational elementary and secondary schools under Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, the coreligionist housing provision of the Fair Housing Act, and a discrepancy between the agency's religious employer exemption at 13 CFR 113.3-1(h) and section 702 of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act. It was effective on 8 May 2020.

events.instrument: Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue, 591 U.S. 464 (2020)
events.summary: The Supreme Court held that applying Montana's constitutional no-aid provision to bar religious schools from a tax credit scholarship program violated the Free Exercise Clause. The exclusion imposed a disability on the basis of religious status and did not survive strict scrutiny. The Montana Supreme Court had invalidated the entire scholarship program rather than sever the religious exclusion; that judgment was reversed and the case remanded. The decision restricts the operation of state Blaine and anti-aid provisions against religious schools in publicly supported scholarship programs.

events.instrument: Department of Education interim final rule, CARES Act Programs; Equitable Services to Students and Teachers in Non-Public Schools, 85 FR 39479 (34 CFR 76.665)
events.summary: The Department of Education issued an interim final rule, effective on the day of publication, interpreting the CARES Act requirement that local educational agencies provide equitable services to students and teachers in non-public schools. The rule added 34 CFR 76.665, applying the consultation framework of section 1117(b) of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act to the CARES Act programs and permitting methods of calculating the proportional share other than the Title I low-income formula. The Department waived notice and comment and the delayed effective date on grounds of the pandemic emergency.

events.instrument: Our Lady of Guadalupe School v. Morrissey-Berru, 591 U.S. 732 (2020)
events.summary: The Supreme Court held that the ministerial exception barred employment discrimination claims by two teachers at Catholic elementary schools who taught religion, prayed with students, and were expected to template the faith, even though they lacked the title of minister and had limited formal religious training. The Court stated that what matters is what an employee does, and it rejected a rigid checklist drawn from Hosanna-Tabor. The Ninth Circuit judgments in both consolidated cases were reversed and remanded. The decision extends religious employment autonomy to a broad class of religious school teachers.

events.instrument: National Association for the Advancement of Colored People v. DeVos, No. 20-cv-1996 (DLF) (D.D.C. 4 Sept. 2020)
events.summary: The United States District Court for the District of Columbia granted the plaintiffs' expedited motion for summary judgment against the Department of Education's interim final rule at 85 FR 39479, holding the rule unlawful. The opinion records that the plaintiffs acknowledged that none of their remaining claims would survive if the rule were vacated, and it quotes the rule that when a reviewing court determines that agency regulations are unlawful, the ordinary result is that the rules are vacated rather than that their application to individual petitioners is proscribed. Section 76.665 does not appear in the current Code of Federal Regulations. This is a reversal of a federal action that had increased the share of pandemic relief flowing to non-public school students.

events.instrument: Department of Education final rule, Direct Grant Programs, State-Administered Formula Grant Programs, and related programs, 85 FR 59916 (34 CFR 75.500, 76.500)
events.summary: The Department of Education issued a final rule, effective 23 November 2020, amending 34 CFR 75.500 and 76.500 to address constitutional rights, free inquiry, and grant conditions. The rule added provisions at 34 CFR 75.500(d) and 76.500(d) governing religious student organizations at public institutions of higher education that receive a direct grant from the Department or a subgrant under a state-administered formula grant program, and it added free inquiry conditions applicable to grantees. The state-administered formula grant provisions reach programs through which elementary and secondary education funds are distributed.

events.instrument: Equal Participation of Faith-Based Organizations in the Federal Agencies' Programs and Activities, 85 FR 82037
events.summary: Nine federal agencies, including the Department of Education, issued a joint final rule on the participation of faith-based organizations in federal programs and activities, effective 19 January 2021. The rule implements Executive Order 13831 and revised each agency's regulations governing the terms on which religious organizations may receive federal financial assistance and the notice and referral requirements applied to them. It is the governing federal framework for religious providers that receive federal grants, including religious schools and school-affiliated organizations.

events.instrument: CRRSAA sec. 312(a)(2), (d), Pub. L. 116-260, div. M, 134 Stat. 1925
events.summary: The Coronavirus Response and Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2021 created the Emergency Assistance to Non-Public Schools program. Section 312(a)(2) reserved $2,750,000,000 for allotments to governors to provide services or assistance to non-public schools, and section 312(d) set the program terms. A state's allotment is proportional to the number of children aged five through seventeen at or below 185 percent of poverty enrolled in non-public schools in the state. Governors were required to apply, and the Secretary was required to issue a notice inviting applications within thirty days of enactment and to act on applications within fifteen days of receipt.

events.instrument: American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 sec. 2002, Pub. L. 117-2, 135 Stat. 23
events.summary: Section 2002 of the American Rescue Plan Act appropriated a further $2,750,000,000 to the Department of Education for fiscal year 2021, available through 30 September 2023, for allocations to governors under the Emergency Assistance to Non-Public Schools program, to provide services or assistance to non-public schools that enroll a significant percentage of low-income students and are most affected by the qualifying emergency. Subsection (b) provides that these funds may not be used to reimburse any non-public school. Together with the $2,750,000,000 reserved by the Coronavirus Response and Relief Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2021, the two appropriations total $5,500,000,000.

events.instrument: Peltier v. Charter Day School, Inc., No. 20-1001 (4th Cir. 14 June 2022) (en banc)
events.summary: Sitting en banc, the Fourth Circuit held that in operating a school that is part of the North Carolina public school system, a charter school performs a function traditionally and exclusively reserved to the state, and that the charter school acted under color of state law for purposes of 42 U.S.C. 1983. The court reached a different conclusion as to the school's for-profit management contractor. The Supreme Court denied the charter school's petition for a writ of certiorari on 26 June 2023 in Charter Day School, Inc. v. Peltier, No. 22-238, after inviting and receiving the views of the Solicitor General. The state action holding bears directly on whether a charter school may be operated by a religious entity.

The Supreme Court held that Maine's requirement that schools receiving town tuitioning payments be nonsectarian violates the Free Exercise Clause. Once a state elects to pay tuition for students at private schools, it may not disqualify some private schools solely because they are religious. The Court rejected the distinction between religious status and religious use on which the First Circuit had relied, and reversed and remanded that judgment. The decision extends Espinoza from a tax credit scholarship program to a direct tuition payment program.

events.instrument: SBA final rule, Regulatory Reform Initiative: Streamlining and Modernizing the 7(a), Microloan, and 504 Loan Programs, 87 FR 38900 (removing 13 CFR 120.110(k))
events.summary: The Small Business Administration removed paragraph (k) of 13 CFR 120.110, which had made businesses principally engaged in teaching, instructing, counseling, or indoctrinating religion or religious beliefs ineligible for agency financial assistance. The rule states that the removal was proposed on the basis of Trinity Lutheran and the principle that government may not deny a public benefit to an entity solely because of its religious status, character, or identity. Of the 2,667 unique comments received, 2,651 concerned the removal and all but one opposed it. The paragraph is now reserved in the Code of Federal Regulations, so religious schools are eligible for the agency's standing loan programs and not only for pandemic-era programs.

events.instrument: Fellowship of Christian Athletes v. San Jose Unified School District Board of Education, No. 22-15827 (9th Cir. 13 Sept. 2023) (en banc)
events.summary: Sitting en banc, the Ninth Circuit reversed the denial of a preliminary injunction and directed the district court to enter an order reinstating the Fellowship of Christian Athletes as an official approved student club. The district had revoked the club's status because the organization requires its student leaders to affirm a statement of faith that includes the belief that sexual relations should be within a marriage between a man and a woman. The en banc court held that the plaintiffs had standing, that their claims were not moot, and that they were entitled to preliminary relief on their free exercise and free speech claims.

events.instrument: Partnerships With Faith-Based and Neighborhood Organizations, 89 FR 15671
events.summary: Nine federal agencies, including the Department of Education, issued a joint final rule revising the 2020 regulations on the participation of faith-based organizations in federal programs. The rule was effective on 3 April 2024. It amends the framework established at 85 FR 82037 that governs the terms on which religious organizations receive federal financial assistance, including provisions on notice to beneficiaries and referral to alternative providers.

events.instrument: Loffman v. California Department of Education, No. 23-55714 (9th Cir. 28 Oct. 2024)
events.summary: The Ninth Circuit held that parent plaintiffs plausibly alleged that California's requirement that a private school be nonsectarian in order to be certified as a nonpublic school serving students with disabilities under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act violates the Free Exercise Clause. The statute burdens parents on its face by prohibiting them from advocating for a sectarian placement, is not neutral toward religion, and the state did not demonstrate that the requirement satisfies strict scrutiny or is narrowly tailored. The panel affirmed the dismissal of the school plaintiffs' and one family's claims for lack of standing, reversed the dismissal of the parent plaintiffs' free exercise and equal protection claims, vacated the denial of a preliminary injunction, and remanded.

events.instrument: Department of Education withdrawal of proposed rule, Direct Grant Programs, State-Administered Formula Grant Programs; Withdrawal, 89 FR 104935 (withdrawing 88 FR 10857)
events.summary: The Department of Education withdrew, as of 20 December 2024, the notice of proposed rulemaking published at 88 FR 10857 on 22 February 2023. That proposal would have rescinded the regulations on religious student organizations at public institutions of higher education that receive a direct grant from the Department or a subgrant under a state-administered formula grant program, which the Department had adopted at 85 FR 59916. The withdrawal left the 2020 provisions in force.

events.instrument: IRS Notice 2025-70, Request for Comments on Individual Tax Credit for Qualified Contributions to Scholarship Granting Organizations
events.summary: The Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service announced their intention to issue proposed regulations implementing 26 U.S.C. 25F and requested public comments on the issues that guidance should address, including state certification processes, the requirement that a scholarship granting organization spend at least 90 percent of income on scholarships, income verification, the treatment of organizations operating in more than one state, reporting and recordkeeping, and the definition of disqualified persons. Written comments were requested on or before 26 December 2025. The notice is undated on its face in the copy retrieved, so the day and month of issuance are not established here; the comment deadline places it in 2025.

events.instrument: Executive Order 14191, Expanding Educational Freedom and Opportunity for Families, 90 FR 8859
events.summary: The President signed Executive Order 14191 on 29 January 2025, published in the Federal Register on 3 February 2025. Section 3 directs the Secretary of Education to issue guidance within sixty days on how states can use federal formula funds to support K-12 educational choice initiatives. Section 4 directs the Secretary to include education freedom as a priority in discretionary grant programs as appropriate and consistent with applicable law, and directs the Secretary of Labor and the Secretary of Education to submit plans within ninety days. Section 5 directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to issue guidance on whether and how states may use block grants, including the Child Care and Development Block Grant, to support families choosing private and faith-based options. Section 6 directs the Secretary of Defense to review mechanisms for military-connected families to attend private, faith-based, or public charter schools.

events.instrument: Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board v. Drummond, 605 U.S. 165 (2025) (Nos. 24-394, 24-396)
events.summary: The Supreme Court disposed of the consolidated appeals concerning St. Isidore of Seville Catholic Virtual School with a one-line per curiam order stating that the judgment is affirmed by an equally divided Court. Justice Barrett took no part in the consideration or decision of the cases. The judgment left standing is that of the Oklahoma Supreme Court in Drummond v. Oklahoma Statewide Virtual Charter School Board, 2024 OK 53, which barred the establishment of the religious virtual charter school. An affirmance by an equally divided Court sets no precedent, so the question whether a state may authorize a religious charter school remains unresolved by the Supreme Court, and no later Supreme Court merits decision through 7 September 2026 addresses it.

events.instrument: Catholic Charities Bureau, Inc. v. Wisconsin Labor and Industry Review Commission, 605 U.S. 238 (2025) (No. 24-154)
events.summary: The Supreme Court held that the Wisconsin Supreme Court's application of the state unemployment compensation tax exemption for organizations operated primarily for religious purposes violated the First Amendment. Eligibility for the exemption turned on inherently religious choices, such as whether to proselytize or to serve only co-religionists in charitable work, rather than on secular criteria, and that regime imposed a denominational preference subject to strict scrutiny. The decision bears on the tax and employment treatment of entities affiliated with churches, including schools and school-affiliated ministries.

The Supreme Court held that parents challenging a school board's introduction of storybooks with sexuality and gender story lines into the elementary curriculum, together with the board's withdrawal of notice and opt outs, are entitled to a preliminary injunction. The Court held that the parents are likely to succeed on the claim that the policies unconstitutionally burden their religious exercise, relying on the recognized right of parents to direct the religious upbringing of their children. The decision concerns public school instruction and the family's position rather than the position of a religious school.

Section 70411 of Public Law 119-21 added section 25F to the Internal Revenue Code, allowing an individual a nonrefundable credit for qualified cash contributions to a scholarship granting organization, capped at $1,700 per taxable year and reduced by any state tax credit claimed for the same contributions. A covered state is one of the states, or the District of Columbia, that voluntarily elects to participate and to identify scholarship granting organizations in the state under subsection (g). An eligible student is a member of a household with income not greater than 300 percent of area median gross income. The section applies to taxable years ending after 31 December 2026. This is the first federal tax credit for contributions funding elementary and secondary scholarships.

events.instrument: Pulsifer v. Westshore Christian Academy, No. 24-2092 (6th Cir. 9 July 2025)
events.summary: The Sixth Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment for a Christian academy, holding that the ministerial exception barred the employment claim because the employee performed vital religious duties supporting the academy's religious mission. The decision applies the functional approach of Our Lady of Guadalupe School v. Morrissey-Berru to a staff position at a Christian elementary and secondary school.

events.instrument: Mid Vermont Christian School v. Saunders, No. 24-1704 (2d Cir. 9 Sept. 2025)
events.summary: The Second Circuit held that the Vermont Principals' Association's expulsion of Mid Vermont Christian School was not neutral because it displayed hostility toward the school's religious beliefs, that the plaintiffs are therefore likely to prevail on their Free Exercise claim, and that they satisfy the remaining requirements for injunctive relief. The court reversed the district court's order and remanded with instructions to grant the motion for a preliminary injunction insofar as it seeks the school's reinstatement in the association. The ruling is preliminary and the case was remanded for further proceedings, so the final outcome is outstanding.

events.instrument: Rev. Proc. 2026-6, announced by IR-2025-121 (advance election to participate under 26 U.S.C. 25F; Form 15714)
events.summary: The Department of the Treasury and the Internal Revenue Service issued Revenue Procedure 2026-6, which provides the exclusive procedure for a state to elect to be a covered state before identifying scholarship granting organizations under 26 U.S.C. 25F(g). A state submits Form 15714, Advance Election to Participate Under Section 25F for 2027, on or after 1 January 2026 and before the final date on which the state is permitted to submit its list of scholarship granting organizations. The advance election must be perfected by submitting the complete list before that deadline, and the list cannot be submitted with the election form. The revenue procedure was announced in news release IR-2025-121 dated 12 December 2025.

events.instrument: Hellman v. Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education, No. 25-1417 (1st Cir. 20 Mar. 2026)
events.summary: The First Circuit affirmed the dismissal of a challenge by parents of two children with disabilities enrolled in private schools to Massachusetts regulations that permit public school students to receive publicly funded special education services at their schools of enrollment while private school students may receive them only at a public school or another public or neutral location. The court noted that the distinction reflects in part a provision of the Massachusetts Constitution prohibiting direct aid to private schools. The parents argued that the regulation violates the Due Process, Equal Protection, and Privileges or Immunities Clauses by interfering with a fundamental right to enroll their children in private school; the court held that the regulation survives rational basis review. This is a loss for private school families.

events.instrument: Woolard v. Thurmond, No. 24-4291 (9th Cir. 11 Sept. 2025, amended 23 Mar. 2026)
events.summary: The Ninth Circuit affirmed the dismissal of a 42 U.S.C. 1983 action by parents and guardians of students in independent study programs at two California charter schools that had refused to purchase or permit sectarian curricular materials, as required by California laws prohibiting the teaching of sectarian or denominational doctrine in public schools. The panel held that the legal requirements applicable to the programs make them public school programs, applying the features identified in Carson v. Makin, 596 U.S. 767, and that a public school curriculum is government speech not subject to Free Speech Clause scrutiny. The panel amended its opinion and denied rehearing en banc; five judges dissented from the denial. This is a loss for families seeking religious curricular materials through publicly funded programs.

events.instrument: IRS news release IR-2026-76, states electing to participate in the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit under 26 U.S.C. 25F
events.summary: In news release IR-2026-76 dated 8 June 2026, the Internal Revenue Service announced that 27 states had elected to participate in the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program. The release names Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, West Virginia, and Wyoming. The release states that participation is voluntary, that taxpayers must contribute to a scholarship granting organization located in a participating state that has submitted a list of qualified organizations, and that the agency will maintain and update the official list. The credit is not yet in effect, and states must complete the election and submission process.

events.instrument: Crosspoint Church v. Makin, No. 24-1590 (1st Cir. 2 July 2026)
events.summary: In a companion decision to St. Dominic Academy v. Makin, the First Circuit affirmed in part and reversed in part the denial of a permanent injunction sought by a church operating a school against conditions Maine attaches to participation in its tuition assistance program. The court affirmed as to the absence of a case or controversy on the Employment Rule and as to the Religious Nondiscrimination Rule and the Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity Nondiscrimination Rule, reversed as to the Religious Expression Rule, and remanded for further proceedings. The final outcome is outstanding.

events.instrument: St. Dominic Academy v. Makin, No. 24-1739 (1st Cir. 2 July 2026)
events.summary: The First Circuit affirmed in part and reversed in part the denial of a preliminary injunction sought by a Catholic school and a family against conditions Maine attaches to participation in its tuition assistance program through the Maine Human Rights Act. The court affirmed the determination that no case or controversy exists with respect to the Employment Rule and that the school had not shown a likelihood of success on the merits of its claims against the Religious Nondiscrimination Rule and the Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity Nondiscrimination Rule. It reversed as to the Religious Expression Rule and remanded with instructions to enter a preliminary injunction against that rule as applied to the school. The case was remanded for further proceedings, so the final outcome is outstanding.

events.instrument: 26 U.S.C. 25F advance elections; Internal Revenue Service list of participating states for 2027
events.summary: The Internal Revenue Service page on the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit states that the following states have made an advance election to participate under Section 25F for 2027, as of 24 July 2026, and lists 30 states: Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Dakota, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, West Virginia, and Wyoming. The page was last reviewed or updated on 27 July 2026. This confirms the reported figure of 30 states as of 24 July 2026 against a primary Internal Revenue Service source rather than a news report. The page also states that beginning 1 January 2027 individual taxpayers may be able to claim the credit for cash contributions up to $1,700, and that a state must choose to participate and provide a list of scholarship granting organizations before a taxpayer may claim the credit for a contribution in that state. The count is a snapshot; the elections must still be perfected by submission of the organization lists.

events.instrument: Carson Smith Scholarship Program, Utah Code §§ 53F-4-301 to 53F-4-307
events.summary: Utah created the Carson Smith Scholarship Program, a state-funded voucher for students with disabilities, codified at Utah Code sections 53F-4-301 through 53F-4-307. The enacting bill number is not given by the source consulted.

events.instrument: Special Needs Opportunity Scholarship Program, Utah Code §§ 53E-7-401 to 53E-7-410
events.summary: Utah created the Special Needs Opportunity Scholarship Program, codified at Utah Code sections 53E-7-401 through 53E-7-410. The program combined private donations to scholarship granting organizations, for which donors received tax credits, with legislative appropriations, and it served students with disabilities under federal education law together with their siblings attending the same qualifying school. Homeschooled students could participate.

events.instrument: Utah Fits All Scholarship Program, Utah Code §§ 53F-6-401 to 53F-6-414
events.summary: Utah created the Utah Fits All Scholarship Program, an education savings account codified at Utah Code sections 53F-6-401 through 53F-6-414. The enacting legislation passed by margins sufficient to place it beyond the reach of a citizen referendum. The enacting bill number is not given by the source consulted.

The Utah Legislature passed Senate Bill 44 in 2024, merging the Special Needs Opportunity Scholarship, then a tax-credit scholarship, with the state-funded Carson Smith Scholarship Program to form the Carson Smith Opportunity Scholarship. The legacy Carson Smith voucher lapses when its last participating students leave the program.

events.instrument: Litigation challenging the Utah Fits All Scholarship Program, Utah Code §§ 53F-6-401 to 53F-6-414
events.summary: Utah's largest teachers' union filed suit in May 2024 challenging the constitutionality of the Utah Fits All Scholarship Program, and the Partnership for Educational Choice intervened in defense of the program on behalf of participating parents. The source consulted, last updated on 16 August 2024, records the matter as pending in the trial court with no ruling entered. Any later trial court judgment and its appellate treatment remain outstanding and have not been verified against a retrieved primary source.

events.instrument: Valente v. French (D. Vt.), resolution of September 9, 2020 complaint challenging 16 V.S.A. sections 166, 821, 822, and 828
events.summary: The challenge to Vermont's exclusion of religious schools from town tuitioning was resolved on terms under which parents qualifying for tuition benefits may use those funds at private schools regardless of whether the school is religious. Rutland Town School District and Hartland School District were to reimburse residents denied tuition on religious grounds from the 2019-2020 school year forward, and Ludlow Mount Holly Unified Union School District from the 2020-2021 school year forward, with reimbursement due by April 10, 2023.

events.instrument: Vitale v. Bellows Falls Union High School, 2023 VT 15
events.summary: The Vermont Supreme Court ruled against parents who challenged unequal access to town tuitioning. The court stated that Vermont children have a fundamental right to education under the Education Clause, and held that school choice is permitted but not required and need not be made universally available across districts.

events.instrument: Education Improvement Scholarships Tax Credits Program, Va. Code sections 58.1-439.25 through 58.1-439.28
events.summary: Virginia created the Education Improvement Scholarships Tax Credits Program in 2012, a tax-credit scholarship program codified at Va. Code sections 58.1-439.25 through 58.1-439.28 and administered by the Virginia Department of Education.

events.instrument: Wash. Admin. Code sections 250-40-030(6) and 250-40-050(8), sectarian employer exclusion from the State Work Study Program
events.summary: Washington repealed the regulatory exclusion that barred sectarian employers from the State Work Study Program, which allowed work-study students to choose among religious and non-religious employers alike. The exclusion had been challenged in Summit Christian Academy v. Meotti, No. 3:18-cv-05656-TLF (W.D. Wash.), on which the amended complaint was filed September 11, 2018. The state agency had defended the exclusion on the ground that the Washington Constitution prevents an organization involved in religious activity from participating in the program, invoking article I, section 11 and article IX, section 4.

events.instrument: Hope Scholarship Program, W. Va. Code ch. 18 art. 31
events.summary: West Virginia enacted the Hope Scholarship Program in March 2021, creating an education savings account that families may apply to private school tuition and to expenses including online learning, tutoring, and therapy. Related provisions appear at W. Va. Code sections 18-8-1 and 18-9A-25.

events.instrument: Beaver v. Moore (W. Va. Cir. Ct., Kanawha County), preliminary injunction
events.summary: The Circuit Court of Kanawha County issued a preliminary injunction halting the Hope Scholarship Program, accepting the plaintiffs' constitutional arguments against it. The suit had been filed on January 19, 2022.

events.instrument: State v. Beaver (W. Va.), order dissolving preliminary injunction
events.summary: The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals entered an order in October 2022 dissolving the injunction against the Hope Scholarship Program and reversing the Kanawha County Circuit Court ruling that had declared the program unconstitutional, which allowed families to use Hope Scholarship accounts for tuition and education expenses. Retrieved secondary accounts give the order date as either October 5 or October 6, 2022, so the date is recorded here to month precision.

events.instrument: State v. Beaver, No. 22-616 (W. Va.), opinion
events.summary: The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals released its written opinion, by a vote of four to one, holding that the West Virginia Constitution does not prohibit the Legislature from enacting the Hope Scholarship Act in addition to providing for a thorough and efficient system of free schools. The opinion permanently overturned the July 2022 injunction and left the program in operation.

The Wisconsin Supreme Court issued its decision upholding the amended Milwaukee Parental Choice Program, including the participation of religious schools. The decision date is established by the court's own later order in the same docket, which refers to the decision of June 10, 1998.

The Wisconsin Supreme Court dismissed a motion to vacate its June 10, 1998 decision upholding the Milwaukee Parental Choice Program. The court found the motion untimely, holding that the respondents waited nearly two years after the relevant information became public, that the delay waived any disqualification claim, and it remanded the matter to the Dane County Circuit Court for a determination of attorney fees.

events.instrument: Racine Parental Choice Program, Wis. Stat. sec. 118.60; Wis. Admin. Code ch. PI 48
events.summary: Wisconsin extended a parental choice voucher program to the Racine Unified School District in 2011, governed by Wis. Stat. section 118.60 and Wisconsin Administrative Code chapter PI 48. The program was enacted and launched in the same year.

events.instrument: Wisconsin Parental Choice Program (statewide), Wis. Stat. sec. 118.60
events.summary: Wisconsin created a statewide parental choice voucher program in 2013 under Wis. Stat. section 118.60, extending eligibility beyond the Milwaukee and Racine programs.

events.instrument: Wisconsin K-12 Private School Tuition Deduction, Wis. Stat. sec. 71.05(6)(b)49
events.summary: Wisconsin created an individual income tax deduction for private school tuition in 2013, codified at Wis. Stat. section 71.05(6)(b)49.

events.instrument: Wisconsin Special Needs Scholarship Program, Wis. Stat. sec. 115.7915; Wis. Admin. Code ch. PI 49
events.summary: Wisconsin created the Special Needs Scholarship Program in 2015, a voucher for students with disabilities, codified at Wis. Stat. section 115.7915 and implemented through Wisconsin Administrative Code chapter PI 49.

events.instrument: Underwood v. Vos, No. 2023AP001896 (Wis.), petition for original action
events.summary: A petition filed on October 12, 2023 asked the Wisconsin Supreme Court to hear a challenge to the state's parental choice programs, including the statewide program and the Special Needs Scholarship Program. The petitioners alleged violations of the Uniform Taxation Clause and the public purpose doctrine, and contended that superintendents are not given sufficient control over participating private schools. The Wisconsin Supreme Court declined to hear the case in December 2023.

events.instrument: Steamboat Legacy Scholarship Act, Wyo. Stat. sections 21-2-901 through 21-2-909
events.summary: Wyoming enacted the Steamboat Legacy Scholarship Act in 2024, creating an education savings account program codified at Wyo. Stat. sections 21-2-901 through 21-2-909, with related provisions at Wyo. Stat. sections 21-4-102, 21-4-301, and 21-13-310.

events.instrument: 2025 expansion of the Steamboat Legacy Scholarship Act, Wyo. Stat. sections 21-2-901 through 21-2-909
events.summary: Wyoming expanded the education savings account program in 2025. The program provides up to 7,000 dollars annually per participating student for educational expenses including tuition, tutoring, curriculum, and therapies.

events.instrument: Wyoming Education Association v. Degenfelder, No. 2025-CV-0203366 (Wyo. Dist. Ct., 1st Jud. Dist., Laramie County), Order Granting Preliminary Injunction
events.summary: The District Court of the First Judicial District, Laramie County, granted a preliminary injunction restraining the State of Wyoming, the Superintendent of Public Instruction, and the State Treasurer from transferring, expending, reimbursing, releasing, or distributing state funds to education service providers under the Steamboat Legacy Scholarship Act. The court relied on article 3, section 36, article 1, section 19, and article 7 of the Wyoming Constitution, and applied strict scrutiny to educational funding affecting the right to education. The order was preliminary, so the constitutional merits remained outstanding.

events.instrument: Degenfelder v. Wyoming Education Association, 2026 WY 54, Nos. S-25-0203 and S-25-0204
events.summary: The Wyoming Supreme Court held that the district court abused its discretion in granting a preliminary injunction against the Steamboat Legacy Scholarship Act, because the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate possible irreparable personal injury absent the injunction. The court reversed and remanded for further proceedings consistent with the opinion. The constitutional challenge to the Act was not resolved and remains to be decided on remand, so this matter is not final.

events.instrument: Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board v. Drummond, Nos. 24-394 and 24-396 (U.S. May 22, 2025) (per curiam), affirming Drummond v. Oklahoma Statewide Virtual Charter School Board, 2024 OK 53, No. 121694 (Okla. June 25, 2024)
events.summary: On May 22, 2025 the Supreme Court of the United States issued a one-line judgment in Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board, et al. v. Gentner Drummond, Attorney General of Oklahoma, ex rel. Oklahoma, Nos. 24-394 and 24-396, stating: "The judgment is affirmed by an equally divided Court." Justice Barrett took no part in the consideration or decision of the cases. The judgment affirmed was that of the Supreme Court of the State of Oklahoma in Drummond v. Oklahoma Statewide Virtual Charter School Board, 2024 OK 53, No. 121694, decided June 25, 2024, in which that court assumed original jurisdiction and granted a writ of mandamus and declaratory relief, holding that the contract between the Oklahoma Statewide Virtual Charter School Board and St. Isidore of Seville Catholic Virtual School violated the Oklahoma Constitution, the Oklahoma Charter Schools Act, and the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. The Oklahoma court relied on article 2, section 5 and article 1, section 5 of the Oklahoma Constitution and on 70 O.S. Supp. 2022, section 3-132. Chief Justice Kane recused; Vice Chief Justice Rowe concurred in part and dissented in part; Justice Kuehn dissented. Because the affirmance was by an equally divided Court, it resolved the Oklahoma judgment without setting nationwide precedent.

events.instrument: Chittenden Town School District v. Department of Education, No. 97-275, 169 Vt. 310, 738 A.2d 539 (Vt. June 11, 1999)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of Vermont decided Chittenden Town School District v. Department of Education, No. 97-275, on June 11, 1999, reported at 169 Vt. 310, 738 A.2d 539. The Chittenden Town School District, a town tuitioning district without its own high school, adopted a policy paying tuition under 16 V.S.A. section 822 to Mount Saint Joseph Academy, a sectarian school; the Commissioner of Education terminated state aid to the district, and the district sued for declaratory relief and restoration of aid. The Rutland Superior Court entered summary judgment for the defendants on June 27, 1997 and prohibited the district from making the tuition payments. The Supreme Court affirmed, holding that a school district violates Chapter I, Article 3 of the Vermont Constitution, the Compelled Support Clause, when it reimburses tuition for a sectarian school under section 822 in the absence of adequate safeguards against the use of such funds for religious worship. The panel was Dooley, Morse, and Johnson, JJ., with Allen, C.J. (Ret.) and Gibson, J. (Ret.), specially assigned. The Vermont Judiciary's own published-opinion database begins at 2021 and does not carry this opinion; the text was retrieved from a full reproduction of the published opinion and cross-checked against a second reproduction.

events.instrument: Florida Constitutional Amendment No. 8 (2012), "Religious Freedom," proposed by CS/HJR 1471 (2011 Regular Session), amending article I, section 3 of the Florida Constitution
events.summary: Florida Constitutional Amendment No. 8, titled "Religious Freedom" on the ballot, was placed before voters at the general election of November 6, 2012 by CS/HJR 1471 of the 2011 Regular Session, which passed the House 81 yeas to 35 nays on April 27, 2011 and the Senate 26 yeas to 10 nays on May 6, 2011, and was signed by the officers and filed with the Secretary of State on July 1, 2011. The measure would have deleted from article I, section 3 of the Florida Constitution the prohibition on using revenues from the public treasury directly or indirectly in aid of any church, sect, or religious denomination or in aid of any sectarian institution, and would have provided that no individual or entity may be discriminated against or barred from receiving funding on the basis of religious identity or belief. The Florida Department of State, Division of Elections, reports under the heading "Official Results" for the November 6, 2012 General Election that the amendment received 3,441,128 votes Yes for Approval, or 44.5 percent, and 4,286,376 votes No for Rejection, or 55.5 percent. Article XI, section 5 of the Florida Constitution requires approval by 60 percent of voters, so the amendment failed.

events.instrument: 2025 Vt. Acts and Resolves No. 73, Sec. 21 (H.454), codified at 16 V.S.A. Sec. 828(a)(2)(D)
events.summary: 16 V.S.A. Sec. 828(a) provides that a school district shall not pay the tuition of a student except to a list of recipients, one of which is an approved independent school that satisfies five cumulative conditions in subdivision (a)(2). Condition (D) requires that the school "had at least 25 percent of its student enrollment composed of students attending on a district-funded tuition basis pursuant to chapter 21 of this title during the 2023-2024 school year." The other conditions are that the school is located in Vermont, is approved under 16 V.S.A. Sec. 166 on or before July 1, 2025, is located within a supervisory district or a supervisory union with a member district that does not operate a public school for some or all grades as of July 1, 2024, and complies with the minimum class size requirements of 16 V.S.A. Sec. 165(a)(9) and State Board rule, subject to a State Board waiver for geographic isolation or an implementation plan. The section's history note states that this text was added by 2025, No. 73, Sec. 21, effective July 1, 2025; the immediately prior amendment was 2021, No. 127 (Adj. Sess.), Sec. 21, effective July 1, 2024. The Vermont General Assembly's bill status record for H.454 records "Governor approved bill on July 1, 2025" and the assignment of Act 73. The 2023-2024 school year functions as the historical measurement window for the enrollment-composition test rather than as the year the requirement took effect; the requirement itself dates from Act 73 of 2025. The enacted act PDF at legislature.vermont.gov/Documents/2026/Docs/ACTS/ACT073 could not be retrieved.

events.instrument: 2023 Wisconsin Act 11 (2023 Senate Bill 330), amending Wis. Stat. sec. 118.60(4)(bg)3., 5.a., 5.b. and sec. 119.23(4)(bg)3., 5.a., 5.b.
events.summary: The enrolled act states "Date of enactment: June 20, 2023" and "Date of publication: June 21, 2023," and is titled an act "relating to: increasing the per pupil payments in parental choice programs and the Special Needs Scholarship program and the per pupil payments made to independent charter schools and increasing the revenue ceiling for school districts." Sections 5 through 16 amend Wis. Stat. sec. 118.60(4)(bg)3., 5.a., and 5.b. (the statewide and Racine parental choice programs) and sec. 119.23(4)(bg)3., 5.a., and 5.b. (the Milwaukee parental choice program). The amendments add to the annual payment formula, for the 2023-24 school year, an amount equal to 10 percent of the revenue ceiling as defined in sec. 121.905(1) for a pupil enrolled in a grade from kindergarten to 8, and 26.8 percent of that revenue ceiling for a pupil enrolled in a grade from 9 to 12. Section 17 creates sec. 121.905(1)(b)8., defining "revenue ceiling" as the amount under subdivision 7. plus $1,000, first applicable to the revenue ceiling in the 2023-24 school year. Section 9434 provides that the treatment of the annual adjustment formula provisions takes effect on July 1, 2024. The act states percentages rather than dollar figures. The Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction's 2023-24 Wisconsin Parental Choice Program facts and figures document states the resulting maximum payment as $9,893 per full-time pupil in grades K-8 and $12,387 per full-time pupil in grades 9-12. 2023 Wisconsin Act 19, the 2023-25 biennial budget act (2023 Senate Bill 70, date of enactment July 5, 2023, date of publication July 6, 2023, vetoed in part), does not amend sec. 118.60(4)(bg) or sec. 119.23(4)(bg); the payment increase is Act 11, not Act 19.

events.instrument: Columbus City School Dist. v. State of Ohio, Franklin C.P. No. 22CV000067, Decision and Entry on the Parties' Motions for Summary Judgment (June 24, 2025), on appeal, 10th Dist. No. 25-AP-000603
events.summary: Judge Jaiza N. Page of the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas filed a Decision and Entry on the Parties' Motions for Summary Judgment in Case No. 22 CV 67 on June 24, 2025, electronically signed at 15:00:12. The plaintiffs, including Columbus City School District, Cleveland Heights-University Heights City School District, Richmond Heights Local School District, Lima City School District, Barberton City School District, individual parents, and the Ohio Coalition for Equity and Adequacy of School Funding, challenged the EdChoice voucher program codified in R.C. Chapter 3310 under Article VI, Section 2 and Article I, Section 2 of the Ohio Constitution. The court granted the plaintiffs' motion and denied the defendants' motions on Count One (creation of one or more systems of uncommon schools), Count Two (failure to secure a thorough and efficient system of common schools), and Count Four (State funding of religious schools, alleging that a religion or other sect is given the exclusive right to, or control of, part of the school funds). All motions were denied as to Count Three (segregation in violation of the thorough and efficient system of common schools). The defendants' motions were granted and the plaintiffs' denied on Count Five (Article I, Section 2). The entry states that "the EdChoice program is unconstitutional and shall be enjoined," that the decision is a final appealable order under Civ.R. 54(B) and R.C. 2505.02(B)(8) with no just reason for delay, and that the judgment "shall be stayed pursuant to Civ.R. 62(B)" with no bond ordered. The Franklin County Clerk of Courts docket for 22CV000067 records notices of appeal filed July 23, 2025, a notice of cross appeal filed July 31, 2025, the record transmitted to the court of appeals on September 9, 2025, and Court of Appeals No. 25AP-603. The Tenth District docket for case 25-AP-000603 shows a date filed of July 24, 2025, status ACTIVE, reply briefs filed January 12, 2026, an order granting additional oral argument time on February 19, 2026, a hearing notice issued March 31, 2026 for 9:30 AM, oral argument held May 12, 2026, and no decision or judgment entry through the most recent docket activity on August 14, 2026. As of September 7, 2026 the appeal is pending and the trial court judgment remains stayed, so the EdChoice program continues to operate. Outstanding: the Tenth District's opinion and judgment entry, and any further appeal to the Supreme Court of Ohio.

events.instrument: House Bill 2 (2024 Regular Session), 2024 Ky. Acts ch. 8
events.summary: The Kentucky General Assembly passed House Bill 2, an Act proposing to create a new section of the Constitution of Kentucky relating to education funding. The proposed section reads: "The General Assembly may provide financial support for the education costs of students outside the system of common schools. The General Assembly may exercise this authority by law, Sections 59, 60, 171, 183, 184, 186, and 189 of this Constitution notwithstanding." The Act directed that the question be submitted to the voters at the next regular election at which members of the General Assembly are to be voted for, in the form: "To give parents choices in educational opportunities for their children, are you in favor of enabling the General Assembly to provide financial support for the education costs of students in kindergarten through 12th grade who are outside the system of common (public) schools by amending the Constitution of Kentucky as stated below?" The House passed the bill with committee substitute on 13 March 2024 by 65 to 32, the Senate passed it on 15 March 2024 by 27 to 8, and the enrolled bill was signed by the presiding officers and delivered to the Secretary of State on 21 March 2024 as chapter 8 of the 2024 Acts.

events.instrument: Kentucky Constitutional Amendment 2 (2024), submitted under 2024 Ky. Acts ch. 8 (H.B. 2)
events.summary: At the general election held on 5 November 2024 the voters of Kentucky rejected Constitutional Amendment 2, which would have added a section to the Constitution of Kentucky permitting the General Assembly to provide financial support for the education costs of students in kindergarten through grade 12 outside the system of common schools, notwithstanding Sections 59, 60, 171, 183, 184, 186, and 189. The official results published by the Kentucky State Board of Elections record 706,942 votes for YES and 1,298,967 votes for NO on the amendment, out of 2,005,909 votes cast on the question. The published results state totals only and do not state percentages. The amendment failed in every county. Kentucky therefore retains the anti-aid provisions that its Supreme Court has read to bar public support of nonpublic schools, and no private school choice program was authorized. This is a loss event for Christian and other nonpublic school families in Kentucky.

events.instrument: Toney v. Bower, 318 Ill. App. 3d 1194, 744 N.E.2d 351 (4th Dist. 2001) (No. 4-00-0401)
events.summary: The Appellate Court of Illinois, Fourth District, affirmed the dismissal of a challenge to the education expense tax credit at section 201(m) of the Illinois Income Tax Act, 35 ILCS 5/201(m), which allows a credit of 25 percent of qualified education expenses above $250, capped at $500, for tuition, book fees, and lab fees paid to a public or nonpublic school. The plaintiffs, taxpayers and public school personnel, argued that the credit violated section 3 of article I, section 3 of article X, section 1(a) of article VIII, and section 2 of article IX of the Illinois Constitution, as well as the Establishment Clause. The court held that a tax credit is neither an appropriation nor a payment of public funds, so the article VIII and article X limits on public funds and on aid to sectarian schools were not engaged; that the credit has a secular legislative purpose, does not have the primary effect of advancing religion because any benefit reaches religious schools only through the independent choices of parents, and does not create excessive entanglement; and that the classification drawn by the credit is reasonable. The judgment for the Director of Revenue was affirmed. A national association reports that the Supreme Court of Illinois denied leave to appeal on 6 June 2001; that denial was not verified against a court record.

events.instrument: Griffith v. Bower, 319 Ill. App. 3d 993, 747 N.E.2d 423 (5th Dist. 2001) (No. 5-99-0829)
events.summary: The Appellate Court of Illinois, Fifth District, affirmed the dismissal of a separate challenge to the same education expense credit, enacted by Public Act 91-9 and codified at 35 ILCS 5/201(m). The plaintiffs argued that the credit violated section 3 of article I and section 3 of article X of the Illinois Constitution. The court held that the credit involves no appropriation or payment of public funds and instead allows Illinois parents to keep more of their own money, that it is available on equal terms to parents of public school and nonpublic school students, and that any money reaching a religious school does so only through the private choices of individual parents, so the credit neither aids a sectarian school within the meaning of article X nor has the primary effect of advancing religion. The judgment for the Director of Revenue was affirmed. A national association reports that the Supreme Court of Illinois denied leave to appeal on 29 June 2001; that denial was not verified against a court record.

events.instrument: Strout v. Albanese, 178 F.3d 57 (1st Cir. 1999) (No. 98-1986), cert. denied sub nom. Strout v. Albanese, No. 99-254 (12 Oct. 1999)
events.summary: The United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit affirmed judgment for the state and upheld the exclusion of sectarian schools from Maine's town tuitioning program under 20-A M.R.S.A. section 2951(2), which pays tuition at an approved private school for a student whose administrative unit maintains no public school of the student's grade level. Parents who wished to direct the payment to a religious school argued that the exclusion violated the Establishment Clause, the Free Exercise Clause, the Equal Protection Clause, the Due Process Clause, and the Free Speech Clause. The court rejected each claim, reasoning that there was no binding authority holding that direct payment of tuition by the state to a private sectarian school is constitutionally permissible, and that direct aid of that kind is invalid absent mechanisms restricting the funds to secular purposes; on that view Maine's exclusion was a permissible, indeed a required, response to Establishment Clause constraints rather than an impermissible discrimination against religion. The Supreme Court of the United States denied the petitions for writs of certiorari on 12 October 1999 in No. 99-254. This decision states the position of federal law on Maine town tuitioning until Carson v. Makin, 596 U.S. 767 (2022), held the sectarian exclusion to violate the Free Exercise Clause. It is recorded as a loss event.

events.instrument: Matter of Parents for Educational and Religious Liberty in Schools v. Young, 2025 NY Slip Op 03689 (N.Y. 18 June 2025) (No. 56)
events.summary: The New York Court of Appeals affirmed, with costs, in a proceeding brought against Lester W. Young Jr., as Chancellor of the Board of Regents, the Commissioner of Education, the Board of Regents, and the State Education Department, challenging the substantial equivalency regulations for nonpublic schools at 8 NYCRR part 130. The two provisions still at issue, 8 NYCRR 130.6(c)(2)(i) and 8 NYCRR 130.8(d)(7)(i), provide that a nonpublic school that receives a final determination of failure to meet the substantial equivalency requirement shall no longer be deemed a school that provides compulsory education fulfilling the requirements of article 65 of the Education Law. Judge Rivera wrote for the Court, which held that the Commissioner acted within the authority delegated by the Education Law: the provisions neither compel parents to unenroll their children nor authorize the closure of a school, and instead state a consequence that follows from the statutory text itself. The Supreme Court, Albany County, had annulled those two provisions in Matter of Parents for Educ. & Religious Liberty in Schs. v Young, 79 Misc 3d 454, 2023 NY Slip Op 23081 (23 March 2023), and the Appellate Division reversed on that point with one justice dissenting. The regulations therefore stand, and the compliance burden on New York's religious and other nonpublic schools remains in force.

events.instrument: Indian Appropriation Act of June 7, 1897, ch. 3, 30 Stat. 62, 79
events.summary: Congress attached to the Indian appropriation act a declaration that it is the settled policy of the government to make no appropriation whatever for education in any sectarian school, language first used in the act of 1896 and repeated in this act. The policy was carried out through successive percentage reductions in public appropriations for contract schools operated by religious bodies, and the Supreme Court later held in Reuben Quick Bear v. Leupp that the declaration reached only public money and not tribal treaty and trust funds.

The Supreme Court held that a congressional appropriation for a building at Providence Hospital, a corporation chartered by Congress and managed by members of a Roman Catholic sisterhood, did not violate the Establishment Clause. The Court reasoned that the corporate charter defined a secular corporation and that the religious affiliation of its members was immaterial to the character of the appropriation.

events.instrument: Reuben Quick Bear v. Leupp, 210 U.S. 50 (1908)
events.summary: The Supreme Court held that the congressional prohibition on appropriating public funds for education in sectarian schools does not reach tribal treaty and trust funds, which belong to the Indians themselves. Indians could direct their own funds to sectarian schools of their choice, provided the petitions were genuine and payments were limited to the pro rata share of the petitioning Indians.

The Supreme Court upheld a Kentucky statute forbidding a private chartered college to teach white and Black students together, holding that a state may withhold from its corporations privileges and powers of which it could not constitutionally deprive individuals. The Court decided the case on the statute's application to the corporation and did not resolve its validity as applied to individuals. The reasoning was superseded by later equal protection decisions and by Runyon v. McCrary, 427 U.S. 160 (1976), which held that federal law bars racially discriminatory admissions at private nonsectarian schools.

The Supreme Court, in a unanimous decision, struck down a Nebraska statute forbidding the teaching of modern foreign languages to children who had not passed the eighth grade, as applied to a teacher of German in a parochial school. The Court held that the liberty protected by the Fourteenth Amendment includes the right of a teacher to teach and the right of parents to engage a teacher to instruct their children, and that the state's means exceeded the limitations on its power.

events.instrument: Pierce v. Society of the Sisters of the Holy Names of Jesus and Mary, 268 U.S. 510 (1925)
events.summary: The Supreme Court held that the Oregon Compulsory Education Act, which required nearly every child between eight and sixteen to attend a public school, unreasonably interfered with the liberty of parents to direct the upbringing and education of their children under the Fourteenth Amendment. The Court stated that the child is not the mere creature of the state and that a statute standardizing children through public instruction alone conflicts with the fundamental theory of liberty on which governments in the Union rest. The vote is not reported on the source page.

The Supreme Court held that the Territory of Hawaii's Foreign Language School Act infringed rights protected by the Fifth Amendment by giving the government control over the intimate and essential details of private schools, including curriculum, teachers, and textbooks. The Court found the measure went beyond reasonable regulation of private schools without adequate justification. The vote is not reported on the source page.

events.instrument: Cochran v. Louisiana State Board of Education, 281 U.S. 370 (1930)
events.summary: The Supreme Court upheld Louisiana's use of tax revenue to supply free textbooks to school children, including children attending private and parochial schools, against a Fourteenth Amendment taxation challenge. The Court reasoned that the books furnished for private schools are not granted to the schools themselves but only to or for the use of the children, and that the appropriation served the public purpose of education. This reasoning became known as the child-benefit doctrine. The vote is not reported on the source page.

events.instrument: Minersville School District v. Gobitis, 310 U.S. 586 (1940)
events.summary: The Supreme Court held that a public school may require students to salute the flag and recite the Pledge of Allegiance notwithstanding the students' religious objections, reasoning that fostering national unity fell within legislative authority. The decision was overruled three years later by West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette, 319 U.S. 624 (1943). The vote is not reported on the source page.

The Supreme Court held that the concept of liberty embodied in the Fourteenth Amendment embraces the liberties guaranteed by the First Amendment, applying the Free Exercise Clause to the states. The Court struck down Connecticut's licensing requirement for religious solicitation as a prior restraint on religious exercise. The vote is not reported on the source page.

events.instrument: West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette, 319 U.S. 624 (1943)
events.summary: By a vote of 6 to 3, the Supreme Court held that a state may not compel students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance, and that no official may prescribe what shall be orthodox in politics, nationalism, religion, or other matters of opinion. The decision overruled Minersville School District v. Gobitis, 310 U.S. 586 (1940).

The Supreme Court upheld the application of a state child labor law to a guardian who had her ward distribute religious literature in public, holding that the power of the state to control the conduct of children reaches beyond its authority over adults. The Court held that parental religious rights do not exempt children from reasonable state regulations enacted for child welfare. The vote is not reported on the source page.

events.instrument: Everson v. Board of Education of the Township of Ewing, 330 U.S. 1 (1947)
events.summary: By a vote of 5 to 4, the Supreme Court held that the Establishment Clause applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment, and that New Jersey's reimbursement of parents for bus fares paid to transport children to parochial schools did not violate it. The Court treated the reimbursement as a general welfare benefit extended to all citizens without regard to religious affiliation.

events.instrument: National Defense Education Act of 1958, Pub. L. 85-864, 72 Stat. 1580
events.summary: Congress enacted the National Defense Education Act, which extended several federal education programs to nonpublic schools and their pupils. Title III authorized loans to private nonprofit elementary and secondary schools for laboratory and other equipment and materials in science, mathematics, and modern foreign languages; Title V permitted testing in secondary schools beyond public institutions where state law allowed; and Title VI made teachers from private as well as public schools eligible for stipends at federally supported language institutes.

By a vote of 8 to 1, the Supreme Court held that a state may not impose a substantial burden on the free exercise of religion unless the burden is justified by a compelling state interest and no alternative regulation could serve that interest without infringing First Amendment rights. This standard governed free exercise claims, including the claim sustained in Wisconsin v. Yoder, until Employment Division v. Smith, 494 U.S. 872 (1990), confined it.

events.instrument: Civil Rights Act of 1964, Pub. L. 88-352, 78 Stat. 241
events.summary: Congress enacted the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Section 601 provides that no person shall, on the ground of race, color, or national origin, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any program or activity receiving federal financial assistance. Section 702 of Title VII exempts a religious corporation, association, or society with respect to the employment of individuals of a particular religion to perform work connected with the carrying on of its religious activities, and exempts an educational institution with respect to the employment of individuals to perform work connected with its educational activities.

events.instrument: Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965, Pub. L. 89-10, 79 Stat. 27
events.summary: Congress enacted the Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965, which for the first time directed substantial federal education funds toward pupils enrolled in private elementary and secondary schools. Title I required local educational agencies to make provision for including special educational services and arrangements, such as dual enrollment, educational radio and television, and mobile educational services and equipment, in which educationally deprived children attending private schools can participate. Title II required states to allocate library resources, textbooks, and other instructional materials on an equitable basis for the use of children and teachers in private elementary and secondary schools, limited to materials approved for use in the public schools of the state.

events.instrument: Board of Education v. Allen, 392 U.S. 236 (1968)
events.summary: By a vote of 6 to 3, the Supreme Court upheld a New York statute requiring public school boards to lend textbooks free of charge to all students in grades seven through twelve, including students at parochial schools. The Court treated the loan as a neutral educational benefit to students and parents rather than direct aid to religious institutions, extending the child-benefit reasoning of Cochran and Everson.

events.instrument: Walz v. Tax Commission of the City of New York, 397 U.S. 664 (1970)
events.summary: The Supreme Court upheld New York's property tax exemption for real property used solely for religious worship against an Establishment Clause challenge. The Court held that the exemption serves secular purposes shared with other nonprofit institutions and produces only minimal and remote involvement between church and state, less than the involvement that taxation would entail. The vote is not stated on the source page.

A three-judge district court held that the Internal Revenue Code does not permit exemption under section 501(c)(3), or charitable deductions under section 170, for private schools that maintain racially discriminatory admissions policies. Schools were required to adopt and publicize genuinely nondiscriminatory policies as to admissions, scholarships, and other programs to qualify for federal tax benefits. The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment summarily in Coit v. Green, 404 U.S. 997 (1971), and the ruling was the direct antecedent of Bob Jones University v. United States, 461 U.S. 574 (1983).

events.instrument: Lemon v. Kurtzman, 403 U.S. 602 (1971), decided with Earley v. DiCenso and Robinson v. DiCenso
events.summary: The Supreme Court struck down Rhode Island's salary supplements for teachers of secular subjects in nonpublic schools and Pennsylvania's reimbursement of nonpublic schools for teachers' salaries, textbooks, and instructional materials, holding that the programs required pervasive state surveillance and produced excessive entanglement between government and religion. The Court announced a three-part test requiring a secular legislative purpose, a principal effect that neither advances nor inhibits religion, and the absence of excessive government entanglement with religion. The vote was 8 to 1, with Justice Marshall taking no part in No. 89. The test governed Establishment Clause adjudication for roughly five decades and was abandoned by the Supreme Court in Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, 597 U.S. 507 (2022).

The Supreme Court sustained federal construction grants to church-related colleges and universities under the Higher Education Facilities Act of 1963, but struck down the provision limiting the federal interest in the financed facilities to twenty years, holding that unrestricted use of the property after that period would be a contribution to a religious body. Chief Justice Burger announced the judgment joined by Justices Harlan, Stewart, and Blackmun, Justice White concurred in the judgment, Justices Douglas, Black, and Marshall dissented in part, and Justice Brennan dissented.

The Supreme Court held that the Free Exercise Clause protects Old Order Amish parents from a compulsory school attendance law requiring formal schooling after the eighth grade, where the requirement conflicts with sincere religious belief and the state cannot show that an exemption would harm a sufficiently compelling interest. The vote was 6 to 1, with Justices Powell and Rehnquist taking no part and Justice Douglas dissenting in part.

events.instrument: Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, Pub. L. 92-318, 86 Stat. 235, 373
events.summary: Congress enacted Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, providing that no person shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving federal financial assistance. Clause (3) of section 901(a) provides that the section shall not apply to an educational institution controlled by a religious organization if application would not be consistent with the religious tenets of that organization.

events.instrument: Levitt v. Committee for Public Education and Religious Liberty, 413 U.S. 472 (1973)
events.summary: The Supreme Court struck down New York's lump sum per pupil reimbursement of nonpublic schools for testing and record keeping, holding that the state made no effort to ensure that internally prepared tests were free of religious instruction. The Court held that courts could not sever the secular portion of an undifferentiated payment covering both secular and potentially religious services. The Court reached a contrary result on a redrawn New York statute in Committee for Public Education and Religious Liberty v. Regan, 444 U.S. 646 (1980).

events.instrument: Committee for Public Education and Religious Liberty v. Nyquist, 413 U.S. 756 (1973)
events.summary: By a vote of 6 to 3, the Supreme Court struck down New York's maintenance and repair grants to nonpublic schools, its tuition reimbursement for low income parents of nonpublic school pupils, and its tax relief for other nonpublic school parents. The Court held that each measure had the primary effect of advancing religion, the grants because they lacked safeguards confining the money to secular functions, and the tax relief because it operated in the same manner as the tuition grants. The decision's reasoning as applied to programs of true private choice was later confined by Zelman v. Simmons-Harris, 536 U.S. 639 (2002).

By a vote of 6 to 3, the Supreme Court struck down Pennsylvania's Parent Reimbursement Act for Nonpublic Education, which reimbursed parents for a portion of tuition paid to nonpublic schools. The Court found no constitutionally significant difference between the Pennsylvania program and the New York tuition reimbursement struck down the same day in Nyquist, holding that both singled out a class of citizens for a special economic benefit whose intended consequence was to preserve and support religion oriented institutions.

By a vote of 6 to 3, the Supreme Court upheld the application of South Carolina's Educational Facilities Authority Act to revenue bond financing of facilities at a Baptist college. The Court held that the statute had a secular purpose, did not have the primary effect of advancing religion because the institution was not pervasively sectarian, and did not create excessive entanglement.

By a vote of 7 to 0, the Supreme Court held that Mississippi could not lend free textbooks to students attending private schools that practice racial discrimination. The Court held that free textbooks, like tuition grants directed to private school students, are a form of financial assistance that benefits the schools, and that a state may not provide tangible support to institutions that discriminate on the basis of race.

events.instrument: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, Pub. L. 93-112, title V, 87 Stat. 355, 394
events.summary: Congress enacted section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, providing that no otherwise qualified individual with a disability shall, solely by reason of the disability, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any program or activity receiving federal financial assistance. The provision reaches nonpublic schools to the extent they receive federal financial assistance and operates alongside the special education statutes enacted two years later.

By a vote of 6 to 1, the Supreme Court held that Title I of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act requires states to provide educationally deprived private school children with services comparable in quality, scope, and opportunity to those provided to public school children, and that comparable does not mean identical. The Court held that Title I does not mandate any particular method of delivery, so a state may accommodate its own constitutional restrictions through arrangements such as neutral sites or summer programs.

The Supreme Court upheld Pennsylvania's loan of textbooks to nonpublic school children but struck down the direct loan of instructional materials and equipment to nonpublic schools and the provision of auxiliary services such as counseling, testing, and remedial instruction on nonpublic school premises. The Court held that the material and equipment loans advanced the religious mission of predominantly church related schools and that the auxiliary services required comprehensive, discriminating, and continuing state surveillance. The vote was fractured across the several provisions. The instructional materials holding was overruled by Mitchell v. Helms, 530 U.S. 793 (2000), and the auxiliary services holding was overruled by Agostini v. Felton, 521 U.S. 203 (1997).

events.instrument: Education for All Handicapped Children Act of 1975, Pub. L. 94-142, 89 Stat. 773
events.summary: Congress enacted the Education for All Handicapped Children Act, conditioning federal funds on state assurances of a free appropriate public education for all handicapped children, with availability for ages three through eighteen by September 1, 1978, and ages three through twenty-one by September 1, 1980. The act required child identification and evaluation, individualized education programs, nondiscriminatory evaluation procedures, procedural safeguards for children and parents, and education alongside children who are not handicapped to the maximum extent appropriate.
