States were required to assure that handicapped children placed in or referred to private schools by a state or local agency receive special education and related services at no cost to their parents or guardian and in conformity with an individualized education program.

events.instrument: Roemer v. Board of Public Works of Maryland, 426 U.S. 736 (1976)
events.summary: By a vote of 5 to 4, the Supreme Court upheld Maryland's noncategorical annual grants to private colleges, including Roman Catholic affiliated institutions, subject to a statutory prohibition on use for sectarian purposes. The Court held that the recipient colleges were not pervasively sectarian and that the annual character of the subsidy and its administrative review did not create excessive entanglement.

By a vote of 7 to 2, the Supreme Court held that 42 U.S.C. 1981 prohibits private, commercially operated, nonsectarian schools from denying admission on the basis of race, and that this application does not violate parental rights or freedom of association. The Court expressly reserved the question of the statute's application to private sectarian schools that practice racial exclusion on religious grounds.

The Supreme Court upheld Ohio's provision to nonpublic school pupils of textbooks, standardized testing and scoring, diagnostic services, and therapeutic, guidance, and remedial services delivered at neutral sites, while striking down the loan of instructional materials and equipment and the funding of field trip transportation and services. The decision, together with Meek v. Pittenger, marked the outer limits of permissible aid under the Lemon test. The vote was fractured across the several categories. The instructional materials holding was overruled by Mitchell v. Helms, 530 U.S. 793 (2000).

events.instrument: New York v. Cathedral Academy, 434 U.S. 125 (1977)
events.summary: By a vote of 6 to 3, the Supreme Court struck down New York's Chapter 996, which authorized payments to nonpublic schools for testing and record keeping services performed before the statute at issue in Levitt was enjoined. The Court held that reimbursement for the identical services already held unconstitutional would either aid religion or require entanglement, and that a legislature may not override a federal court injunction by invoking the schools' reliance on the invalidated statute.

events.instrument: NLRB v. Catholic Bishop of Chicago, 440 U.S. 490 (1979)
events.summary: By a vote of 5 to 4, the Supreme Court held that the National Labor Relations Act does not confer jurisdiction on the National Labor Relations Board over lay teachers employed by church operated schools. The Court rested on statutory construction, finding no clear expression of an affirmative intention of Congress to cover such teachers, and so did not reach the First Amendment question of government entanglement with religion.

events.instrument: Committee for Public Education and Religious Liberty v. Regan, 444 U.S. 646 (1980)
events.summary: By a vote of 5 to 4, the Supreme Court upheld a New York statute reimbursing nonpublic schools for the cost of administering state prepared tests and maintaining state required records. The Court distinguished Levitt on the ground that the state controlled the content of the tests and that audit safeguards prevented any appreciable risk of religious use of the funds.

events.instrument: St. Martin Evangelical Lutheran Church v. South Dakota, 451 U.S. 772 (1981)
events.summary: By a vote of 8 to 1, the Supreme Court held that employees of church operated schools that are not separately incorporated from the church are in the employ of the church for purposes of 26 U.S.C. 3309(b)(1)(A), so that the schools are outside the federal unemployment tax coverage requirement imposed on the states. The decision turned on statutory construction of the Federal Unemployment Tax Act.

events.instrument: Board of Education of the Hendrick Hudson Central School District v. Rowley, 458 U.S. 176 (1982)
events.summary: By a vote of 5 to 3, the Supreme Court held that a state satisfies the free appropriate public education requirement of the Education for All Handicapped Children Act by providing personalized instruction with sufficient support services to permit the child to benefit educationally, where the services meet state educational standards and conform to the individualized education program. The act does not require a state to maximize the potential of each handicapped child commensurate with the opportunity provided to other children.

events.instrument: Bob Jones University v. United States, 461 U.S. 574 (1983), decided with Goldsboro Christian Schools, Inc. v. United States
events.summary: By a vote of 8 to 1, the Supreme Court held that private schools maintaining racially discriminatory admissions or dating policies do not qualify for tax exempt status under section 501(c)(3), because an institution seeking that exemption must serve a public purpose and must not act contrary to established public policy. The Court held that the governmental interest in eradicating racial discrimination in education outweighs the burden on the schools' exercise of their religious beliefs, and that no less restrictive means were available.

By a vote of 5 to 4, the Supreme Court upheld a Minnesota income tax deduction for tuition, textbooks, and transportation expenses, available to the parents of public and nonpublic school children alike. The Court held that the deduction satisfied the Lemon test because it had a secular purpose, was available for educational expenses incurred by all parents, and directed any benefit to religious schools only through the independent decisions of individual taxpayers. The decision is the foundation of later tax deduction and tax credit scholarship programs.

events.instrument: School Committee of the Town of Burlington v. Department of Education of Massachusetts, 471 U.S. 359 (1985)
events.summary: In a unanimous decision, the Supreme Court held that a reviewing court may order a school district to reimburse parents for private school expenses where the court determines that the private placement rather than the district's proposed individualized education program was appropriate under the Education of the Handicapped Act. The Court held that a parental change of placement contrary to the stay put provision does not waive the right to reimbursement, though parents bear the financial risk if the district's proposed program is ultimately found appropriate.

events.instrument: School District of the City of Grand Rapids v. Ball, 473 U.S. 373 (1985)
events.summary: By a vote of 5 to 4, the Supreme Court struck down Grand Rapids' Shared Time and Community Education programs, under which public employees taught supplementary classes in classrooms leased from nonpublic schools, holding that the programs had the principal effect of advancing religion. The Court identified three defects: the risk that state paid instructors would inculcate religion, the message of state endorsement conveyed by placing public instruction inside religious schools, and the subsidy to the religious mission of the schools whose secular teaching burdens the state assumed. The decision was overruled in relevant part by Agostini v. Felton, 521 U.S. 203 (1997).

By a vote of 5 to 4, the Supreme Court struck down New York City's use of Title I funds to send public school teachers into parochial schools to provide remedial instruction to eligible children, holding that the monitoring required to keep the instruction secular produced excessive entanglement of church and state and a permanent and pervasive state presence in sectarian schools. The decision was overruled by Agostini v. Felton, 521 U.S. 203 (1997).

events.instrument: Witters v. Washington Department of Services for the Blind, 474 U.S. 481 (1986)
events.summary: In a unanimous decision, the Supreme Court held that the Establishment Clause does not bar a state vocational rehabilitation program from paying aid to a blind student who chose to use it at a Christian college to prepare for the ministry. The Court reasoned that the aid is paid to the student, who transmits it to the institution of his choice, so that any aid ultimately flowing to a religious institution results from the genuinely independent and private choices of aid recipients.

events.instrument: Ohio Civil Rights Commission v. Dayton Christian Schools, Inc., 477 U.S. 619 (1986)
events.summary: The Supreme Court held that a federal court should abstain under Younger v. Harris from enjoining a state civil rights agency's administrative proceeding against a religious school over the nonrenewal of a teacher's contract, where the school has an adequate opportunity to raise its constitutional objections in the state proceedings and on state judicial review. The Court held that the elimination of prohibited sex discrimination is a sufficiently important state interest to support abstention, and it did not reach the merits of the school's First Amendment defense. The majority opinion was by Justice Rehnquist, with Justice Stevens concurring in the judgment.

events.instrument: Education of the Handicapped Act Amendments of 1986, Pub. L. 99-457, 100 Stat. 1145
events.summary: Congress amended the Education of the Handicapped Act to add Part H, a program of grants to states for coordinated, multidisciplinary early intervention services for handicapped infants and toddlers from birth through age two, and to extend the preschool grant program to children ages three through five. Services were defined to cover physical, cognitive, language, psychosocial, and self help development and to include family training, counseling, and home visits.

events.instrument: Corporation of the Presiding Bishop of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints v. Amos, 483 U.S. 327 (1987)
events.summary: The Supreme Court held that the section 702 exemption permitting religious organizations to prefer coreligionists in employment does not violate the Establishment Clause when applied to the secular nonprofit activities of a religious organization. The Court held that the exemption serves the permissible purpose of reducing governmental interference with the ability of religious organizations to define and carry out their missions, that the government itself does not advance religion by leaving them free to do so, and that the exemption avoids entanglement.

By a vote of 5 to 4, the Supreme Court held that the Adolescent Family Life Act, which authorized federal grants to public and nonprofit private organizations including religious organizations for counseling services, is not invalid on its face under the Establishment Clause, because it has a legitimate secular purpose and does not impermissibly advance religion. The Court remanded for consideration of whether particular grants had been administered unconstitutionally.

events.instrument: Employment Division, Department of Human Resources of Oregon v. Smith, 494 U.S. 872 (1990)
events.summary: By a vote of 5 to 4, the Supreme Court held that the Free Exercise Clause does not require an exemption from a neutral law of general applicability that incidentally burdens religious conduct, so that individuals may not claim an exemption from such a law on the ground that their religious beliefs conflict with it. Congress responded with the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993, which the Supreme Court held exceeded congressional power as applied to the states in City of Boerne v. Flores, 521 U.S. 507 (1997).

events.instrument: Education of the Handicapped Act Amendments of 1990, Pub. L. 101-476, 104 Stat. 1103
events.summary: Congress amended the Education of the Handicapped Act, replacing the statutory term handicapped children with children with disabilities throughout and adding autism and traumatic brain injury to the categories of qualifying disability. The amended statute is the successor to the Education for All Handicapped Children Act of 1975 and is commonly known as the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act.

events.instrument: Lamb's Chapel v. Center Moriches Union Free School District, 508 U.S. 384 (1993)
events.summary: By a vote of 6 to 3 on the judgment, the Supreme Court held that a school district that opens its property to after hours community use may not deny a church access to exhibit a film series on family and child rearing, because the denial discriminated against the religious viewpoint from which the otherwise permissible subject was addressed. The Court held that permitting the use would not violate the Establishment Clause, since the showing would occur outside school hours, would not be sponsored by the school, and would be open to the public.

events.instrument: Zobrest v. Catalina Foothills School District, 509 U.S. 1 (1993)
events.summary: By a vote of 5 to 4, the Supreme Court held that the Establishment Clause does not bar a school district from providing a sign language interpreter under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act to a deaf student attending a Roman Catholic high school. The Court reasoned that the service is part of a general government program distributing benefits neutrally to any child qualifying as disabled, and that the aid reaches the religious school only as a result of the private decision of the parents.

events.instrument: Florence County School District Four v. Carter, 510 U.S. 7 (1993)
events.summary: In a unanimous decision, the Supreme Court held that parents may obtain reimbursement for a unilateral private school placement even where the private school is not approved by the state, provided the public school district failed to provide a free appropriate public education and the private placement was otherwise proper under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act. The Court held that the statutory requirements for state approved placements do not apply to parental placements.

events.instrument: Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993, Pub. L. 103-141, 107 Stat. 1488
events.summary: Congress enacted the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, providing that government may substantially burden a person's exercise of religion only if it demonstrates that the burden is in furtherance of a compelling governmental interest and is the least restrictive means of furthering that interest. The findings identify Employment Division v. Smith, 494 U.S. 872 (1990), as having virtually eliminated the requirement that government justify burdens on religious exercise imposed by laws neutral toward religion. The Supreme Court held the act unconstitutional as applied to the states in City of Boerne v. Flores, 521 U.S. 507 (1997), leaving it in force against the federal government.

events.instrument: Board of Education of Kiryas Joel Village School District v. Grumet, 512 U.S. 687 (1994)
events.summary: By a vote of 6 to 3, the Supreme Court struck down a New York statute creating a separate public school district whose boundaries followed those of a village inhabited by members of the Satmar Hasidic community, holding that the statute delegated governmental authority on the basis of religious identity. The Court held that the state could address the community's need for special education services through generally applicable legislation rather than a measure directed at one religious group.

events.instrument: Improving America's Schools Act of 1994, Pub. L. 103-382, 108 Stat. 3518
events.summary: Congress reauthorized the Elementary and Secondary Education Act as the Improving America's Schools Act of 1994. Section 1120 governs the equitable participation of private school children in Title I services, and sections 1112 and 1115 require local educational agencies to consult and coordinate with private school officials in identifying eligible children and designing services. Section 1111(f) provides that nothing in the part authorizes a federal officer or employee to mandate, direct, or control a state, local educational agency, or school's specific instructional content. The reauthorization followed the invalidation of on premises Title I instruction in Aguilar v. Felton and preceded its restoration by Agostini v. Felton, 521 U.S. 203 (1997).

events.instrument: Elementary and Secondary Education Act sec. 14508, as added by Pub. L. 103-382, title I, sec. 101, 108 Stat. 3905 (20 U.S.C. 8898)
events.summary: The Improving America's Schools Act of 1994 added section 14508 to the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, codified at 20 U.S.C. 8898 and titled by the codifiers as relating to the applicability of the chapter to home schools. The section was enacted on October 20, 1994, and has since been repealed. The operative statutory text was not retrieved from a primary source, so only the existence, enactment date, codification, and subject of the provision are recorded here.

Article I, Section 4 of the Alaska Constitution provides: "No law shall be made respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." The clause tracks the federal First Amendment rather than adding an independent state prohibition on aid, and it sits alongside the far more restrictive funding bar in Article VII, Section 1.

The Arkansas Constitution of 1874 contains no anti-aid or no-sectarian-appropriation clause. The education article was retrieved and checked; Article 14, Section 2, the only funding restriction it carries, provides: "No money or property belonging to the public school fund, or to this State, for the benefit of schools or universities, shall ever be used for any other than for the respective purposes to which it belongs." The restriction is one of purpose rather than of recipient, and it names neither sectarian institutions nor private schools. Arkansas is accordingly recorded as a jurisdiction with no Blaine-type provision.

Article V, Section 34 of the Colorado Constitution, also adopted in 1876, provides: "No appropriation shall be made for charitable, industrial, educational or benevolent purposes to any person, corporation or community not under the absolute control of the state, nor to any denominational or sectarian institution or association." The clause is of the broad type: it bars educational appropriations to any recipient outside the absolute control of the state, which takes in secular private schools as well as denominational ones.

The Connecticut Constitution contains no anti-aid or no-sectarian-appropriation provision. The education article was retrieved and checked: Article Eighth requires free public elementary and secondary schools, maintains a system of higher education, confirms the charter of Yale College, and preserves the perpetual School Fund, and it carries no clause barring appropriation to sectarian or private schools. The constitution was adopted December 14, 1965, and proclaimed December 30, 1965. Connecticut is accordingly recorded as a jurisdiction with no Blaine-type provision.

Article Seventh of the Connecticut Constitution is a compelled-support clause that cuts against, rather than for, a funding bar: "no person shall by law be compelled to join or support, nor be classed or associated with, any congregation, church or religious association," and "No preference shall be given by law to any religious society or denomination in the state. Each shall have and enjoy the same and equal powers, rights and privileges, and may support and maintain the ministers or teachers of its society or denomination." The article protects individual conscience and equality among denominations; it does not prohibit appropriations.

events.instrument: District of Columbia Home Rule Act, Pub. L. 93-198, 87 Stat. 774
events.summary: The District of Columbia has no constitution of its own and therefore no state constitutional anti-aid provision. Its charter is the District of Columbia Home Rule Act, Public Law 93-198, 87 Stat. 774, enacted December 24, 1973, which delegates legislative powers to an elected Council subject to the retention by Congress of ultimate legislative authority over the District. The text of the Act was retrieved and checked: it contains no provision restricting the use of public funds for religious or sectarian schools, and its education provisions concern the Board of Education and the budget rather than the recipients of school money. Through 1994 the District is accordingly recorded as a jurisdiction with no anti-aid provision.

events.instrument: Fla. Const. of 1885, Decl. of Rights, § 6
events.summary: Section 6 of the Declaration of Rights of the Florida Constitution of 1885 provides: "No preference shall be given by law to any church, sect or mode of worship, and no money shall ever be taken from the public treasury directly or indirectly in aid of any church, sect or religious denomination, or in aid of any sectarian institution." This is the antecedent of the anti-aid language carried into the revision of 1968; the bar runs to churches, sects, denominations, and sectarian institutions rather than to private schools as a class.

Article I, Section 3 of the Florida Constitution, as revised in 1968, carries the anti-aid language forward into the religious freedom section: "No revenue of the state or any political subdivision or agency thereof shall ever be taken from the public treasury directly or indirectly in aid of any church, sect, or religious denomination or in aid of any sectarian institution." The clause is sectarian-specific and does not reach secular private schools; it applies to all state and local revenue rather than only to school funds.

events.instrument: Ga. Const. of 1877, art. I, § I, ¶ XIV
events.summary: Georgia's anti-aid clause entered the constitution as Article I, Section I, Paragraph XIV of the Constitution of 1877, as ratified: "No money shall ever be taken from the public treasury, directly or indirectly, in aid of any church, sect, or denomination of religionists, or of any sectarian institution." The bar is sectarian-specific and applies to all money taken from the public treasury rather than to school funds alone.

events.instrument: Ga. Const. art. I, § II, ¶ VII
events.summary: The Georgia anti-aid clause of 1877 is carried forward in the present constitution with changed numbering, appearing as Article I, Section II, Paragraph VII: "No money shall ever be taken from the public treasury, directly or indirectly, in aid of any church, sect, cult, or religious denomination or of any sectarian institution." The operative language is that of 1877 with the word "cult" added; the original adoption year is 1877 and the paragraph number reflects later renumbering rather than a fresh enactment.

Hawaii's no-aid clause was framed by the Constitutional Convention of 1950 and stood in the education article as Article IX, Section 1: "nor shall public funds be appropriated for the support or benefit of any sectarian or private educational institution." The clause is of the broad type, reaching private educational institutions of every kind rather than sectarian ones alone. It survived the amendments of 1964, which concerned the board of education and the superintendent, without change to the funding bar.

events.instrument: Haw. Const. art. X, § 1 (renumbered from art. IX by the Constitutional Convention of 1978)
events.summary: The education article was renumbered from Article IX to Article X by the Constitutional Convention of 1978 and the election of November 7, 1978. As renumbered, Article X, Section 1 requires a statewide system of public schools "free from sectarian control" and provides that "nor shall public funds be appropriated for the support or benefit of any sectarian or nonsectarian private educational institution," subject to an exception permitting the proceeds of special purpose revenue bonds authorized under Article VII, Section 12 to finance or assist certain not-for-profit early childhood facilities and private schools. The section was further amended in 1994 and in 2002.

Article IX, Section 5 of the Idaho Constitution, adopted with the constitution framed in 1889 and effective at statehood in 1890, provides that neither the legislature nor any county, city, town, township, school district, or other public corporation "shall ever make any appropriation, or pay from any public fund or moneys whatever, anything in aid of any church or sectarian or religious society," and bars grants or donations of land, money, or property to any church or for any sectarian or religious purpose. The bar is sectarian-specific rather than directed at private schools generally. A later proviso permits a health facilities authority to finance private not-for-profit health facilities owned or operated by a church or sectarian religious society.

Article X, Section 3 of the Illinois Constitution of 1970 provides that neither the General Assembly nor any county, city, town, township, school district, or other public corporation "shall ever make any appropriation or pay from any public fund whatever, anything in aid of any church or sectarian purpose," and that public funds shall not be used to aid or maintain any school, academy, seminary, college, university, or other educational institution controlled in whole or in part by any church or religious denomination. The bar is sectarian-specific: it turns on church or denominational control rather than on private status. The constitution was framed by a convention sitting from December 8, 1969, to September 3, 1970, and took effect in 1970.

Article 1, Section 6 of the Indiana Constitution, adopted February 10, 1851, and effective November 1, 1851, provides: "No money shall be drawn from the treasury, for the benefit of any religious or theological institution." The clause is directed at religious and theological institutions and says nothing of private schools as a class, which has left the Indiana courts to decide whether aid that reaches a religious school through the choice of a parent is money drawn for the benefit of the institution.

Article 1, Section 4 of the Indiana Constitution of 1851 is a compelled-support and no-preference clause: "No preference shall be given, by law, to any creed, religious society, or mode of worship; and no man shall be compelled to attend, erect, or support any place of worship, or to maintain any ministry, against his consent." The no-preference language cuts against singling out religious schools for exclusion as readily as it cuts against favoring them.

The Iowa Constitution of 1857 contains no anti-aid or no-sectarian-appropriation clause. The education article was retrieved and checked: Article IX, Second Division, Section 3 makes the proceeds of the federal school land grant a perpetual fund whose interest is "inviolably appropriated to the support of common schools throughout the state," which restricts the use of that particular fund rather than barring appropriations to sectarian or private schools. Iowa is accordingly recorded as a jurisdiction with no Blaine-type provision.

Article I, Section 3 of the Iowa Constitution is a compelled-support clause: "The general assembly shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; nor shall any person be compelled to attend any place of worship, pay tithes, taxes, or other rates for building or repairing places of worship, or the maintenance of any minister, or ministry." It restrains compelled taxation for worship and ministry and does not address appropriations to schools.

Article 6, Section 6(c) of the Kansas Constitution provides: "No religious sect or sects shall control any part of the public educational funds." The clause is a bar on sectarian control of school funds rather than a prohibition on appropriations to private or religious schools, which makes it markedly narrower than the appropriation bans of neighboring states. The present Article 6 was proposed at the special session of 1966 and took effect November 8, 1966, replacing the education article carried from the constitutional convention of 1859.

Section 189 of the Kentucky Constitution provides: "No portion of any fund or tax now existing, or that may hereafter be raised or levied for educational purposes, shall be appropriated to, or used by, or in aid of, any church, sectarian or denominational school." The bar is sectarian-specific and confined to funds and taxes raised for educational purposes. The section was ratified August 3, 1891, and revised September 28, 1891, and it has not been amended since.

The Louisiana Constitution of 1974 contains no anti-aid or no-sectarian-appropriation clause. The education article was retrieved and checked section by section: Article VIII provides for the public educational system, the state superintendent, the boards, parish school boards, appropriations to state boards and to higher education, funding and apportionment, and Tulane University, and none of its sixteen sections bars appropriation to sectarian, religious, or nonpublic schools. Section 4 contemplates nonpublic schooling directly, requiring the State Board of Elementary and Secondary Education to approve a private school on application where the standards are met. Louisiana is accordingly recorded as a jurisdiction with no Blaine-type provision.

Article I, Section 8 of the Louisiana Constitution of 1974 provides: "No law shall be enacted respecting an establishment of religion or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." The clause follows the federal formulation and adds no independent state restriction on the appropriation of public money to religious schools.

The Maine Constitution contains no anti-aid or no-sectarian-appropriation clause. The education article was retrieved and checked: Article VIII, Part First, Section 1 requires the Legislature to compel the towns to make suitable provision for the support and maintenance of public schools, and it authorizes the Legislature to "encourage and suitably endow, from time to time, as the circumstances of the people may authorize, all academies, colleges and seminaries of learning within the State" — an affirmative grant of power to aid institutions outside the public system rather than a bar. Maine is accordingly recorded as a jurisdiction with no Blaine-type provision, which is why its town tuitioning litigation has turned on the federal religion clauses rather than on a state anti-aid provision.

Article I, Section 3 of the Maine Constitution protects the natural and unalienable right of all individuals to worship according to conscience, provides that no person shall be hurt, molested, or restrained in liberty or estate for worshipping God according to conscience, and forbids the establishment by law of any subordination or preference of one sect or denomination to another. The no-preference language is an affirmative protection that cuts against excluding religious schools from a generally available benefit.

The Maryland Constitution of 1867 contains no anti-aid or no-sectarian-appropriation clause. The education article was retrieved and checked in full: Article VIII, Section 1 directs the General Assembly to establish a system of free public schools, Section 2 continues the existing system until the close of the first session, and Section 3 provides that "The School Fund of the State shall be kept inviolate, and appropriated only to the purposes of Education." The restriction in Section 3 is one of purpose and names neither sectarian institutions nor private schools. Maryland is accordingly recorded as a jurisdiction with no Blaine-type provision.

Article 36 of the Maryland Declaration of Rights provides that as it is the duty of every man to worship God in the manner he thinks most acceptable, "all persons are equally entitled to protection in their religious liberty," and that no person ought by any law to be molested in person or estate on account of religious persuasion. The article is a guarantee of religious liberty and equality and imposes no restriction on the appropriation of public funds.

The Massachusetts anti-aid amendment was ratified May 23, 1855, as Article XVIII of the Articles of Amendment. As adopted it provided that all moneys raised by taxation in the towns and cities for the support of public schools, and all moneys appropriated by the state for the support of common schools, "shall be applied to, and expended in, no other schools than those which are conducted according to law, under the order and superintendence of the authorities of the town or city in which the money is to be expended; and such moneys shall never be appropriated to any religious sect for the maintenance exclusively of its own schools." The original bar was of the broad type, confining school money to schools under public superintendence.

Article XLVI of the Articles of Amendment, adopted by the delegates August 30, 1917, and ratified by the people November 6, 1917, was adopted in place of and in substitution for Article XVIII, broadening the anti-aid rule beyond school money to grants, appropriations, and uses of public money or property, and beyond schools to charitable and religious undertakings not publicly owned and controlled.

Article CIII of the Articles of Amendment, agreed to by the General Court in the political years 1972 and 1973 and approved by the voters November 5, 1974, replaced Section 2 of Article XVIII in its 1917 form. In its present shape the section provides that "No grant, appropriation or use of public money or property or loan of credit shall be made or authorized by the Commonwealth or any political subdivision thereof for the purpose of founding, maintaining or aiding any infirmary, hospital, institution, primary or secondary school, or charitable or religious undertaking which is not publicly owned and under the exclusive control, order and supervision of public officers or public agents authorized by the Commonwealth or federal authority or both," subject to stated exceptions. The bar turns on public ownership and control rather than on religion, which is why it reaches secular private schools as fully as religious ones.

Article VIII, Section 2 of the Michigan Constitution of 1963, effective January 1, 1964, required the legislature to maintain and support a system of free public elementary and secondary schools and required every school district to educate its pupils without discrimination as to religion, creed, race, color, or national origin. As adopted the section carried no anti-aid language; the prohibition now associated with it was added by the initiated amendment of 1970.

Article XIII, Section 2 of the Minnesota Constitution, adopted October 13, 1857, provides: "In no case shall any public money or property be appropriated or used for the support of schools wherein the distinctive doctrines, creeds or tenets of any particular Christian or other religious sect are promulgated or taught." The bar turns on what is taught rather than on who owns the school, so it reaches a religious school by reason of its instruction and leaves a secular private school untouched. The constitution was generally revised on November 5, 1974, without change to the substance of this section.

Article I, Section 16 of the Minnesota Constitution guarantees liberty of conscience, forbids compelling any person to attend, erect, or support any place of worship or to maintain any religious or ecclesiastical ministry against his consent, forbids any preference by law to any religious establishment or mode of worship, and closes with a funding bar: "nor shall any money be drawn from the treasury for the benefit of any religious societies or religious or theological seminaries." The section combines an affirmative protection of conscience with a second, narrower appropriations restriction.

Article 8, Section 208 of the Mississippi Constitution of 1890 provides: "No religious or other sect or sects shall ever control any part of the school or other educational funds of this state; nor shall any funds be appropriated toward the support of any sectarian school, or to any school that at the time of receiving such appropriation is not conducted as a free school." The section joins a sectarian-specific bar to a broader one: an appropriation to any school not conducted as a free school is forbidden whether or not the school is religious.

Montana's original anti-aid provision was Article XI, Section 8 of the Constitution of 1889, which forbade any direct or indirect appropriation "in aid of any church, or for any sectarian purpose, or to aid in the support of any school, academy, seminary, college, university, or other literary, scientific institution, controlled in whole or in part by any church, sect or denomination whatever." The bar turns on church, sect, or denominational control.

The Constitution of 1972 carried the anti-aid rule forward as Article X, Section 6, which forbids the legislature, counties, cities, towns, school districts, and public corporations to make "any direct or indirect appropriation or payment from any public fund or monies, or any grant of lands or other property for any sectarian purpose or to aid any church, school, academy, seminary, college, university, or other literary or scientific institution, controlled in whole or in part by any church, sect, or denomination." Subsection (2), which has no counterpart in the text of 1889, provides that the section does not apply to funds from federal sources provided to the state for distribution to non-public education.

Nebraska's no-aid provision entered the constitution in 1875 as Article VIII, Section 11. It was transferred to Article VII, Section 11 by the constitutional convention of 1919 and 1920, and it has been amended three times since, in 1920, 1972, and 1976.

events.instrument: Neb. Const. art. VII, § 11 (as amended 1976, Laws 1976, LB 666, § 1)
events.summary: As it stands after the amendment of 1976, Article VII, Section 11 of the Nebraska Constitution provides: "Notwithstanding any other provision in the Constitution, appropriation of public funds shall not be made to any school or institution of learning not owned or exclusively controlled by the state or a political subdivision thereof," with a limited exception permitting contracts with non-state institutions for nonsectarian educational services for children with disabilities, a requirement that public schools remain free of sectarian instruction, a restriction on the state's acceptance of money for sectarian purposes, and a bar on religious tests for teachers or students. The provision is of the broad type: it turns on public ownership and control, so it reaches secular private schools as well as religious ones. The third paragraph, on federal grants, was restored following the 1980 decision in Cunningham v. Exon.

Article 11, Section 9 of the Nevada Constitution, adopted with the constitution of 1864, provides: "No sectarian instruction shall be imparted or tolerated in any school or University that may be established under this Constitution." The clause bars sectarian instruction in state schools; it is not itself an appropriations restriction.

New Hampshire's anti-aid language was added in 1877 to Part Second, Article 83 of the constitution, the article on the encouragement of literature and trade. The added sentence provides: "no money raised by taxation shall ever be granted or applied for the use of the schools of institutions of any religious sect or denomination." The bar is sectarian-specific and confined to money raised by taxation; it does not by its terms reach secular private schools.

events.instrument: N.J. Const. of 1947, art. VIII, § IV, ¶¶ 1-3
events.summary: The New Jersey Constitution of 1947 contains no anti-aid or no-sectarian-appropriation clause. The education section was retrieved and checked: Article VIII, Section IV, Paragraph 1 requires a thorough and efficient system of free public schools, Paragraph 2 makes the school fund a perpetual fund whose income is annually appropriated to the support of free public schools and forbids the Legislature to borrow, appropriate, or use it for any other purpose, and Paragraph 3 authorizes the Legislature to provide for the transportation of children "to and from any school." The restriction in Paragraph 2 runs to a particular fund rather than to a class of recipient, and Paragraph 3 expressly contemplates transportation to nonpublic schools. New Jersey is accordingly recorded as a jurisdiction with no Blaine-type provision.

Article I, Paragraph 3 of the New Jersey Constitution is a compelled-support clause: no person shall be deprived of the privilege of worshipping according to conscience, "nor shall any person be obliged to pay tithes, taxes, or other rates for building or repairing any church or churches, place or places of worship, or for the maintenance of any minister or ministry, contrary to what he believes to be right or has deliberately and voluntarily engaged to perform." Paragraph 4 adds that there shall be no establishment of one religious sect in preference to another. The protections are individual and comparative; neither bars an appropriation to a school.

Article XII, Section 3 of the New Mexico Constitution provides that the schools, colleges, universities, and other educational institutions provided for by the constitution "shall forever remain under the exclusive control of the state, and no part of the proceeds arising from the sale or disposal of any lands granted to the state by congress, or any other funds appropriated, levied or collected for educational purposes, shall be used for the support of any sectarian, denominational or private school, college or university." The clause names private schools alongside sectarian and denominational ones, which places it in the broad category. It was part of the constitution under which New Mexico entered the Union in 1912 and has not been amended.

New York's anti-aid clause entered the constitution at the convention of 1894 as Article IX, Section 4. It forbids the state and its subdivisions to use property, credit, or public money, directly or indirectly, in aid or maintenance of any school or institution of learning wholly or in part under the control or direction of any religious denomination, or in which any denominational tenet or doctrine is taught, other than for examination or inspection.

The New York anti-aid clause was renumbered and amended by the Constitutional Convention of 1938 and approved by the people November 8, 1938, the amendment adding the proviso that the legislature may provide for the transportation of children to and from any school or institution of learning. It was renumbered again, without substantive change, by the amendment approved November 6, 1962, at which time the former Section 4 was repealed. The bar turns on denominational control or denominational teaching rather than on private status, so it does not reach a secular private school.

The North Carolina Constitution contains no anti-aid or no-sectarian-appropriation clause. The education article was retrieved and checked: Article IX, Section 1 declares that "Religion, morality, and knowledge being necessary to good government and the happiness of mankind, schools, libraries, and the means of education shall forever be encouraged"; Section 2 requires a general and uniform system of free public schools; and Section 6 requires the State school fund to be "faithfully appropriated and used exclusively for establishing and maintaining a uniform system of free public schools." The restriction in Section 6 runs to a particular fund rather than to a class of recipient. North Carolina is accordingly recorded as a jurisdiction with no Blaine-type provision.

Article I, Section 13 of the North Carolina Constitution provides: "All persons have a natural and inalienable right to worship Almighty God according to the dictates of their own consciences, and no human authority shall, in any case whatever, control or interfere with the rights of conscience." The section is an affirmative protection of conscience and carries no funding restriction.

Article VIII, Section 5 of the North Dakota Constitution provides: "No money raised for the support of the public schools of the state shall be appropriated to or used for the support of any sectarian school." Section 1 of the same article requires a system of public schools "free from sectarian control." The bar is sectarian-specific and confined to money raised for the support of the public schools; it does not by its terms reach secular private schools or public money raised for other purposes. The constitution was adopted by the constitutional convention on August 17, 1889, and ratified by the voters on October 1, 1889.

Article II, Section 5 of the Oklahoma Constitution, adopted with the constitution of 1907, provides: "No public money or property shall ever be appropriated, applied, donated, or used, directly or indirectly, for the use, benefit, or support of any sect, church, denomination, or system of religion, or for the use, benefit, or support of any priest, preacher, minister, or other religious teacher or dignitary, or sectarian institution as such." The clause is sectarian-specific but unusually wide in the conduct it reaches, covering indirect application and donation as well as appropriation.

Article I, Section 5 of the Oregon Constitution of 1857 provides: "No money shall be drawn from the Treasury for the benefit of any religeous, or theological institution, nor shall any money be appropriated for the payment of any religeous services in either house of the Legislative Assembly." The archaic spelling is that of the original text. Oregon has no education-specific anti-aid article; the restriction is this Bill of Rights clause, which is directed at religious and theological institutions and does not reach secular private schools.

Sections 2, 3, and 4 of Article I of the Oregon Constitution secure the natural right to worship Almighty God according to conscience, provide that "No law shall in any case whatever control the free exercise, and enjoyment of religeous opinions, or interfere with the rights of conscience," and forbid any religious test as a qualification for office. These are affirmative protections standing alongside the appropriations bar of Section 5.

Article III, Section 15 of the Pennsylvania Constitution provides: "No money raised for the support of the public schools of the Commonwealth shall be appropriated to or used for the support of any sectarian school." The clause entered the constitution with the Constitution of 1874 and carries its present section number following the revisions of 1967 and 1968. The bar is sectarian-specific and confined to money raised for the support of the public schools.

Article III, Section 29 of the Pennsylvania Constitution provides: "No appropriation shall be made for charitable, educational or benevolent purposes to any person or community nor to any denomination and sectarian institution, corporation or association." The clause is the broader of the pair, reaching educational appropriations to any person or community as well as to denominational and sectarian institutions.

The Rhode Island Constitution contains no anti-aid or no-sectarian-appropriation clause. The education article was retrieved and checked: Article XII makes it the duty of the General Assembly to promote public schools and public libraries, makes the school fund a perpetual fund, requires donations for education to be applied on the donors' terms, and forbids the General Assembly to divert the fund from those uses. The restriction runs to a particular fund rather than to a class of recipient. Rhode Island is accordingly recorded as a jurisdiction with no Blaine-type provision.

Article I, Section 3 of the Rhode Island Constitution is a compelled-support clause: "No person shall be compelled to frequent or to support any religious worship, place, or ministry whatever, except in fulfillment of such person's voluntary contract." The section further provides that no person shall be penalized, disqualified from office, or otherwise burdened on account of religious belief. It restrains compulsion of the individual and does not restrict appropriations.

Article XI, Section 4 of the South Carolina Constitution provides: "No money shall be paid from public funds nor shall the credit of the State or any of its political subdivisions be used for the direct benefit of any religious or other private educational institution." The clause is of the broad type, reaching private educational institutions of every kind, and it turns on whether the benefit is direct. It took its present form when Act No. 42 of 1973 revised and rewrote Article XI, substituting the present Sections 1 through 4 for the former Sections 1 through 12.

Article VIII, Section 16 of the South Dakota Constitution, adopted with the constitution of 1889, provides: "No appropriation of lands, money or other property or credits to aid any sectarian school shall ever be made by the state, or any county or municipality within the state, nor shall the state or any county or municipality within the state accept any grant, conveyance, gift or bequest of lands, money or other property to be used for sectarian purposes, and no sectarian instruction shall be allowed in any school or institution aided or supported by the state." The bar is sectarian-specific and reaches receipts as well as appropriations.

The Tennessee Constitution contains no anti-aid or no-sectarian-appropriation clause. The education section was retrieved and checked: Article XI, Section 12, in the text as presently published, recognizes the inherent value of education, requires the General Assembly to provide for the maintenance, support, and eligibility standards of a system of free public schools, and permits the General Assembly to establish and support such post-secondary educational institutions as it determines. The section carries no bar on appropriations to sectarian or private schools and no restriction confining school money to public schools. Tennessee is accordingly recorded as a jurisdiction with no Blaine-type provision.

Article I, Section 3 of the Tennessee Constitution is a compelled-support and no-preference clause: all men have a natural and indefeasible right to worship according to conscience, "no man can of right be compelled to attend, erect, or support any place of worship, or to maintain any minister against his consent," no human authority may control or interfere with the rights of conscience, "and that no preference shall ever be given, by law, to any religious establishment or mode of worship." The no-preference language is an affirmative protection that cuts against excluding religious schools from a generally available benefit.

Article I, Section 7 of the Texas Constitution, adopted February 15, 1876, provides: "No money shall be appropriated, or drawn from the Treasury for the benefit of any sect, or religious society, theological or religious seminary." The bar is sectarian-specific and names no schools beyond theological and religious seminaries, which leaves ordinary religious day schools and secular private schools outside its express terms. Texas has no education-specific anti-aid article.

Article X, Section 9 of the Utah Constitution provides: "Neither the state of Utah nor its political subdivisions may make any appropriation for the direct support of any school or educational institution controlled by any religious organization." Section 1 of the same article requires the state's public education and higher education systems to be "free from sectarian control," and Section 8 forbids any religious or partisan test as a condition of employment, admission, or attendance. The bar turns on religious control and on directness of support, so it does not by its terms reach secular private schools. The constitution took effect with statehood in 1896; the section carries its present number following later revision of the education article.

The Vermont Constitution contains no anti-aid or no-sectarian-appropriation clause. The education provision was retrieved and checked: Chapter II, Section 68 requires that "a competent number of schools ought to be maintained in each town unless the general assembly permits other provisions for the convenient instruction of youth," and provides that "All religious societies, or bodies of people that may be united or incorporated for the advancement of religion and learning, or for other pious and charitable purposes, shall be encouraged and protected." The section protects religious societies rather than barring aid to them. Vermont is accordingly recorded as a jurisdiction with no Blaine-type provision, which is why its town tuitioning disputes have turned on the federal religion clauses and on the compelled-support clause of Chapter I.

Chapter I, Article 3rd of the Vermont Constitution is a compelled-support clause: all persons have a natural and unalienable right to worship Almighty God according to the dictates of their own consciences, "and that no person ought to, or of right can be compelled to attend any religious worship, or erect or support any place of worship, or maintain any minister, contrary to the dictates of conscience." The article further provides that no person may be deprived of civil rights on account of religious sentiment. It restrains compulsion of the individual taxpayer rather than appropriation by the state.

Article VIII, Section 10 of the Virginia Constitution, effective July 1, 1971, provides: "No appropriation of public funds shall be made to any school or institution of learning not owned or exclusively controlled by the State or some subdivision thereof, except (a) a general law may permit students to attend, upon a tuition basis, schools or institutions of learning not so owned or controlled, and (b) appropriations may be made to nonsectarian institutions for the reform of youthful criminals and to such other institutions as the General Assembly may deem proper." The bar is of the broad type, turning on public ownership and exclusive control rather than on religion, and the tuition exception is written into the clause itself.

Article VIII, Section 11 of the Virginia Constitution permits the General Assembly to provide for loans and grants to or on behalf of students attending nonprofit institutions of higher education whose primary purpose is to provide collegiate or graduate education "and not to provide religious training or theological education." The section is an express carve-out from the appropriations bar of Section 10 and conditions the aid on the institution's purpose rather than on its ownership.

Article I, Section 11 of the Washington Constitution, adopted with the constitution of 1889, provides: "No public money or property shall be appropriated for or applied to any religious worship, exercise or instruction, or the support of any religious establishment." The bar runs to religious worship, exercise, instruction, and establishments; because it reaches religious instruction it has been read to restrict aid that flows to religious schooling, while leaving secular private schools outside its terms.

Article IX, Section 4 of the Washington Constitution provides: "All schools maintained, supported or assisted by the public funds shall be forever free from sectarian control or influence." The clause conditions public support on freedom from sectarian control rather than prohibiting support outright, which makes it a control provision rather than an appropriations ban, though in practice it has the same effect on aid to a church-controlled school.

The West Virginia Constitution of 1872 contains no anti-aid or no-sectarian-appropriation clause. The education article was retrieved and checked: Article XII, Section 1 requires the Legislature to provide by general law for a thorough and efficient system of free schools, and Section 4 provides that the interest of the school fund "shall be annually applied to the support of free schools throughout the state, and to no other purpose whatever." The restriction runs to a particular fund rather than to a class of recipient, and no section names sectarian or private schools. West Virginia is accordingly recorded as a jurisdiction with no Blaine-type provision.

Article III, Section 15 of the West Virginia Constitution is an unusually full compelled-support clause: "No man shall be compelled to frequent or support any religious worship, place or ministry whatsoever," no man shall suffer on account of religious opinion, the Legislature shall not prescribe any religious test "or confer any peculiar privileges or advantages on any sect or denomination," and it shall not authorize any religious society or the people of any district to levy a tax for the erection or repair of a house of public worship or for the support of any church or ministry, "but it shall be left free for every person to select his religious instructor, and to make for his support, such private contracts as he shall please." The clause restrains compelled support and the conferral of peculiar privileges; it does not bar appropriations to schools.

Article I, Section 18 of the Wisconsin Constitution of 1848 combines a compelled-support clause with an appropriations bar. It provides that the right to worship according to conscience shall never be infringed, "nor shall any person be compelled to attend, erect or support any place of worship, or to maintain any ministry, without consent," nor shall any preference be given by law to any religious establishment or mode of worship, "nor shall any money be drawn from the treasury for the benefit of religious societies, or religious or theological seminaries." The funding bar names religious societies and religious or theological seminaries rather than religious schools generally, and it does not reach secular private schools. The section was amended in November 1982.

Article 1, Section 19 of the Wyoming Constitution, adopted with the constitution of 1889, provides: "No money of the state shall ever be given or appropriated to any sectarian or religious society or institution." The bar is sectarian-specific and applies to state money generally rather than to school funds alone.

Article 3, Section 36 of the Wyoming Constitution provides: "No appropriation shall be made for charitable, industrial, educational or benevolent purposes to any person, corporation or community not under the absolute control of the state, nor to any denominational or sectarian institution or association." The clause is of the broad type: an educational appropriation to any recipient outside the absolute control of the state is barred whether or not the recipient is religious.

Article 7, Section 8 of the Wyoming Constitution provides that no portion of any public school fund "shall ever be used to support or assist any private school, or any school, academy, seminary, college or other institution of learning controlled by any church or sectarian organization or religious denomination whatsoever." The clause names private schools first and church-controlled institutions second, which places it in the broad category; taken with Article 1, Section 19 and Article 3, Section 36 it gives Wyoming three overlapping bars.

Alabama has no separate home education statute. The route by which families educate their children at home is the church school, and the definition of a church school in the compulsory attendance article was rewritten by Acts 1982, No. 82-218, which defines a church school to include only schools that offer instruction in grades K-12, or any combination of them, including preschool, "through on-site or home programs." The history line for the section reads: School Code 1927, s. 302; Code 1940, T. 52, s. 299; Acts 1982, No. 82-218, p. 260, s. 1; Act 2014-245, p. 785, s. 4. A church school operates under the authority of a church, and no teacher certification, testing, or state approval is imposed on it by this section.

Alaska exempted from compulsory attendance a child who "is being educated in the child's home by a parent or legal guardian." The Coalition for Responsible Home Education states that Alaska passed the statute in 1997 and characterizes it as one of the most minimal home education statutes in the country, imposing no notification, no qualification standard for the parent, no required days or hours, no required subjects, no record keeping, and no assessment. The exemption is the operative provision; the year here rests on the association summary rather than on the session law, which was not retrieved.

Arizona Families for Home Education, the statewide home education association, states that home instruction became lawful in Arizona in 1982 through HB 2116, signed by Governor Bruce Babbitt. The association describes what the 1982 law required: an affidavit had to be filed with the county school superintendent, parents had to pass a proficiency examination before being permitted to teach their own children, students had to take annual standardized tests whose results went to the county superintendent, and county superintendents had discretion to evaluate a student's progress, to require follow-up testing, or to terminate the home education program. The current codification, A.R.S. s. 15-802, retains the affidavit of intent filed with the county school superintendent and has dropped the parent examination and the testing requirement.

events.instrument: Ark. Code Ann. s. 6-15-503 (Acts 1985 (1st Ex. Sess.), No. 40, s. 3; Acts 1985 (1st Ex. Sess.), No. 42, s. 3)
events.summary: Arkansas created a home school subchapter in the first extraordinary session of 1985. The history line for the prerequisites section reads: Acts 1985 (1st Ex. Sess.), No. 40, s. 3; 1985 (1st Ex. Sess.), No. 42, s. 3; A.S.A. 1947, s. 80-1503.6; Acts 1987, No. 260, s. 1, followed by later amendments. The section requires the parent or legal guardian to give written notice of intent to the school district superintendent by a set date each year or before withdrawing a student, to identify the child and the home school, and to sign the notice. No teacher qualification and no state approval are imposed by the section as it now stands, and it bars districts from demanding criteria or information beyond what the section lists.

events.instrument: C.R.S. s. 22-33-104.5 (L. 88: entire section added, p. 766, s. 1, effective July 1, 1988)
events.summary: Colorado added a home-based education section to the School Attendance Law of 1963. The source annotation reads: "L. 88: (6) amended, p. 812, s. 12, effective May 24; entire section added, p. 766, s. 1, effective July 1," followed by amendments in 1993, 1994, 1996, and later years. The section requires written notification to a school district 14 days before the program begins and annually after that, at least 172 days of instruction averaging four instructional contact hours per day, instruction in reading, writing, speaking, mathematics, history, civics, literature, science, and the Constitution of the United States, evaluation in grades 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11 by a nationally standardized achievement test or by a qualified evaluator, and the keeping of attendance, test, and immunization records.

events.instrument: Connecticut State Board of Education policy on home instruction, adopted November 7, 1990; C.G.S. s. 10-184
events.summary: Connecticut has never enacted a home education statute. The compulsory attendance statute, C.G.S. s. 10-184, excuses a parent who can "show that the child is elsewhere receiving equivalent instruction in the studies taught in the public schools." The Connecticut State Department of Education home schooling information packet records that the State Board of Education adopted its policy on home instruction on November 7, 1990, acknowledging the right of parents to instruct their children at home as an alternative to public school attendance where equivalent instruction is shown. The suggested procedures that follow from that policy, including the notice of intent, are not statutory and carry no approval requirement.

Delaware did not put home schools into its code during the 1980s. The Delaware General Assembly's session law record for volume 74 of the Delaware Laws lists chapter 79, Senate Bill 103, titled "An Act to Amend Title 14 of Delaware Code Relating to Compulsory School Attendance and Homeschools, and Non-Public School Attendance and Enrollment Reporting Requirements." That act, of the 142nd General Assembly sitting in 2003 and 2004, is the measure that placed home schools in Title 14 and tied them to the compulsory attendance provisions and to enrollment reporting. The year is recorded as it actually fell rather than being forced into the 1980 to 1994 window.

events.instrument: Compulsory School Attendance Act, Act of Feb. 4, 1925, 43 Stat. 806, ch. 140, art. I, ss. 1, 2; D.C. Code s. 38-202
events.summary: The District's compulsory attendance requirement originates in the Act of February 4, 1925, 43 Stat. 806, ch. 140, article I, sections 1 and 2, as the historical note to D.C. Code s. 38-202 records. Until 2013 the section required a person having custody of a minor to place the minor in regular attendance in "a public, independent, private, or parochial school, or in private instruction," so private instruction at home stood on the face of the statute as an alternative to attendance at a school. D.C. Law 20-17 replaced that language in 2013 with a requirement of regular attendance in an educational institution, and the modern home schooling framework is administrative rather than statutory.

events.instrument: Fla. Stat. s. 232.0201 (ss. 2, 3, ch. 85-144, Laws of Fla.)
events.summary: Florida created the home education program in 1985. The history line for section 232.0201 reads: "ss. 2, 3, ch. 85-144; s. 1, ch. 87-64; s. 16, ch. 87-252; s. 11, ch. 89-70; s. 26, ch. 90-306; s. 19, ch. 91-57," followed by later amendments, and the section provides that regular attendance may be achieved by attendance in a home education program and that the parent or guardian is not required to hold a Florida teaching certificate. The parent must notify the county superintendent of intent, maintain a portfolio of a log of educational activities and samples of the student's work, and obtain an annual educational evaluation of the student's progress. The section was carried into the K-20 Education Code as s. 1002.41 in 2002.

Georgia recognized the home study program by statute in 1984. The history line reads: "Code 1981, s. 20-2-690, enacted by Ga. L. 1984, p. 1266, s. 1; Ga. L. 1985, p. 149, s. 20; Ga. L. 1986, p. 10, s. 20," followed by later amendments. A parent must submit a declaration of intent within 30 days of establishing the program and annually after that, must hold at least a high school diploma or a state approved high school equivalency diploma, must teach reading, language arts, mathematics, social studies, and science, must provide 180 school days of at least four and one-half school hours, must have the child take a nationally standardized test every three years beginning at the end of the third grade, and must write an annual progress assessment report retained for three years.

events.instrument: Haw. Admin. R. ch. 8-12, Compulsory Attendance Exceptions (Eff. 11/7/91)
events.summary: Hawaii's home schooling framework is administrative. Chapter 8-12 of the Hawaii Administrative Rules, adopted by the Board of Education, carries the history note "Eff. 11/7/91" on its home schooling provisions, with a later compilation and amendment effective May 13, 2000. The rules require the parent to give the principal of the local public school a notice of intent to home educate before beginning, to keep a record of the planned curriculum, to submit an annual report of the child's progress evidenced by standardized testing, a professional evaluation, or the parent's own documentation, and to notify the principal if home schooling is terminated. No prior approval by the department is required.

Idaho's compulsory education statute does not command attendance at a school. It provides that the parent or guardian of a child who has attained the age of seven but not the age of sixteen "shall cause the child to be instructed in subjects commonly and usually taught in the public schools of the state of Idaho." The duty runs to instruction rather than to enrollment, so instruction given at home satisfies it, and the statute imposes no notice, no testing, no approval, and no qualification on the parent. The history note reads: 33-202, added 1963, ch. 13, sec. 25, p. 27; am. 1992, ch. 243, sec. 1, p. 721; am. 2009, ch. 103, sec. 2, p. 318.

The Supreme Court of Illinois held that instruction given at home may qualify as attendance at a private school under the compulsory attendance law where the instruction meets adequate standards, and it reversed the parents' conviction. The parents were Seventh Day Adventists who objected to public school on religious grounds. The court reasoned that the object of the compulsory education law is that children shall be educated, not that they shall be educated in a particular place or manner, while placing on parents who claim the exemption the burden of showing that they have in good faith provided an adequate course of instruction. The decision long predates the 1980 to 1994 wave, and the year is recorded as it fell.

events.instrument: Mazanec v. North Judson-San Pierre School Corp., 614 F. Supp. 1152 (N.D. Ind. 1985)
events.summary: The United States District Court for the Northern District of Indiana held that Indiana's compulsory attendance statute, which requires instruction equivalent to that given in the public schools, does not violate the Free Exercise Clause as applied to home education, and that parents hold a constitutional interest in educating their children at home consistent with Pierce v. Society of Sisters and Wisconsin v. Yoder, subject to the state's authority to enforce minimum educational standards. On the facts the court found that the instruction the Mazanec children received satisfied the statutory equivalency requirement and entered judgment for the defendants. Indiana enacted no separate home education statute in the period.

events.instrument: Iowa Code ch. 299A, competent private instruction (91 Acts, ch 200, s. 22)
events.summary: Iowa placed competent private instruction on a statutory footing in 1991. The credit line for the duties section of chapter 299A reads: "91 Acts, ch 200, s. 22; 2013 Acts, ch 121, s. 88; 2021 Acts, ch 88, s. 6." The parent, guardian, or legal custodian providing competent private instruction must complete and send the report required under section 299.4 to the school district of residence, must ensure that the child is evaluated annually to determine whether the child is making adequate progress, and must ensure that the results of the annual evaluation are reported to the district of residence and to the department of education by August 1 of the following year.

The Kansas Supreme Court held that instruction given at home by an uncertified mother did not constitute a private, denominational, or parochial school under K.S.A. 72-1111, and so did not satisfy the compulsory attendance requirement. The court set the standard that a qualifying nonpublic school must have a competent instructor and must be substantially equivalent to a public school in time and structure, and it found that the arrangement before it failed on the instructor's lack of certification and experience, the absence of a consistent schedule or lesson planning, and the mixing of instruction with child care. Kansas enacted no home education statute in the period, and home schools continue to operate as nonaccredited private schools.

events.instrument: Kentucky State Board for Elementary and Secondary Education v. Rudasill, 589 S.W.2d 877 (Ky. 1979)
events.summary: The Kentucky Supreme Court held that the state may not require private and church schools to meet its accreditation standards, to use state approved textbooks, or to employ certified teachers, resting on section 5 of the Kentucky Constitution, which protects a citizen from being compelled to send a child to any school to which he is conscientiously opposed. The state may require that private schools teach the basic subjects rationally related to the education of children to exercise the right of suffrage and to take part in the democratic system, and it may monitor compliance through standardized achievement testing, but it may not dictate the manner in which private or parochial schools teach. The decision is the foundation on which Kentucky families educating their children at home operate as private schools.

events.instrument: La. R.S. 17:236.1, approval of home study programs (Acts 1984, No. 446, s. 1)
events.summary: Louisiana enacted a home study program statute in 1984. The credit line for La. R.S. 17:236.1 reads: "Acts 1984, No. 446, s. 1; Acts 1988, No. 837, s. 1; Acts 2000, 1st Ex. Sess., No. 118, s. 2, eff. April 19, 2000; Acts 2010, No. 677, s. 1." The section requires the parent or legal guardian to apply to the Board of Elementary and Secondary Education for approval of the home study program, which makes Louisiana an approval state rather than a notice state, and approval is renewed on the terms the section sets out.

Maine's compulsory attendance section permits equivalent instruction through a home instruction program that complies with the conditions the section sets out: written notice to school officials and to the commissioner within ten calendar days of starting the program, at least 175 days of instruction each year covering English, mathematics, science, social studies, physical education, health, library skills, fine arts, and Maine studies, and an annual assessment of the child's academic progress by one of five listed methods. The history line records that the section was enacted by PL 1983, c. 806, s. 49 and amended by PL 1985, c. 123, ss. 1 and 2, the amendment that corresponds to the year Maine's statewide home instruction rules were settled; the source consulted does not itself state which act first added the home instruction program.

events.instrument: COMAR 13A.10.01.01, Home Instruction Program, adopted effective July 27, 1987
events.summary: Maryland's home instruction framework is a bylaw of the State Board of Education rather than a statute. The administrative history for COMAR 13A.10.01.01 records that the regulation was adopted effective July 27, 1987, with later amendments effective in 2016 and 2019. It requires the parent to sign a statement on a form prescribed by the State Department of Education at least 15 days before the home instruction program begins, to provide instruction in English, mathematics, science, social studies, art, music, health, and physical education, to maintain a portfolio of materials showing regular, thorough instruction, to permit a representative of the local school system to review the portfolio no more than three times a school year, and to verify continuation of the program before each school year. The regulation replaced a 1984 bylaw that had barred home instruction by a parent without a teaching certificate.

events.instrument: Care and Protection of Charles, 399 Mass. 324, 504 N.E.2d 592 (1987)
events.summary: The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts upheld the compulsory education statute, G.L. c. 76, s. 1, and held that a school committee may require its approval of a home education proposal in advance, while confining the approval inquiry to factors essential to ensuring that the children receive an adequate education. The court vacated the trial judge's order and remanded. It recognized that parents hold a liberty interest in directing the education of their children under the Fourteenth Amendment that is not absolute and must accommodate the state's interest in an educated citizenry. The parents were motivated by Christian belief and sought to give Bible centered instruction, and the court held that religious motivation does not entitle a family to more protection than a secular family receives.

The Michigan Supreme Court reversed the convictions of Mark and Chris DeJonge and held that the teacher certification requirement, as applied to families whose sincere religious beliefs forbid the use of certified instructors, violates the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment. The court held that the certification mandate is neither essential to nor the least restrictive means of achieving the state's asserted interest in the education of children, and it exempted families holding such convictions from the requirement. The decision is the point at which Michigan families educating their children at home for religious reasons ceased to be prosecuted for the absence of a certified teacher.

events.instrument: 1987 Minn. Laws ch. 178 (H.F. No. 432); Minn. Stat. s. 120A.22
events.summary: Minnesota rewrote its compulsory attendance provisions in 1987. Chapter 178 of the 1987 session laws, House File No. 432, is titled an act relating to education and modifying certain provisions of the compulsory attendance laws, and it was approved May 20, 1987. The act recognizes a home school as a place in which a child is provided instruction, requires the person in charge of providing instruction to report the name, age, and address of each child to the superintendent by October 1 of each school year, sets alternative qualifications for the instructor including a valid Minnesota teaching license, direct supervision by a licensed person, or a teacher competency examination, and requires that the performance of every child not enrolled in a public school be assessed each year using a nationally norm-referenced standardized achievement examination.

events.instrument: Miss. Code Ann. s. 37-13-91, Mississippi Compulsory School Attendance Law (Laws, 1982, Ex Sess, ch. 17, s. 21)
events.summary: Mississippi restored compulsory school attendance in the extraordinary session of 1982 and wrote the home instruction exception into the same law. The sources line for section 37-13-91 reads: "Laws, 1977, ch. 483, s. 1; Laws, 1982, Ex Sess, ch. 17, s. 21; Laws, 1987, ch. 460, 1991, ch. 308, s. 1," followed by later amendments. The statute permits a child to be educated in a legitimate home instruction program in place of a public or legitimate nonpublic school, defines a legitimate program as one not operated or instituted for the purpose of avoiding or circumventing the compulsory attendance law, and requires the parent to file a certificate of enrollment with the school attendance officer each year describing the education the child is receiving.

Missouri wrote the home school into its compulsory attendance statute in 1986. The history line reads: "(L. 1963 p. 200 s. 8-3, A.L. 1977 H.B. 130, A.L. 1986 S.B. 795, A.L. 1990 S.B. 740, A.L. 1993 S.B. 380, A.L. 2004 S.B. 968 and S.B. 969)." The statute defines a home school as a school, whether incorporated or unincorporated, that offers private or religious based instruction to no more than four unrelated pupils and charges no tuition, requires at least 1,000 hours of instruction of which at least 600 are in reading, language arts, mathematics, social studies, and science and at least 400 of those 600 at the regular home school location, and requires the parent to keep a plan book or diary, a portfolio of the child's work, and records of evaluations. Production of the daily log is made a defense to any prosecution.
