events.instrument: Mont. Code Ann. s. 20-5-109 (En. Sec. 2, Ch. 355, L. 1983; amd. Sec. 3, Ch. 498, L. 1989; amd. Sec. 9, Ch. 138, L. 2005)
events.summary: Montana enacted the nonpublic and home school requirements for the compulsory enrollment exemption in 1983. The history line reads: "En. Sec. 2, Ch. 355, L. 1983; amd. Sec. 3, Ch. 498, L. 1989; amd. Sec. 9, Ch. 138, L. 2005." A home school qualifies for the exemption if it maintains attendance and immunization records available to the county superintendent, provides at least the minimum aggregate hours of pupil instruction required of public schools, is housed in a building that complies with local health and safety regulations, provides an organized course of study that includes the subjects required of public schools, and notifies the county superintendent of the county in which it is located in each school fiscal year. No teacher certification and no approval are required.

events.instrument: Neb. Rev. Stat. s. 79-1601 (Laws 1984, LB 928, s. 3)
events.summary: Nebraska created the exempt school in 1984, after the litigation over the Faith Baptist Church school at Louisville. The statute allows a school to elect not to meet the requirements for approval and accreditation on the ground that those requirements "violate sincerely held religious beliefs," and requires an authorized representative of the school to submit an annual assurance to the Commissioner of Education that the statutory conditions are and will continue to be satisfied. The source line for the section includes "Laws 1984, LB 928, s. 3" among entries running from Laws 1919, c. 155, s. 1 to the present. The compulsory attendance section, 79-201, correspondingly excuses attendance at a school that has made the election under 79-1601, and that election is the route Nebraska families use to educate their children at home.

Nevada replaced the former regime, under which a family had to obtain the approval of the board of trustees for equivalent instruction, with a notice regime in 2007. The credit line for the homeschool provisions of chapter 388D of the Nevada Revised Statutes reads "Added to NRS by 2007, 3032," with amendments in 2011, 2013, 2015, and 2023. The statute requires the parent of a child subject to compulsory enrollment who wishes to homeschool the child to file a written notice of intent with the superintendent before homeschooling begins, within ten days of a formal withdrawal from a public school, or within thirty days of establishing residence in Nevada. The year is recorded as it actually fell rather than being forced into the 1980 to 1994 window.

New Hampshire enacted a home education chapter in 1990. The source notes running through RSA 193-A begin "1990, 279:3" and continue with amendments in 1996, 2006, 2008, 2012, and 2022. A parent commencing a home education program must notify the commissioner of the department of education, the resident district superintendent, or the principal of a nonpublic school within five business days of commencing the program, must maintain a portfolio of records and materials relating to the program and preserve it for two years from the end of the instruction, and must provide for an annual educational evaluation documenting the child's progress at a level commensurate with the child's age, ability, or disability.

events.instrument: State v. Massa, 95 N.J. Super. 382, 231 A.2d 252 (1967)
events.summary: The court held that instruction given at home by a parent can satisfy New Jersey's compulsory attendance requirement, reading N.J.S.A. 18:14-14, which excused a child receiving equivalent instruction elsewhere than at school, to require academic equivalence only and not social development. Barbara and Frank Massa were found to have given their daughter educationally equivalent instruction, and her truancy conviction was reversed. The court stated that the object of the statute was that all children shall be educated, not that they shall be educated in a particular way. New Jersey enacted no home education statute in the 1980 to 1994 period, and this decision remains the basis of the position.

events.instrument: NMSA 1978, s. 22-1-2.1 (enacted by Laws 1985, ch. 21, s. 2)
events.summary: New Mexico wrote home school requirements into the Public School Code in 1985. The history line reads: "1978 Comp., 22-1-2.1, enacted by Laws 1985, ch. 21, s. 2; 1993, ch. 62, s. 2; 1993, ch. 226, s. 1; 2001, ch. 62, s. 1; 2014, ch. 12, s. 3." The section requires the person operating the home school to notify the department on a home school registration form, to maintain records of the child's immunization or a waiver of it, and to provide instruction by a person holding at least a high school diploma or its equivalent. No approval by a district or by the department is required.

New York's home instruction framework is a regulation of the Commissioner of Education rather than a statute, the compulsory attendance law having long allowed instruction elsewhere than at a school. Section 100.10 carries a transitional provision fixing its start: "For the 1988-89 school year only, the written notice of intention to instruct at home required in paragraph (1) of this subdivision shall be due on August 1, 1988," which places the section in force for the 1988-89 school year. The regulation requires the parent to give annual written notice to the superintendent of schools, to file an individualized home instruction plan on the district's form within four weeks of receiving the materials, to furnish quarterly reports on the dates named in the plan, and to file an annual assessment with the fourth quarterly report.

North Carolina wrote home schools into Article 39 of the school law in the 1988 session. The session law credit on each of the three operative sections reads "1987 (Reg. Sess., 1988), c. 891, s. 1." A home school is defined as a nonpublic school consisting of the children of not more than two families or households in which the parents determine the scope and sequence of academic instruction, provide the instruction, and determine additional sources of instruction. The school elects to operate under the qualifications of Part 1 or Part 2 of the Article, testing is annual, safety and sanitation inspections are waived for a school in a private residence, and the person giving instruction must hold at least a high school diploma or its equivalent. Compliance with Part 3 exempts the school from other educational regulation apart from immunization requirements.

The Supreme Court of North Carolina reversed the Court of Appeals and held that instruction given at home can qualify as a nonpublic school under the compulsory attendance statutes, finding that Delconte's program met the express statutory standards and that nothing in the language of the statute barred education at home. The Delcontes were described in the opinion as deeply religious fundamentalist Christians who held that the Bible is authoritative and obliges them to teach their children at home, and the court noted the constitutional difficulty that would arise were the state to forbid home instruction altogether. The decision preceded the statute of 1988 and is the point at which the position changed.

events.instrument: North Dakota home education law of 1989
events.summary: The Coalition for Responsible Home Education records that North Dakota enacted its home education law in 1989 and describes what it changed: home school parents had previously been required to hold teaching certification, and the 1989 law allowed a parent without certification to educate a child at home under the supervision of a certified teacher or on passing the state teachers' examination. The requirements now codified in chapter 15.1-23 of the Century Code carry that structure forward through the statement of intent, the parent qualification, the monitoring of unqualified parents by a certified teacher, and standardized testing in grades four, six, eight, and ten. The session law citation was not retrieved, so the year rests on the association history.

The North Dakota Supreme Court affirmed the convictions of eight parents from four families who kept their children out of school and taught them at home without state certified teachers. The court rejected the parents' free exercise defense, holding the state's interest in teacher certification sufficiently compelling, and it distinguished Wisconsin v. Yoder on the ground that these families lacked the long history of successful self-sufficiency of the Amish and that their children had not completed a basic primary education. The court called certification a reasonably narrow requirement and among the least personally intrusive methods available. The decision marks the position in North Dakota before the law changed at the end of the decade.

events.instrument: Ohio Admin. Code ch. 3301-34, Excuses from Compulsory Attendance for Home Education (prior effective date 08/01/1989)
events.summary: Ohio's home education framework was made by rule of the State Board of Education. The administrative record for the definitions rule of chapter 3301-34 gives its prior effective dates as 08/01/1989, 01/23/2009, and 07/01/2019, which places the first adoption of the chapter on August 1, 1989. The chapter governs the excuse from compulsory attendance for home education and carries the notification and academic assessment rules that a parent must satisfy. The rules superseded the minimum standards regime that the Supreme Court of Ohio had struck down as applied to a religious school in the 1970s.

Oklahoma is the one state whose constitution names an alternative to school attendance. Article XIII, section 4 provides: "The Legislature shall provide for the compulsory attendance at some public or other school, unless other means of education are provided, of all the children in the State who are sound in mind and body, between the ages of eight and sixteen years, for at least three months in each year." The phrase "unless other means of education are provided" is the constitutional basis on which Oklahoma families educate their children at home, and no notice, testing, or approval follows from it. The compilation consulted carries adoption notes for sections 1a and 8, dating them to 1946 and 1944, and carries none for section 4, which is consistent with section 4 standing as adopted with the Constitution at statehood in 1907.

Oregon enacted its provision on teaching by a private teacher, parent, or guardian in 1985. The source note reads: "[1985 c.579 s.2; 1989 c.619 s.4; 1999 c.717 s.1a; 2007 c.70 s.95; 2013 c.1 s.33]." The statute requires that when a child is taught, or is withdrawn from a public school to be taught, by a parent, legal guardian, or private teacher, the parent, legal guardian, or private teacher must notify the education service district in writing, and it requires the child to be examined at grades 3, 5, 8, and 10 under the procedures the section prescribes. No approval and no teacher qualification are required.

events.instrument: Act 169 of 1988; 24 P.S. s. 13-1327.1, home education program
events.summary: The Pennsylvania Department of Education's guide to home education and private tutoring states, under its history of homeschooling in Pennsylvania, that "In 1988, the Pennsylvania General Assembly passed Act 169," which amended the Public School Code in a number of ways, among them adding the home education program as a way of satisfying compulsory attendance. The program is codified at 24 P.S. s. 13-1327.1. The supervisor must hold a high school diploma or its equivalent, must file a notarized affidavit with the district superintendent by August 1 each year with an outline of proposed educational objectives by subject area, must maintain a portfolio with a contemporaneous log and samples of the child's work, must have the child take nationally normed standardized tests in reading and mathematics at grades 3, 5, and 8, and must obtain an annual written evaluation by a licensed psychologist or a certified teacher. School district approval is not required to begin a program.

Rhode Island's compulsory attendance section itself carries the home instruction alternative. It provides that attendance is not obligatory where the person charged proves that the child has attended for the required period a private day school approved by the commissioner "or a course of at-home instruction approved by the school committee of the town where the child resides." Rhode Island is therefore an approval state, and approval rests with the local school committee. The credit line runs from G.L. 1896, ch. 64, s. 1 through G.L. 1938, ch. 181, s. 1, G.L. 1956, s. 16-19-1, and amendments in 1984, 1988, 1989, 1995, 2002, 2003, and 2007. The date recorded is the origin of the section shown by that credit line; the source consulted does not establish which act first added the at-home instruction clause.

South Carolina enacted a home schooling section in 1988. The history line reads: "1962 Code Section 21-757.3; 1967 (55) 181; 1988 Act No. 593, Section 1." The section requires the approval of the district board of trustees, requires the parent to hold at least a high school diploma or the equivalent general educational development certificate and to pass a basic skills examination, or to hold a baccalaureate degree, sets an instructional day of at least four and one-half hours and a year of at least 180 days, prescribes reading, writing, mathematics, science, and social studies, with composition and literature in grades seven through twelve, requires a plan book or diary, a portfolio of the child's work, and semiannual progress reports to the district, and requires participation in statewide testing and the Basic Skills Assessment Program.

events.instrument: SDCL s. 13-27-7, notification of alternative instruction (SL 1981, ch 141, s. 3; SL 1983, ch 131, s. 1)
events.summary: South Dakota excuses a child from public school attendance where the parent provides alternative instruction, which is the term the code uses for home education, and the notification is made on a standard form declaring that the child will be provided with alternative instruction under section 13-27-3, giving the child's name, birth date, and resident district, and signed by the parent. The source line for the notification section reads: "SDC 1939, s. 15.3202; SL 1955, ch 41, ch 15, s. 2; SL 1971, ch 116, s. 3; SL 1981, ch 141, s. 3; SL 1983, ch 131, s. 1; SL 1991, ch 20, ss. 17, 18; SL 1992, ch 128, s. 2," followed by later entries. The date recorded is the earliest of the two acts of the 1980s shown in that line; the source consulted does not state which act first introduced the term alternative instruction.

events.instrument: Tenn. Code Ann. s. 49-6-3050, home schools (Acts 1985, ch. 398, s. 3)
events.summary: Tennessee enacted a home school statute in 1985. The history line reads: "[Acts 1985, ch. 398, s. 3; 1987, ch. 42, ss. 2-5; 1987, ch. 308, s. 33; 1994, ch. 725, ss. 1-3; 1995, ch. 534, s. 1; 1997, ch. 434, ss. 4, 5; 2005, ch. 177, s. 4.]" The parent must notify the local director of schools by August 1 before the school year with the names, ages, and grades of the children, the location of the school, the curriculum, and the qualifications of the instructor, must hold a high school diploma or its equivalent to teach grades kindergarten through eight and a baccalaureate degree to teach grades nine through twelve, subject to annual exemption by the department, and must have the children take state board approved standardized tests in grades five, seven, and nine.

events.instrument: Texas Education Agency v. Leeper, 893 S.W.2d 432 (Tex. 1994)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of Texas affirmed that children taught at home are not required to attend public school, holding that the private school exemption from compulsory attendance then at Texas Education Code s. 21.033(a)(1) reaches children taught at home, in a bona fide manner, a curriculum designed to meet basic education goals including a study of good citizenship. The case was brought as a class action on behalf of Texas families educating their children at home after prosecutions and threatened prosecutions, and it affirmed the judgment entered for the families at trial. Texas has enacted no home education statute; the position rests on this decision, and the Texas Education Agency instructs districts that home schooled students are exempt from compulsory attendance to the same extent as private school students.

events.instrument: Senate Bill 39 (2014 General Session), amending Utah Code s. 53A-11-102, now s. 53G-6-204
events.summary: Utah's exemption from school attendance had long been granted by the local board of education on its approval of the family's program. Senate Bill 39 of the 2014 general session removed the state's educational requirements from the exemption; the Coalition for Responsible Home Education, opposing the bill, quotes its sponsor as saying that parents would be formally exempt from any and all state educational requirements such as classroom time, curriculum standards, testing, or reporting. The section as it now stands, Utah Code s. 53G-6-204, requires a local school board to excuse a school-age minor from attendance where the parent files a signed and notarized affidavit with the district of residence stating that the child will attend a home school and that the parent assumes sole responsibility for the education, and district approval is not required. The year is recorded as it actually fell.

events.instrument: 16 V.S.A. s. 166b, home study program (Added 1987, No. 97, s. 3, eff. June 23, 1987)
events.summary: Vermont created the home study program in 1987. The history line reads: "(Added 1987, No. 97, s. 3, eff. June 23, 1987; amended 1989, No. 44, s. 6, eff. June 1, 1990; No. 118, s. 3; 1991, No. 24, s. 11; 1995, No. 100 (Adj. Sess.), s. 1; 2005, No. 107 (Adj. Sess.), s. 1.)" The parent must file a written notice with the commissioner giving the child's name, age, and birth date, the family's contact details and legal residence, any prior progress assessments, a detailed outline of the curriculum in each subject, and the names and signatures of the instructors, must cover the minimum course of study, and must have the child's progress assessed each year by a report from a Vermont licensed teacher, by a parent prepared report with a portfolio of the child's work, or by an approved standardized achievement test.

events.instrument: Va. Code s. 22.1-254.1, home instruction of children (1984, c. 436)
events.summary: Virginia enacted a home instruction statute in 1984. The history line reads: "1984, c. 436; 1986, c. 215; 1991, c. 306; 1992, c. 131; 1993, c. 992; 1994, c. 854; 1998, c. 435," followed by later chapters. The parent must notify the division superintendent each August of the intention to instruct the child and provide a description of the curriculum by August 15, must satisfy one of four qualifications, namely a high school diploma, a teaching license, the provision of a structured curriculum including a correspondence or distance learning program, or evidence of the ability to provide an adequate education, and must submit by August 1 following the year either a composite score at or above the fourth stanine on a nationally normed standardized achievement test or an evaluation showing adequate progress. Failure to supply that evidence places the family on probation.

Washington enacted home-based instruction in 1985. The history line for the duties section reads: "[2019 c 252 s 109; 2004 c 19 s 107; 1995 c 52 s 1; 1993 c 336 s 1103; 1990 c 33 s 178; 1985 c 441 s 2.]" The parent must ensure that a standardized achievement test approved by the state board of education is administered annually to the child by a qualified individual, or that an annual assessment of the child's academic progress is written by a certificated person currently working in the field of education, and must ensure that test scores or annual assessments and immunization records, together with any other records kept on the instructional and educational activities provided, are forwarded to any other public or private school to which the child transfers.

events.instrument: State v. Riddle, 168 W. Va. 429, 285 S.E.2d 359 (1981)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia affirmed the convictions of Bobby and Esther Riddle, members of a strict Biblical Christian sect who taught their children at home on a formal curriculum out of the conviction that secular education conflicted with their beliefs about sin and salvation. The court held that sincerely held religious conviction is never a defense to total noncompliance with the compulsory attendance law, and it distinguished Wisconsin v. Yoder on the ground that the Riddles had never sought approval under the state's home instruction exemption. The court directed that parents must work through the statutory channel, namely approval of qualified home instruction by the county superintendent, rather than disregard the law and raise constitutional defenses after prosecution.

Wisconsin created the home-based private educational program by 1983 Wisconsin Act 512, enacted May 10, 1984 and published May 18, 1984. The act defines a home-based private educational program as a program of educational instruction provided to a child by the child's parent or guardian or by a person designated by the parent or guardian, and provides that instruction in such a program meeting all the criteria of s. 118.165(1) may be substituted for attendance at a public or private school. The criteria include at least 875 hours of instruction each year, a sequentially progressive curriculum of fundamental instruction in the core subjects, and a vacation period. No notice of approval, no teacher qualification, and no testing are imposed.

Vermont towns that do not maintain a high school pay tuition for their resident pupils to attend a public or an approved independent school chosen by the parent, within or outside the state. The arrangement dates from 1869 and is the oldest publicly funded private school choice program in the country. It is now codified at 16 V.S.A. sections 821 to 836.

events.instrument: Swart v. South Burlington Town School District, 122 Vt. 177, 167 A.2d 514 (1961)
events.summary: The Vermont Supreme Court held that the South Burlington Town School District, although acting within the literal terms of the town tuitioning statute, exceeded the limits of the United States Constitution when it paid tuition to Roman Catholic high schools operated by the Diocese of Burlington. The decree enjoining the payments was affirmed, and Vermont districts stopped paying tuition to sectarian schools.

events.instrument: Campbell v. Manchester Board of School Directors, 161 Vt. 441, 641 A.2d 352 (1994)
events.summary: The Vermont Supreme Court reversed the denial of tuition reimbursement under 16 V.S.A. section 822 for a pupil attending St. Andrews Academy, holding that reimbursement limited to the average public school tuition and paid on the parent's request did not violate the Establishment Clause. The court expressly reserved the question whether reimbursement under the 1991 amendment would be permissible.

Maine towns that do not operate a school of the relevant grade span pay tuition for their resident pupils at a public or an approved private school chosen by the parent. The arrangement dates from 1873 and is the second oldest publicly funded private school choice program in the country.

events.instrument: Exclusion of sectarian schools from Maine town tuitioning, following the Attorney General's opinion of January 7, 1980
events.summary: The Maine Attorney General advised on January 7, 1980, that paying tuition for pupils to attend schools with a pervasively religious atmosphere would violate the First Amendment. Maine then enacted legislation barring religious schools from the tuitioning program, a restriction that stood for more than forty years.

events.instrument: Squires v. Inhabitants of City of Augusta, 155 Me. 151, 153 A.2d 80 (1959)
events.summary: The Maine Supreme Judicial Court held that the City of Augusta had no authority, by statute or by charter, to enact an ordinance appropriating public funds to transport pupils to nonpublic schools. The court did not reach the constitutional question, resting instead on the absence of enabling legislation, and sustained the taxpayers' appeal.

events.instrument: Bangor Baptist Church v. State of Maine, Department of Educational and Cultural Services, 576 F. Supp. 1299 (D. Me. 1983)
events.summary: Ten church schools and their pastors challenged Maine's compulsory education statutes and its private school approval requirements. The court entered findings of fact and conclusions of law on the constitutionality of the approval scheme and granted injunctive relief protecting the pastors' right to preach their interpretation of Scripture, while leaving the state free to pursue legislatively prescribed means of protecting its interests.

events.instrument: 1989 Wisconsin Act 336, s. 228, creating Wis. Stat. s. 119.23 (Milwaukee Parental Choice Program)
events.summary: Section 228 of 1989 Wisconsin Act 336, enacted April 27, 1990, and published May 10, 1990, created Wis. Stat. section 119.23, the Milwaukee Parental Choice Program. The program allowed a limited number of low income pupils in a city of the first class to attend a nonsectarian private school at state expense. The governor vetoed the sunset provision that would have ended the program after five years.

events.instrument: Davis ex rel. Davis v. Grover, 166 Wis. 2d 501, 480 N.W.2d 460 (1992)
events.summary: The Wisconsin Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals and upheld the Milwaukee Parental Choice Program against challenges under the private or local legislation clause, the uniform district schools clause, and the public purpose doctrine of the Wisconsin Constitution. The program was the first modern publicly funded voucher program in the United States to survive review by a state supreme court.

events.instrument: Ch. 648, Laws of 1961, amending Wis. Stat. s. 40.53(1)
events.summary: Chapter 648 of the Laws of 1961 amended the school transportation statute so that school boards would furnish transportation to pupils attending private and parochial schools on the same terms as pupils attending public schools.

events.instrument: State ex rel. Reynolds v. Nusbaum, 17 Wis. 2d 148, 115 N.W.2d 761 (1962)
events.summary: The Wisconsin Supreme Court held that chapter 648 of the Laws of 1961, which required school boards to transport pupils attending private and parochial schools, conferred a benefit on religious groups contrary to article I, section 18 of the Wisconsin Constitution. The court decided the case solely under the state constitution.

events.instrument: State ex rel. Van Straten v. Milquet, 180 Wis. 109, 192 N.W. 392 (1923)
events.summary: The Wisconsin Supreme Court held that a school district board acted beyond its authority when it contracted to transport pupils to a private school. The statutory power to provide transportation extended only to children attending the schools the district was required to support, so the contract was invalid.

events.instrument: Minn. Stat. s. 290.09, subd. 22, deduction for tuition, textbooks, and transportation
events.summary: Minnesota has permitted taxpayers to deduct from gross income the actual expenses of tuition, textbooks, and transportation for their dependent children in elementary and secondary schools under a law originally enacted in 1955 and revised in 1976 and again in 1978. The deduction is available to parents of public and nonpublic school pupils alike.

events.instrument: L. 1971, ch. 944, Nonpublic School Education Costs; Credit
events.summary: The 1971 Minnesota Legislature enacted a tax credit for parents of children attending nonpublic schools, intended to reduce their burden, to maintain plurality of educational opportunity, and to prevent the collapse of the nonpublic school sector.

events.instrument: Minnesota Civil Liberties Union v. State, 302 Minn. 216, 224 N.W.2d 344 (1974)
events.summary: The Minnesota Supreme Court reversed the district court and held the 1971 nonpublic school tax credit unconstitutional, following the intervening decisions of the United States Supreme Court that had narrowed the authorities on which the trial court had relied.

events.instrument: L. 1969, ch. 570, transportation of pupils to sectarian schools; Americans United Inc. v. Independent School District No. 622, 288 Minn. 196, 179 N.W.2d 146 (1970)
events.summary: The Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed the trial court and upheld chapter 570 of the Laws of 1969, which authorized the use of public funds to transport children to sectarian elementary and secondary schools, against challenges under article IX, section 1 of the Minnesota Constitution and the First Amendment.

events.instrument: Protestants and Other Americans United for Separation of Church and State v. Essex, 28 Ohio St. 2d 79, 275 N.E.2d 603 (1971)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of Ohio upheld R.C. 3317.06(H), under which the state appropriated money to local public school districts to buy textbooks that were then lent to pupils attending nonpublic schools. The court held that title remained in the state, that the benefit ran to parents and children rather than to schools, and that no exclusive right to school funds was conferred within the meaning of article VI, section 2 of the Ohio Constitution.

events.instrument: Ohio Rev. Code s. 3317.06 (1976), services and materials for nonpublic school pupils
events.summary: Ohio enacted a program of assistance for nonpublic school pupils that lent instructional materials and equipment to pupils or their parents rather than to the schools, and that provided diagnostic, therapeutic, guidance, testing, and field trip services. The statute was drafted to meet the objections the United States Supreme Court had raised to the Pennsylvania program in Meek v. Pittenger.

events.instrument: Ohio Rev. Code s. 3317.06, as considered in Wolman v. Walter, 433 U.S. 229 (1977)
events.summary: The United States Supreme Court sustained the Ohio provisions for textbooks, standardized testing and scoring, diagnostic services, and therapeutic services, and held unconstitutional the provisions for the loan of instructional materials and equipment and for field trip transportation. The Ohio program therefore survived only in part.

events.instrument: State v. Whisner, 47 Ohio St. 2d 181, 351 N.E.2d 750 (1976)
events.summary: Parents at the Tabernacle Christian School were convicted of failing to send their children to a school that met the Minimum Standards for Ohio Elementary Schools. The Supreme Court of Ohio held that the minimum standards, which reached curriculum, staffing, organization, records, and cooperation with the surrounding community, infringed the parents' right to the free exercise of religion under the First Amendment and section 7, article I of the Ohio Constitution. The judgment was reversed and the defendants discharged.

events.instrument: Nonpublic Elementary and Secondary Education Act, Act of June 19, 1968, No. 109
events.summary: Pennsylvania's Act 109 of 1968, signed by the governor on June 19, 1968, empowered the State Superintendent of Public Instruction to contract with nonpublic schools for the purchase of secular educational services, reimbursing them for teachers' salaries, textbooks, and instructional materials in specified subjects.

events.instrument: Nonpublic Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1968, held unconstitutional in Lemon v. Kurtzman, 403 U.S. 602 (1971)
events.summary: The United States Supreme Court held that Pennsylvania's purchase of secular educational services from church related schools fostered excessive entanglement between government and religion and so violated the Establishment Clause. The Pennsylvania program was ended.

events.instrument: Parent Reimbursement Act for Nonpublic Education, Act of August 27, 1971, No. 92
events.summary: Pennsylvania's Act 92, approved August 27, 1971, and financed by the state cigarette tax, reimbursed parents for tuition paid to nonpublic schools that satisfied the compulsory attendance requirements and Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

events.instrument: Parent Reimbursement Act for Nonpublic Education of 1971, held unconstitutional in Sloan v. Lemon, 413 U.S. 825 (1973)
events.summary: The United States Supreme Court held that Pennsylvania's reimbursement of nonpublic school tuition to parents had the impermissible effect of advancing religion and violated the Establishment Clause, and it declined to sever the benefits to parents of children at nonsectarian schools.

events.instrument: Act 194 and Act 195 of July 12, 1972, Pa. Stat. tit. 24, s. 9-972
events.summary: Act 194 extended to nonpublic school pupils the auxiliary services already furnished to public school pupils, including counseling, testing, psychological services, speech and hearing therapy, and services for the educationally disadvantaged. Act 195 provided for the loan of textbooks to nonpublic school pupils and for the loan of instructional materials and equipment.

events.instrument: Act 194 and the instructional materials provisions of Act 195 of 1972, held unconstitutional in Meek v. Pittenger, 421 U.S. 349 (1975)
events.summary: The United States Supreme Court upheld the textbook loan provision of Act 195 but held unconstitutional the loan of instructional materials and equipment and the provision of auxiliary services under Act 194, on the grounds of impermissible effect and excessive entanglement.

events.instrument: Hysong v. Gallitzin Borough School District, 164 Pa. 629, 30 A. 482 (1894)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania declined to enjoin the Gallitzin borough school directors from employing members of the Sisters of St. Joseph as public school teachers or from permitting them to teach in the habit of their order, there being no evidence of sectarian instruction during school hours. The legislature responded the following year with a statute forbidding religious garb in the public schools.

events.instrument: Act of June 27, 1895, P.L. 395, forbidding religious dress or insignia in the public schools; Commonwealth v. Herr, 39 Pa. Super. 454 (1909)
events.summary: The Superior Court of Pennsylvania upheld the Act of June 27, 1895, which forbade public school teachers to wear dress or insignia indicating membership in a religious order. The court held that the right to wear a particular garb in the schoolroom is not free from legislative control.

events.instrument: Salary Supplement Act, R.I. Pub. Laws ch. 246 (1969)
events.summary: Rhode Island's Salary Supplement Act of 1969 paid state funds directly to teachers of secular subjects in nonpublic elementary schools, supplementing their salaries by up to fifteen percent. In practice the sole beneficiaries were lay teachers in Roman Catholic schools, which enrolled about ninety-five percent of the state's nonpublic elementary pupils.

events.instrument: Salary Supplement Act of 1969, held unconstitutional in Earley v. DiCenso, decided with Lemon v. Kurtzman, 403 U.S. 602 (1971)
events.summary: The United States Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the three judge district court and held that the Rhode Island salary supplement for teachers in nonpublic schools required continuing state surveillance to keep the aid secular, and so fostered excessive entanglement between government and religion.

events.instrument: Members of the Jamestown School Committee v. Schmidt, 122 R.I. 185, 405 A.2d 16 (1979)
events.summary: Answering questions certified by the federal district court, the Rhode Island Supreme Court construed the state's regional school transportation act, which carried pupils attending nonpublic nonprofit schools as well as public school pupils, and held that it did not divert the permanent school fund contrary to article XII of the Rhode Island Constitution.

events.instrument: Judd v. Board of Education of Union Free School District No. 2, 278 N.Y. 200, 15 N.E.2d 576 (1938)
events.summary: The New York Court of Appeals held that furnishing transportation at public expense to pupils attending private and parochial schools was a contribution in aid of the maintenance of those schools and was forbidden by the state constitution. The decision was overtaken by a constitutional amendment adopted later the same year.

events.instrument: L. 1965, ch. 320, amending Education Law s. 701, textbook loan
events.summary: Chapter 320 of the Laws of 1965 directed school authorities to purchase textbooks and to lend them, on individual request, to all children in grades seven to twelve enrolled in a public or private school that complied with the compulsory education law.

events.instrument: Board of Education of Central School District No. 1 v. Allen, 20 N.Y.2d 109, 228 N.E.2d 791 (1967)
events.summary: The New York Court of Appeals upheld section 701 of the Education Law, holding that the loan of secular textbooks to individual pupils entailed no aid to parochial schools and raised no Establishment Clause question. The court declined to follow its earlier reasoning in Judd.

events.instrument: N.Y. Laws of 1972, ch. 414, maintenance and repair grants, tuition reimbursement, and tax relief for nonpublic school parents
events.summary: Chapter 414 of the Laws of 1972 provided direct grants from the state treasury to qualifying nonpublic schools for maintenance and repair, partial tuition reimbursement for low income parents of nonpublic school pupils, and tax relief for parents who did not qualify for reimbursement.

events.instrument: N.Y. Laws of 1972, ch. 414, held unconstitutional in Committee for Public Education and Religious Liberty v. Nyquist, 413 U.S. 756 (1973)
events.summary: The United States Supreme Court held that the maintenance and repair grants, the tuition reimbursement, and the tax relief provisions of chapter 414 each had the impermissible effect of advancing religion and violated the Establishment Clause.

events.instrument: N.J.S.A. 54A:3-1(b), additional exemption for a dependent attending a nonpublic elementary or secondary school
events.summary: When New Jersey instituted a general income tax in 1976 it allowed taxpayers an additional exemption of one thousand dollars for each dependent child attending, on a full time basis, an elementary or secondary institution not deriving its primary support from public money.

events.instrument: Public Funds for Public Schools v. Byrne, 590 F.2d 514 (3d Cir. 1979)
events.summary: The Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit held that New Jersey's additional income tax exemption for parents of nonpublic school pupils had the principal effect of advancing religion, since the great majority of eligible taxpayers supported dependents at religiously affiliated schools, and so violated the Establishment Clause.

events.instrument: Act No. 100, Public Acts of 1970, ch. 2, allowances for lay teachers of secular subjects in nonpublic schools
events.summary: Chapter 2 of Act 100 of the Public Acts of 1970 paid state allowances toward the salaries of certified lay teachers who taught secular subjects in nonpublic elementary and secondary schools. Participation was voluntary, and eligible units had to certify their teachers and keep segregated accounts. The Michigan Supreme Court considered its constitutionality at the request of the legislature.

events.instrument: Sheridan Road Baptist Church v. Department of Education, 426 Mich. 462, 396 N.W.2d 373 (1986)
events.summary: Two church schools challenged Michigan's requirement that teachers in nonpublic schools hold state certification, arguing that engaging only government certified teachers was contrary to Scripture. The Michigan Supreme Court affirmed the requirement against the free exercise and establishment challenges.

events.instrument: Iowa Code ss. 422.9 and 422.12, tuition and textbook deduction and credit
events.summary: In 1987 the Iowa Legislature added subsections to sections 422.9 and 422.12 of the Iowa Code allowing taxpayers with adjusted gross income below forty-five thousand dollars and one or more dependents in kindergarten through grade twelve at an accredited Iowa school to claim a deduction or a credit for tuition and textbook expenses.

events.instrument: Johnson v. Charles City Community Schools Board of Education, 368 N.W.2d 74 (Iowa 1985)
events.summary: The Iowa Supreme Court rejected the claim of a pastor and church school families that the First Amendment barred the state from setting educational standards for a private religious school, and affirmed the trial court. The court noted that the term equivalent instruction required further definition.

events.instrument: Fellowship Baptist Church v. Benton, 815 F.2d 485 (8th Cir. 1987)
events.summary: The Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit sustained Iowa's reporting requirements for private schools and its requirement that pupils receive equivalent instruction from a certified teacher, and it rejected the churches' claim to the exemption reserved for members of established religious groups such as the Amish. The vagueness of the phrase equivalent instruction was remanded for further consideration.

The Iowa Supreme Court affirmed a decree enjoining a school district from spending public money on a school that had been moved into a Roman Catholic parish building and conducted as a parochial school, and requiring the directors to provide a school building elsewhere.

events.instrument: Nebraska Textbook Loan Act, L.B. 659, Laws 1971
events.summary: Legislative Bill 659 of 1971 directed public school district boards to lend secular textbooks to pupils in nonpublic elementary and secondary schools, on a declared policy of aiding education and developing the skills of the state's youth.

events.instrument: Gaffney v. State Department of Education, 192 Neb. 358, 220 N.W.2d 550 (1974)
events.summary: The Nebraska Supreme Court reversed the district court and held the Nebraska Textbook Loan Act unconstitutional under the Constitution of Nebraska.

events.instrument: State ex rel. Douglas v. Faith Baptist Church, 207 Neb. 802, 301 N.W.2d 571 (1981)
events.summary: The Nebraska Supreme Court sustained the State Board of Education's Rule 14, which required approval for the continued legal operation of every school, prescribed curriculum, materials, the length of the school day and year, health and safety requirements, reporting, and state certification of every professional staff member, as applied to a church school that refused to seek approval.

The Supreme Court of Missouri held that public school funds used to carry grade school children part of the way to a Roman Catholic parochial school were not used for maintaining free public schools, and that the transportation at district expense was unlawful and must be enjoined.

events.instrument: Senate Bill 638, 76th General Assembly (1972), ss. 170.051 and 170.055, RSMo
events.summary: Senate Bill 638 of 1972 required the lending of school textbooks to pupils and teachers in nonpublic schools not operated for profit, with the money for the books kept separate from public school fund money.

The Supreme Court of Missouri reversed the judgment upholding the textbook loan statute, except as to the part already forbidding payments for teachers in private schools, holding that the Missouri Constitution of 1945 forbade the lending of textbooks to nonpublic school pupils.

The Supreme Court of Missouri held that a school district violated the Missouri Constitution by taking a Roman Catholic parish school into the public system and maintaining it at public expense with teachers of a religious order. The decree was reversed for entry of relief consistent with that holding.

events.instrument: Berghorn v. Reorganized School District No. 8, 364 Mo. 121, 260 S.W.2d 573 (1953)
events.summary: Taxpayers challenged three schools operated by a reorganized district in former Roman Catholic parish buildings with teachers of a religious order. The Supreme Court of Missouri sustained the judgment that the schools were not free public schools entitled to public money, following Harfst v. Hoegen.

events.instrument: Ch. 66, Acts of 1940, transportation for pupils attending schools other than public schools; Sherrard v. Jefferson County Board of Education, 294 Ky. 469, 171 S.W.2d 963 (1942)
events.summary: The Kentucky Court of Appeals held that chapter 66 of the Acts of 1940, which entitled pupils attending private schools to the same transportation as public school pupils, diverted common school funds and was unconstitutional and void.

events.instrument: Ch. 156, Acts of 1944, KRS 158.115; Nichols v. Henry, 301 Ky. 434, 191 S.W.2d 930 (1945)
events.summary: The Kentucky Court of Appeals upheld the 1944 act providing supplemental transportation along highways without sidewalks for children attending school in compliance with the compulsory attendance laws, distinguishing its earlier decision in Sherrard, and it remanded for a declaration of rights.

A taxpayer challenged the payment of public money to nuns of the Roman Catholic Church who taught in public schools while wearing the garb and emblems of their orders. The Kentucky Court of Appeals declined to enjoin the practice, the plaintiff having conceded the teachers' qualifications and not having alleged that they taught the tenets of their church.

events.instrument: KRS 171.215, Kentucky Acts 1978, ch. 139, textbooks for nonpublic school pupils
events.summary: Chapter 139 of the Kentucky Acts of 1978, effective June 17, 1978, directed the state to supply textbooks to children in Kentucky's nonpublic schools.
The Supreme Court of Kentucky held KRS 171.215, the nonpublic school textbook statute, invalid under the Kentucky Constitution, over a dissent that would have followed Board of Education v. Allen.

events.instrument: Item 210 of the Appropriation Act of 1954; Almond v. Day, 197 Va. 419, 89 S.E.2d 851 (1955)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of Appeals of Virginia held that Item 210 of the 1954 Appropriation Act, which paid tuition and institutional fees for children of deceased and disabled veterans at approved institutions of collegiate or secondary grade, was unconstitutional so far as it authorized payments to sectarian schools, under section 141 of the Constitution of Virginia and the First Amendment.

events.instrument: Education Code s. 16257, transportation of private school pupils; Bowker v. Baker, 73 Cal. App. 2d 653, 167 P.2d 256 (1946)
events.summary: The California District Court of Appeal upheld the statute permitting school districts to carry pupils attending private schools on district buses, holding that the direct benefit ran to the children in providing for their safety and education, with only an indirect benefit to the parochial school.

events.instrument: Education Code ss. 60315 and 60246, textbook loan; California Teachers Association v. Riles, 29 Cal. 3d 794, 632 P.2d 953 (1981)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of California held that the statutes authorizing the Superintendent of Public Instruction to lend public school textbooks to pupils at nonprofit nonpublic schools violated article IX, section 8 and article XVI, section 5 of the California Constitution, distinguishing the bus transportation upheld in Bowker v. Baker.

events.instrument: Ch. 53, Laws of 1941, transportation of private and parochial school pupils; Mitchell v. Consolidated School District No. 201, 17 Wash. 2d 61, 135 P.2d 79 (1943)
events.summary: The Washington Supreme Court sustained a judgment declaring chapter 53 of the Laws of 1941 unconstitutional and enjoining the expenditure of public funds to transport children attending private or parochial schools, notwithstanding the legislature's declaration that the act was an exercise of the police power.

events.instrument: Visser v. Nooksack Valley School District No. 506, 33 Wash. 2d 699, 207 P.2d 198 (1949)
events.summary: Parents sought to compel a school district to carry their children to a religious private school on public school buses. The Washington Supreme Court affirmed the dismissal of the action, holding that the state may not encourage the existence of schools established for religious purposes by direct public subsidy.

events.instrument: Laws of 1972, 1st Ex. Sess., ch. 155, s. 10, grants for needy pupils in grades one to twelve; Weiss v. Bruno, 82 Wash. 2d 199, 509 P.2d 973 (1973)
events.summary: The Washington Supreme Court held that the grants program for needy pupils in grades one to twelve and the tuition supplement program for students at private institutions of higher education could not be funded consistently with article 9, section 4 of the Washington Constitution, and it prohibited the disbursement of funds under both.

events.instrument: ORS 337.150, free textbooks; Dickman v. School District No. 62C, 232 Or. 238, 366 P.2d 533 (1961)
events.summary: The Oregon Supreme Court reversed the trial court and directed a decree for the plaintiff taxpayers, holding that supplying free textbooks to pupils of a parochial school under the free textbook statute used state funds for the benefit of a religious institution contrary to article I, section 5 of the Oregon Constitution.

events.instrument: I.C. s. 33-1501 as amended by S.L. 1970, ch. 91, s. 1, transportation of nonpublic school pupils
events.summary: The 1970 amendment to section 33-1501 of the Idaho Code allocated state funds to school districts for the transportation of pupils attending parochial schools.

The Idaho Supreme Court reversed the trial court, which had upheld the statute, and held that furnishing transportation at public expense to pupils attending parochial schools was forbidden by the Idaho Constitution, following Matthews v. Quinton and Spears v. Honda.

events.instrument: Horace Mann League of the United States of America v. Board of Public Works, 242 Md. 645, 220 A.2d 51 (1966)
events.summary: Maryland taxpayers challenged four statutes granting a total of two and a half million dollars for buildings at four private colleges. The Court of Appeals of Maryland affirmed in part and reversed in part, sustaining the grant to one college and holding the grants to the three church related institutions invalid.

events.instrument: Conn. Gen. Stat. s. 10-281, transportation for pupils in nonprofit private schools, effective October 1, 1957
events.summary: The statute empowered a municipality to provide transportation for pupils attending a nonprofit private school on the same terms as pupils attending public school, where a majority of the private school's pupils came from the municipality.

events.instrument: Snyder v. Town of Newtown, 147 Conn. 374, 161 A.2d 770 (1960)
events.summary: The Connecticut Supreme Court of Errors answered that section 10-281 was not unconstitutional, except as to money derived from the state school fund, which article eighth, section 2 of the Connecticut Constitution reserved to the public schools. The transportation of pupils to a church school was otherwise held not to be support of that church. The United States Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

The Alaska Supreme Court held that furnishing transportation at public expense to pupils attending nonpublic schools was a direct benefit to the school and violated article VII, section 1 of the Alaska Constitution, which forbids the payment of public money for the direct benefit of any religious or other private educational institution.

events.instrument: Act 97, Session Laws of Hawaii 1965, and Act 233, Session Laws of Hawaii 1967, bus transportation subsidies for sectarian and private school pupils
events.summary: The 1965 and 1967 acts, and the State School Board rule issued under the later act, used public funds to subsidize bus transportation for pupils attending sectarian and private schools.

The Supreme Court of Hawaii held that the transportation subsidies violated article IX, section 1 of the Constitution of the State of Hawaii, which forbids the appropriation of public funds for the support or benefit of any sectarian or private educational institution, and it declined to follow the reasoning of the Everson majority in construing the state provision.

The Supreme Court of New Mexico largely affirmed a decree barring the teaching of sectarian religion in the public schools, barring certain members of Roman Catholic religious orders from public school employment, and forbidding the use of state transportation for pupils attending parochial schools, while vacating the injunction as to those teachers against whom no evidence of religious teaching had been shown.

events.instrument: Act No. 100 of 1928, the Free Text-Book Act, and Act No. 143 of 1928
events.summary: Act 100 of 1928 provided free textbooks for the school children of Louisiana and Act 143 appropriated the money to buy them, the funds coming from the severance tax.

events.instrument: Borden v. Louisiana State Board of Education, 168 La. 1005, 123 So. 655 (1929)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of Louisiana refused to annul the Free Text-Book Act and its appropriation, rejecting the taxpayers' contention that supplying books to children attending private and parochial schools was a prohibited loan of state property.

The Supreme Court of Mississippi held that the act of 1878, which would have let pupils at private institutions draw their pro rata share of the common school fund, was contrary to the constitutional scheme of a uniform system of free public schools under state supervision. Private institutions were excluded from participation in the fund.

events.instrument: Ch. 202, Laws of 1940, State Textbook Rating and Purchasing Board; Chance v. Mississippi State Textbook Rating and Purchasing Board, 190 Miss. 453, 200 So. 706 (1941)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of Mississippi sustained the chancellor's refusal to enjoin the loan of free textbooks to pupils in private and sectarian elementary schools, holding that the emphasis of the 1940 act lay on the need of the pupil rather than on aid to the school, over a dissent that it broke down the separation of church and state.

The North Dakota Supreme Court affirmed a judgment for the school officers and refused to restrain teachers who were members of a religious order from wearing the garb of that order while teaching in the public schools, holding that the practice, and the teachers' contribution of part of their salaries to their order, did not violate the state constitution.

Parents who sent their children to a Christian day school that had not been approved by the county superintendent and the Superintendent of Public Instruction, and whose teachers were not state certified, were convicted under the compulsory attendance law. The North Dakota Supreme Court affirmed the convictions.

events.instrument: Synod of Dakota v. State, 2 S.D. 366, 50 N.W. 632 (1891)
events.summary: The South Dakota Supreme Court denied the Synod of Dakota any recovery from the state for instruction given at Pierre University under a territorial contract, holding that the university was a sectarian institution and that section 3 of article 6 and section 16 of article 8 of the state constitution forbade the appropriation of public funds to it.
The 1973 and 1974 session laws directed South Dakota school districts to lend textbooks free of charge, at district expense, to all public and nonpublic school pupils in grades one through twelve.

events.instrument: McDonald v. School Board of Yankton Independent School District No. 1, 90 S.D. 599, 246 N.W.2d 93 (1976)
events.summary: The South Dakota Supreme Court reversed a writ of mandamus compelling a school board to lend textbooks to nonpublic school pupils, holding SDCL 13-34-16.1, and SDCL 13-34-16 so far as it reached private school pupils, unconstitutional under article VI, section 3 and article VIII, section 16 of the South Dakota Constitution. The court rejected the child benefit doctrine.

events.instrument: SDCL 13-34-16.2 and 13-34-16.3, textbook loan as amended by S.L. 1977, ch. 134
events.summary: The 1977 legislature rewrote the textbook loan statutes, adding a statement of legislative policy, in an effort to meet the objections raised in McDonald.

events.instrument: Elbe v. Yankton Independent School District No. 63-3, 372 N.W.2d 113 (S.D. 1985)
events.summary: Answering a question certified by the federal district court, the South Dakota Supreme Court held SDCL 13-34-16.2 and 13-34-16.3 unconstitutional on their face under article VI, section 3 and article VIII, section 16 of the South Dakota Constitution, the added statement of legislative policy making no difference to the result in McDonald.

events.instrument: Section 29-4 of the School Code (Laws of 1933); Board of Education v. Bakalis, 54 Ill. 2d 448, 299 N.E.2d 737 (1973)
events.summary: The Illinois Supreme Court upheld section 29-4 of the School Code, which required a school board to carry nonpublic school pupils on its regular bus routes, holding that the section was enacted for the secular purpose of protecting the health and safety of children, that its primary effect neither advanced nor inhibited religion, and that it did not offend section 3 of article X of the Illinois Constitution of 1970.

events.instrument: Public Acts 77-1890, 77-1891, and 77-1895 (1971); People ex rel. Klinger v. Howlett, 56 Ill. 2d 1, 305 N.E.2d 129 (1973)
events.summary: The Illinois Supreme Court affirmed the judgment as to Public Act 77-1890 and reversed as to Public Acts 77-1891 and 77-1895, striking the program of grants to parents toward the cost of educating their children in nonpublic schools and declining to pass on the many activities authorized by the Illinois Educational Development Act in the absence of any attempt at implementation.

events.instrument: Section 3 of ch. 142, vol. 38, Laws of Delaware, appropriation for transporting pupils attending church schools; State ex rel. Traub v. Brown, 36 Del. 181, 172 A. 835 (1934)
events.summary: Parents sought to compel the State Board of Education to spend a five thousand dollar appropriation on transporting pupils to schools supported by churches. The Delaware court held the appropriation unconstitutional under section 3 of article 10 of the Constitution of the State of Delaware.

events.instrument: House Bill 373, as amended by House Amendment No. 2, free transportation of nonpublic school pupils; Opinion of the Justices, 216 A.2d 668 (Del. 1966)
events.summary: Answering the governor's request, the Justices of the Delaware Supreme Court rejected the child benefit theory and advised that the act requiring free transportation for pupils regularly attending nonpublic elementary and high schools not operated for profit could not stand. They noted a further question whether transporting pupils of nonsectarian private schools would offend the rule against public funds for private purposes.

events.instrument: Laws 1967, ch. 421, distribution of sweepstakes proceeds to parochial and certain private schools
events.summary: Chapter 421 of the Laws of 1967 directed that a proportionate share of the state sweepstakes proceeds be granted to parochial and certain private schools for educational purposes, on the recited ground that those schools lessened the burden on taxpayers supporting public education.

events.instrument: Opinion of the Justices, 108 N.H. 268, 233 A.2d 832 (1967)
events.summary: A majority of the Justices of the Supreme Court of New Hampshire advised that the scheme could not be carried into effect because of the constitutional prohibition in Part II, article 83, and that the whole amendment was void. One Justice dissented, taking the view that sweepstakes proceeds were not money raised by taxation.

events.instrument: W. Va. Code s. 18-5-13(6); State ex rel. Hughes v. Board of Education, 154 W. Va. 107, 174 S.E.2d 711 (1970)
events.summary: Parents of children in Roman Catholic parochial schools sought mandamus to obtain bus transportation from county boards of education. The Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia read the statutory authority to transport all children of school age in its unrestricted form, over a dissent that would have denied the writ.

events.instrument: St. 1973, ch. 1196, amending G.L. c. 71, s. 48, textbook loan
events.summary: The 1973 statute, amended in 1975, required school committees to lend textbooks to pupils attending private schools, both sectarian and nonsectarian.

events.instrument: Bloom v. School Committee of Springfield, 376 Mass. 35, 379 N.E.2d 578 (1978)
events.summary: The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court held that the textbook loan requirement offended the provision of the Constitution of the Commonwealth forbidding the use of public money or property for founding, maintaining, or aiding private schools, and it reversed the judgment dismissing the taxpayers' complaint.

events.instrument: New Life Baptist Church Academy v. Town of East Longmeadow, 885 F.2d 940 (1st Cir. 1989)
events.summary: A church academy objected on religious grounds to submitting to the local school committee's approval of its secular instruction under Mass. Gen. L. ch. 76, section 1, and proposed standardized testing instead. The Court of Appeals for the First Circuit reversed the district court, holding that the committee's proposed procedures, which included gathering written information, reviewing teacher credentials, and a classroom visit, were reasonably necessary to the state's compelling interest and posed no excessive entanglement.

events.instrument: 1979 N.C. Sess. Laws ch. 505, enacting Article 39 of Chapter 115C, Private Church Schools and Schools of Religious Charter
events.summary: The 1979 act placed private church schools and schools of religious charter under a distinct statutory regime, declaring the state's policy of respect for rights of conscience and religious liberty and requiring each school to keep attendance and immunization records, to operate at least nine calendar months a year, and to be open to reasonable fire, health, and safety inspection. It was amended in 1981.

events.instrument: Article 11, ch. 34, Session Laws 1939, transportation of private and parochial school pupils; Gurney v. Ferguson, 190 Okla. 254, 122 P.2d 1002 (1941)
events.summary: The Supreme Court of Oklahoma affirmed a judgment holding the 1939 act unconstitutional under section 5 of article 2 of the Oklahoma Constitution, reasoning that indirect aid to denominational schools would be a first step toward larger aid and toward state control of those schools.

events.instrument: Opinion of the Justices, 291 Ala. 301, 280 So. 2d 547 (1973)
events.summary: The Justices of the Supreme Court of Alabama advised that House Bill 247, providing state aid to church related schools, would involve excessive entanglement between the state and those institutions and would violate the First Amendment and its Alabama counterpart, article XIV, section 263 of the Constitution of Alabama of 1901.

The first compulsory school attendance law in the United States required every person having control of a child between eight and fourteen years of age to send that child to some public school in the city or town of residence for at least twelve weeks a year, six of them consecutive, on penalty of a forfeiture not exceeding twenty dollars. The statute named the public school as the place of attendance. It excused the penalty where the child had been otherwise furnished with the means of education for a like period, had already acquired the branches taught in the public schools, was prevented by bodily or mental condition, or where the parent was too poor to send the child or furnish the means of education. Private and church schooling therefore operated as a defense to prosecution rather than as express compliance.

Congress required every person in the District having control of a child between six and fourteen years of age to send that child annually to some public school in the part of the District where the family resided for at least twelve weeks, six of them consecutive, with a forfeiture not exceeding twenty dollars for neglect. The penalty was not enforced where the party was unable for any cause to send the child, where the child had attended any other school for a like period, or where bodily or mental infirmity prevented attendance. Attendance at a private or church school thus satisfied the duty. The Bureau of Education reported the statute a dead letter from enactment onward because school accommodations were insufficient.

Vermont first required all children between eight and fourteen years of age to attend school in 1867, and amended the act in 1870 to prescribe more particularly the proceedings for enforcing it. The state superintendent later described the law as obsolete and inoperative, its fatal defect being that it did not designate the person who was to execute it. The law was remodeled in 1888, which extended the obligatory period from twelve to twenty weeks and required attendance at a public school unless the child was otherwise educated for that period or had completed the required common school branches. Instruction elsewhere therefore satisfied the requirement.

New Hampshire passed a compulsory education law in 1871 of the same general character as the Michigan law passed the same year, a truant law having been on the statute book for about twenty years previously. The Michigan pattern directed the parent to send the child to a public school for a fixed minimum term unless the district board excused the child, and one ground of excuse was that the child was taught in a private school or at home in the branches usually taught in primary schools. Attendance at a private or church school therefore satisfied the new duty by way of excuse.

Approved April 15, 1871, the act required every parent or guardian having charge of a child between eight and fourteen years of age to send the child to a public school for at least twelve weeks in each school year, six of them consecutive. The district board could excuse the child on a showing that bodily or mental condition prevented attendance, that the child was taught in a private school or at home in such branches as are usually taught in primary schools, or that the child had already acquired the ordinary branches. No liability arose where no public school was kept for three months within two miles of the residence. This statute became the template copied by Kansas, Colorado, Oregon, and other states.

events.instrument: Wash. Terr. Sess. Laws 1871 (compulsory attendance act)
events.summary: Washington Territory enacted a compulsory education law in 1871 requiring parents and guardians to send children between eight and sixteen years of age to school at least three months of each year, on penalty of one hundred dollars for each failure, provided no good reason could be shown for the failure. The statute spoke of attendance at school rather than at a public school. The law was repealed in 1873. A requirement without penalty or enforcement machinery was reintroduced in 1877 for places of more than four hundred inhabitants, the 1871 act was reenacted in 1883, and a general law was adopted in 1890.

Connecticut's modern system of compulsory education dates from the act of 1872, which made the schooling requirement of the 1871 law applicable to all children whether employed or not and incorporated the earlier employment and truant acts into a single revised statute. As the law stood, every person having control of a child of school age whose physical or mental condition did not render instruction impracticable had to cause the child to attend a public day school during the hours and terms the district public schools were in session, or elsewhere to receive thorough instruction during those hours and terms in the studies taught in the public schools. A church or private school giving that instruction satisfied the requirement.

Nevada's compulsory law of 1873 required every parent or other person having control of a child between eight and fourteen to send the child to a public school for sixteen weeks each year, eight of them consecutive, with penalties of fifty to one hundred dollars for a first offense and one hundred to two hundred dollars afterward. The school trustees could excuse the child on account of bodily or mental condition or because the child had been instructed elsewhere. Instruction in a private or church school therefore satisfied the duty as a ground of excuse rather than as express compliance. The state superintendent reported in 1890 that the law had been a dead letter from the beginning.

Kansas adopted a near transcript of the Michigan act of 1871, but in a materially broader form: every parent or guardian having control of a child between eight and fourteen was required to send the child to a public school or private school taught by a competent instructor for at least twelve weeks each year, six of them consecutive. The district or city board could excuse the child where poverty prevented proper clothing, where bodily or mental condition prevented attendance, or where the child was taught at home in such branches as are usually taught in the public schools, subject to the same examination as other pupils. A provision on malicious prosecution was added in 1876.

The act of 1874 required every parent or other person having charge of a child between eight and fourteen years of age to send the child to a public school for two-thirds of the public school term, twelve weeks of which had to be consecutive, unless the child was excused on account of bodily or mental condition, the poverty or sickness of its parents, or unless the child had been instructed elsewhere. Penalties were twenty dollars and costs for a first offense and up to fifty dollars afterward. Deaf, mute, and blind children were to be sent for five years to the institution provided for them. State superintendents repeatedly reported the act a dead letter.

Passed May 11, 1874, the act to secure to children the benefits of an elementary education directed all parents to instruct their children in spelling, reading, writing, English grammar, geography, and arithmetic, and required every person having charge of a child between eight and fourteen to cause the child to attend some public or private day school at least fourteen weeks in each year, eight of them consecutive, or to be instructed regularly at home in those branches for the same period. The duty was excused where physical or mental condition made attendance or instruction impracticable. Private and parochial day schools satisfied the requirement on the same terms as public schools.

In addition to the 1850 authority for town truancy by-laws, Maine in 1875 required the attendance at school, either public or private, of every child between nine and fifteen years of age for at least twelve weeks in each year. School officers could excuse a child for physical or mental disability, for living more than a mile and a half by the shortest traveled road from any school, or for having been taught at home. Parents were fined five dollars for noncompliance. A substitute act of 1887 required attendance at a public school sixteen weeks each year unless the child had been instructed elsewhere or was disabled.

New Jersey first required school attendance by the law of 1875, which was superseded in 1885. Under the superseding act every parent or other person having charge of a child between seven and twelve years of age had to send the child to a public day school for twenty weeks each year, eight of them consecutive, unless the school board excused the child on account of its bodily or mental condition or because it had been instructed elsewhere. Fines ran from ten to twenty-five dollars, with imprisonment of one to three months available, and instruction in a private or church school satisfied the duty as a ground of excuse. Contemporary reports state that the law was practically a dead letter in the cities.

Wyoming Territory adopted compulsory school attendance in 1873, making the attendance of children obligatory for at least three months of each year and imposing a fine of twenty-five dollars for each offense on a parent or guardian who failed to comply. The U.S. Bureau of Education's contemporaneous compilation dated the territorial requirement to 1876 and reported the territorial superintendent's judgment that it was almost a dead letter, particularly in rural districts that ran ten to fifty miles across. Under the revision of 1887 the duty ran to children between six and twenty-one, with penalties applying to those in charge of children between seven and sixteen.

Ohio enacted a compulsory education law in 1877, the original bill to secure to children the benefits of an elementary education having been so amended during passage as to render the act virtually inoperative: the section providing for prosecution of offenses was struck out, leaving the clerk of the board of education without means of enforcement. The act remained on the statute book until 1889, when a fuller law was passed requiring attendance for twenty weeks each year in city districts and sixteen weeks elsewhere. By 1915 the Ohio statute required attendance at a public, private, or parochial school, or instruction at home.

Wisconsin's first compulsory attendance law took effect September 1, 1879. As amended in 1882 it required persons having control of children between seven and fifteen to send them to a public or private school at least twelve weeks each year. A child could be exempted for incapacity of mind or body, where its labor was essential to the support of an indigent parent or sibling, where it was otherwise being furnished with the means of education for a like period, where it had already acquired a fair knowledge of the common school branches, or where it lived more than two miles from the district school. Private and parochial schools satisfied the requirement on their own terms.

Approved June 23, 1883, and in force July 1, 1883, the act to secure to all children the benefit of an elementary education required all persons having control of children between eight and fourteen to send them to a private or public school not less than twelve weeks in each school year. The local school board could excuse a child for unsuitable mental or bodily condition, because the child had been taught in a private school or at home in the branches ordinarily taught in primary or other schools, because the child had already acquired those branches, or because no school had been taught within two miles of the residence. The state superintendent reported the law easy to evade and without practical effect.

Rhode Island first required school attendance of all children in 1883, in an act that also carried provisions on child employment and truancy and that was revised in 1887. Under the act every person having control of a child between seven and fifteen had to cause the child to attend some public day school for at least twelve weeks a year, six of them consecutive. Attendance for the same period at a private day school approved by the town school committee or city superintendent satisfied the duty, as did being otherwise furnished with the means of education. Approval was to be given only where teaching was in the English language and thorough and efficient, but approval could not be refused on account of the religious teaching in the school.

The Montana territorial law of 1883 was virtually identical with the Kansas law of 1874, the only change of note being an alternative penalty of thirty days in the county jail for a second or subsequent offense by a parent. It therefore required parents and guardians of children between eight and fourteen to send them to a public school or a private school taught by a competent instructor for at least twelve weeks each year, with excuses available for poverty, bodily or mental condition, or home instruction in the branches usually taught in the public schools subject to the same examination. The state superintendent reported in 1890 that there had not been a single conviction under it.

The Dakota Territory law of 1883, amended in 1887, required every parent or other person having control of a child between ten and fourteen years of age to send the child to a public school twelve weeks in each year, six of them consecutive. The child was excused on account of bodily or mental infirmity, where the child had been instructed elsewhere, or where the child had already completed the public school branches. The subdistrict director was to identify children not attending and to complain before a justice of the peace, with a fine of ten to twenty-five dollars, the director himself becoming liable to the same penalty for failure to complain. The territorial requirement carried into both states on their admission in 1889.

The Dakota Territory law of 1883, amended in 1887, required every parent or other person having control of a child between ten and fourteen years of age to send the child to a public school twelve weeks in each year, six of them consecutive. The child was excused on account of bodily or mental infirmity, where the child had been instructed elsewhere, or where the child had already completed the public school branches. The subdistrict director was to identify children not attending and to complain before a justice of the peace, with a fine of ten to twenty-five dollars, the director himself becoming liable to the same penalty for failure to complain. The territorial requirement carried into both states on their admission in 1889.

Minnesota adopted compulsory education in 1885 by a law that was a literal transcript of the Kansas law of 1874 except that the compulsory age ran from eight to sixteen and the penalties were ten to twenty-five dollars for a first offense and twenty-five to fifty dollars afterward. It therefore required attendance at a public school or a private school taught by a competent instructor for at least twelve weeks a year. State Superintendent Kiehle criticized the act for allowing children to be educated in other than public schools while leaving the conditions so indefinite that there was no guaranty that the children received the equivalent of a common school education.

The Nebraska law of 1887 made it unlawful for any parent or guardian to neglect or refuse to compel a child under their control to attend and comply with the rules of some one or more public or private school for a term of twelve weeks or more during each successive year from the age of eight until the age of fourteen inclusive. The duty was excused for illness, poverty, inability, or the child's already being proficient, in which case the district board of education was to excuse the child. Violations carried a fine of ten to fifty dollars for each offense, payable into the general school fund.

Idaho Territory's law of 1887 required every parent, guardian, or other person having control of a child between eight and fourteen years of age to send the child to a public school twelve weeks each year, eight of them consecutive.
