The child was excused on account of bodily or mental condition, if the child was being instructed elsewhere, if the child had completed the ordinary branches of the public schools, if the child did not live within two miles of a public school, or if the child was compelled to labor for the support of its parents. Fines ran from five to twenty dollars for a first offense and ten to fifty dollars afterward. Instruction in a private or church school satisfied the duty as an excuse.

The act to secure to children the benefit of elementary education required every parent or guardian having control of a child between eight and fourteen to send the child to a public school, or a private school taught by a competent instructor, for at least twelve weeks in each year, eight of them consecutive. The district board could excuse the child for bodily or mental condition, or where the child was taught at home in such branches as are usually taught in the public schools subject to the same examination as other pupils of the district, or where no school was taught within two miles. Where poverty prevented clothing the child, the board was to furnish clothing out of district funds. The Bureau of Education noted that the operative sections were based on the Michigan law of 1871.

Approved February 25, 1889, the act required every parent, guardian, or other person having charge of a child between eight and fourteen to send the child to a public school for at least twelve weeks in every school year, eight of them consecutive, unless the bodily or mental condition of the child prevented attendance, unless the child was taught in a private school or at home in such branches as are usually taught in primary schools, or unless the child had already acquired the ordinary branches taught in the public schools. No liability arose where no public school was kept within two miles of the residence. Fines ran from five to twenty-five dollars for a first offense and twenty-five to fifty dollars afterward.

Approved March 13, 1890, the Utah territorial law required every parent, guardian, or other person having control of a child between ten and fourteen years of age to send the child to a public, district, or private school in the district of residence at least sixteen weeks in each school year, ten of them consecutive. The school board was to excuse the duty where the child was taught at home in the branches provided by law for the same length of time, where the child had already acquired the branches taught in the district schools, where physical or mental condition rendered attendance impracticable, where the child was attending some public, district, or private school, or where the child's services were necessary to support a widowed mother or an invalid father.

The school act approved February 12, 1891 empowered and required the school directors of every district to compel parents, guardians, and others having control of children, when such children did not attend some private school, to send them to the public school for at least three months in each year, the requirement running to children between eight and sixteen. Physical disability certified by a practicing physician, inability to buy books, and the absence of any school within two miles excused attendance. Fines ran from one to twenty-five dollars, or up to ten days in the county jail. Earlier territorial compulsion existed on paper from 1870 onward, and an 1887 act was so defective in wording that it compelled nothing.

Approved May 16, 1895, Pennsylvania's first compulsory attendance law required children between the ages of eight and thirteen to attend school for at least sixteen weeks each year, and Governor Hastings noted on signing that this was the first compulsory educational law in the history of the Commonwealth, similar measures having been vetoed in 1891 and 1893. The statute directed attendance at school rather than specifically at a public school, so a private or parochial day school could satisfy the duty. The act was amended in 1897 to require that attendance begin at the opening of the term, to extend the upper age limit to sixteen, and to raise the required annual attendance to seventy percent of the school year. Enforcement was left wholly to the local boards.

Kentucky's first compulsory attendance law reached the cities rather than the whole state. As digested by the Bureau of Education in 1915, the statute required a parent or guardian in a city of the first, second, third, or fourth class having control of a child between seven and sixteen inclusive to cause the child to attend some public or private day or parochial school regularly for the full term of that school, provided the term was not shorter than that of the public schools. The act did not apply where the child was taught at home in the same branches for a like period and subject to the same examination, which the court could order the city superintendent to conduct. The board of education could excuse a child not in proper physical or mental condition.

Act 57 of the Republic of Hawaii created the Department of Public Instruction and, in section 24, made the attendance of all children between six and fifteen years of age inclusive, at either a public or a private school, obligatory, with exemptions only for distance beyond four miles, physical or mental inability certified by a physician, instruction by a competent tutor in the family, and completion of the primary and grammar grades by a child of at least thirteen. Section 25 provided that no child was considered to comply with the attendance law by attending a private school that did not comply with the Act. Section 21 required a departmental permit to establish a private school, section 22 subjected every private school to departmental supervision, and section 30 made English the medium and basis of instruction in all public and private schools, with nonconforming schools not recognized by the Department.

Indiana's first compulsory attendance law was enacted in 1897 after repeated failures in earlier sessions. As digested by the Bureau of Education in 1915, the statute required every parent or guardian having control of a child between seven and fourteen, or between fourteen and sixteen if not lawfully employed, to cause the child to attend a public, private, or parochial school during the term the common school was in session, unless the child was physically or mentally unfit as shown by a physician's certificate. Private and parochial schools were placed on the same footing as public schools for satisfying the duty, and no approval or inspection condition was attached to them.

West Virginia enacted its first compulsory school attendance law in 1897, under which counties could opt out of the requirement. As digested by the Bureau of Education in 1915, the statute required every person having control of a child between the ages of eight and fifteen to cause the child to attend some free school for a prescribed period. The county opt-out meant the obligation was not uniform across the state at enactment. A statewide requirement without county exemption followed in later sessions.

Arizona Territory adopted a compulsory attendance law in 1875, repealed it in 1883, and enacted the law that endured in 1899. As digested by the Bureau of Education in 1915, the statute required every person having control of a child between eight and sixteen to cause the child to attend a public or private school during the time the public school was in session, with attendance excused where the child was taught at home by a competent teacher in the common school branches, where the child was attending an approved private or parochial school, where physical or mental condition rendered attendance impracticable, or where the child had completed the grammar school course. Fines ran from five to twenty-five dollars for each offense.

Iowa's first compulsory attendance law was enacted in 1902. As digested by the Bureau of Education in 1915, the statute required any person in charge of a child between seven and sixteen in proper physical and mental condition to cause the child to attend some public, private, or parochial school, or to attend upon equivalent instruction by a competent teacher elsewhere, for at least twenty-four consecutive school weeks in each school year. Children living more than two miles from school without transportation, children excused by a court of record, children temporarily receiving religious instruction, and employed children over fourteen were outside the requirement. Principals of private and parochial schools were required to report annually, and on individual cases when required, the attendance of all children in those schools.

Maryland's first compulsory attendance law of 1902 reached Baltimore City. As digested by the Bureau of Education in 1915, every child residing in Baltimore City between eight and fourteen had to attend some day school regularly during the entire period of each year unless the child was elsewhere receiving regularly thorough instruction, and children between fourteen and sixteen were subject to the same requirement unless regularly and lawfully employed. The superintendent could excuse necessary absence or attendance made impracticable by mental or physical condition. The duty ran to attendance at some day school, so a private or church day school satisfied it, as did thorough instruction received elsewhere.

Missouri's first general compulsory attendance law was enacted in 1905. As digested by the Bureau of Education in 1915, every person in charge of a child between eight and fourteen had to cause the child to attend some day public, private, or parochial school during at least three-fourths of the time such school was in session, or give the child approved instruction at home; children between fourteen and sixteen not lawfully employed were also required to attend. Exemptions covered inability to provide clothing, physical or mental incapacity, the absence of a public school within two and a half miles, and completion of the common school course. Private and parochial schools satisfied the duty on the same terms as public schools.

Tennessee's first compulsory attendance act, passed in 1905, applied only to specified counties rather than to the state as a whole; a statewide law followed in 1913. As digested by the Bureau of Education in 1915, the requirement ran to children between eight and fourteen, who had to attend school for at least eighty consecutive days or for the full term where the term was shorter, with full-term attendance in separate city systems having a school population of five thousand or more. A court or county or city board could temporarily excuse a child for inability to provide clothing, mental or physical incapacity, distance beyond two miles without transportation, or completion of the eight elementary grades.

Delaware's first compulsory attendance law was enacted in 1907. As digested by the Bureau of Education in 1915, every person in control of a child between seven and fourteen had to send the child to school for not less than five months each year, unless excused by the district school committee with the approval of the county superintendent on satisfactory evidence of mental, physical, or other urgent reasons; the annual district meeting could reduce the period to three months. Attendance at a public school was not required where the child received in a private school or otherwise instruction approved by the county superintendent. The private school route therefore depended on the county superintendent's approval from the outset.

North Carolina enacted its first compulsory attendance law in 1907 as a local option measure, laws for specific counties having been passed as early as 1904, and adopted a statewide law in 1913. As digested by the Bureau of Education in 1915, the person in charge of a child between eight and twelve had to cause the child to attend school four months in the year. Attendance at a private school could be accepted in lieu of attendance at a public school, but such a private school had to keep records and make the reports required. Exemptions covered physical or mental condition, residence beyond two and a half miles, need of the child's services for support, and inability to provide books and clothing.

Oklahoma's first compulsory attendance law was passed in 1908 during the 1907-1908 legislature, the first after statehood. As digested by the Bureau of Education in 1915, every person in control of a child over eight and under sixteen had to cause the child to attend the public or other schools, or to be otherwise instructed, for at least sixty-six percent of the time school was in session, unless the child was mentally or physically unable to attend as determined by a qualified physician. The statute's reference to other schools and to being otherwise instructed placed private and church schools and home instruction on an equal footing with the public schools. Violation was a misdemeanor.

Virginia's first compulsory attendance law of 1908 was a local option measure that did not apply in any county, city, town, or magisterial district constituting a separate school district until the qualified voters of that unit voted to accept it; a statewide requirement followed in 1918. As digested by the Bureau of Education in 1915, every person having control of a child between eight and twelve had to send the child to a public school for at least twelve weeks in the year, with exemptions for children excused by the school board, those weak in body or mind, those who could read and write, those attending a private school, and those living more than two miles from the nearest public school.

Arkansas enacted its first compulsory attendance law in 1909, exempting forty-four counties; further acts in 1911 and 1917 narrowed and then removed the county exemptions. As digested by the Bureau of Education in 1915, the person in charge of a child between eight and sixteen had to cause the child to attend a public, private, or parochial school not less than one-half of the time the school was in session, or provide equivalent instruction at home. Exemptions covered inability to provide clothing, mental or physical incapacity, residence beyond two and a half miles, need of the child's labor for family support, and completion of seven elementary grades. Fines ran from ten to twenty-five dollars.

Louisiana's compulsory attendance act of 1910 applied to the parish of Orleans, and the Bureau of Education's 1915 digest records a companion requirement reaching children between eight and fourteen in cities of over twenty-five thousand inhabitants outside Orleans, together with a parish local option procedure under which a parish board could call a special election to make attendance compulsory in elementary and high schools. The digest records that the regulations as to compulsory attendance were to apply to other schools as well as to public schools. A statewide act of 1916 required parents of children between seven and fourteen to send them to a public or private school for one hundred forty days each year.

Alabama's first compulsory attendance law required persons in parental relation to any child between eight and fifteen years of age to cause the child to attend a public school, or a private, denominational, or parochial school taught by a competent person, for at least eighty days in each school year, with county and city boards permitted to reduce the period to not less than sixty days. Exemptions covered completion of seven elementary grades, residence beyond two and a half miles without public transportation, temporary excuse by a teacher with the attendance officer's approval, mental or physical incapacity, and need of the child's services for support. All school officers, including those in private, denominational, and parochial schools, had to make the reports required under the act. The act took effect in October 1917.

Florida's first compulsory attendance law took effect in a county or special tax school district only after an election, called on the petition of one-fourth of the registered white voters, carried the question by three-fifths of the votes cast; a statewide law followed in 1919. Where adopted, the act required attendance of children between eight and fourteen for not less than eighty days of each year. Similar attendance at a private or church school was accepted if reports were made. Exemptions covered physical or mental condition, residence more than two miles from school without transportation, need of the child's services for support, and lack of books and clothing the parents could not supply.

Approved February 20, 1915, South Carolina's first compulsory attendance act required every parent, guardian, or other person in charge of a child between eight and fourteen to cause the child to attend school for the full term of the public school, or for at least four months in agricultural districts. Attendance at a private or church school could be accepted in lieu of attendance at the local public school, but attendance records had to be kept and reported. The act went into effect in a district only on petition of one-fourth of the qualified electors and a favorable majority vote, and a statewide requirement followed in 1919. Exemptions covered physical or mental unfitness, distance, poverty, and lack of books and clothing.

Approved March 13, 1915, the Texas act compelled attendance upon the public schools of Texas by children between the ages of eight and fourteen, fixing the required term at sixty days for the scholastic year beginning September 1, 1916, eighty days for the year beginning September 1, 1917, and one hundred days for each year thereafter. The act prescribed exemptions from the attendance requirement, provided for county-furnished textbooks for children whose parents could not buy them, prohibited the employment of children under fourteen during school hours, and provided for the appointment of school attendance officers in larger counties and independent districts. Texas had briefly had a compulsory attendance law in the 1870s that was repealed in 1876.

Georgia's first compulsory attendance law required every unexempted child between the ages of eight and fourteen to attend school for a stated period in each year, attendance to commence at the beginning of the school term. A child attending some other school giving instruction in the ordinary branches was exempt, so a private or church school satisfied the requirement. Further exemptions covered a child who had completed the work of the fourth grade, a child with family members dependent on his earnings, a child whose parents could not furnish necessary books and clothing, a child physically or mentally unfit, a child living beyond a stated distance, and a child excused by the school board for other good reasons. The act took effect in 1917.

Mississippi was the last state to adopt compulsory school attendance, and the U.S. Bureau of Education described the enactment as the last of the series that brought compulsory attendance to all forty-eight states. The act of 1918 applied to children between seven and fourteen years of age and required attendance for sixty days, with a county board permitted to reduce the period to forty days, subject to liberal exemptions. It became applicable in a county or district only when approved by a vote of the qualified electors of that county or district, and counties could still opt out under the 1920 act. The act expressly required reports from private or parochial schools, which accordingly satisfied the attendance requirement.

The first Territorial Legislature of Alaska required every parent, guardian, or other person having possession or control of any white child or child of mixed blood living a civilized life, between the ages of eight and sixteen, residing within two miles of a school outside an incorporated town or within the limits of an incorporated town where a school the child was entitled to attend was maintained, to cause the child regularly to attend school during the entire school year. The duty was excused where physical or mental condition rendered attendance inexpedient or impracticable, where the school board excused the child in writing, or where the child had completed a course of study equal to that of the territorial public schools. The statute spoke of attendance at school and set no separate approval condition on nonpublic schools.

Approved May 24, 1889, the Edwards Law replaced the act of 1883 and tightened the terms on which instruction outside the public schools counted. It required every person having control of a child between seven and fourteen to cause the child to attend some public day school in the city, town, or district of residence for at least sixteen weeks, eight of them consecutive. The penalty was avoided only where the child had attended for a like period a private day school approved by the board of education or directors of the district in which the child resided, or had otherwise been given instruction in the branches commonly taught in the public school. The act further provided that no school counted unless reading, writing, arithmetic, United States history, and geography were taught there in the English language.

events.instrument: 1893 Ill. Laws, An act concerning the education of children
events.summary: The Illinois act concerning the education of children, in force July 1, 1893, replaced the Edwards Law of 1889. It carried the same requirement of sixteen weeks' school attendance during the year and extended the required period of consecutive attendance from eight to twelve weeks. The old provision that the compulsory regulations could be met only by attendance at schools offering instruction in English was dropped to please the friends of the parochial schools, and the appointment of truant officers, mandatory on boards of education under the earlier law, was made permissive. Removing the English-language definition of a qualifying school ended the condition that had exposed German-language Lutheran and Catholic parochial schools under the 1889 act.

The Bennett Law required every parent or other person having control of a child between seven and fourteen to cause the child to attend some public or private day school in the city, town, or district in which he resides for a period fixed annually by the local board, not less than twelve weeks and not more than twenty-four. Section 5 provided that no school was to be regarded as a school under the act unless reading, writing, arithmetic, and United States history were taught there in the English language. The English-language definition and the requirement that the school be in the district of residence brought German-language parochial schools within the reach of the act and made the law the central issue of the 1890 state election.

After the Bennett Law became the leading issue of the 1890 election and the party that had opposed it swept the state, the offending measure was promptly repealed and a compulsory attendance law that did not require the use of the English language was enacted in its place. The replacement reduced the compulsory period by one year, closing it at thirteen, allowed any court of record to exempt a child under thirteen, and made the appointment of truant officers optional with school boards. The English-language definition of a qualifying school, which had been the specific threat to German-language parochial schools, was gone.

events.instrument: 1894 N.Y. Laws ch. 671, § 3 (later N.Y. Educ. Law § 623)
events.summary: New York's Compulsory Education Law of 1894, effective in 1895, introduced the substantial equivalency standard that governs nonpublic schooling in the state to this day. As carried into section 623 of the Education Law, instruction given elsewhere than at a public school must be at least substantially equivalent to the instruction given children of like age at the public school of the city or district in which the child resides. Such attendance must be for at least as many hours each day as are required of children of like age at public schools, no greater amount of holidays or vacations may be deducted, and only excuses allowed in the public school will justify absence. The standard replaced the looser 1874 formulation and made a church school's satisfaction of the attendance duty turn on comparison with the local public school.

Approved April 9, 1919, the Nebraska act relating to the teaching of foreign languages provided that no person, individually or as a teacher, should in any private, denominational, parochial, or public school teach any subject to any person in any language other than the English language, and that languages other than English could be taught only to pupils who had passed the eighth grade. The statute reached denominational and parochial schools by its express terms, and a teacher in a Lutheran parochial school was convicted under it for teaching reading in German. It restricted the instruction a church school could give while still satisfying the state's attendance requirement.

events.instrument: Or. Laws § 5259 (Compulsory Education Act, adopted Nov. 7, 1922)
events.summary: Adopted by initiative on November 7, 1922, and set to take effect September 1, 1926, the Oregon Compulsory Education Act required every parent or other person having control of a child between eight and sixteen years of age to send the child to a public school for the period of time a public school was held during the current year in the child's district, with failure a misdemeanor. The act removed the private and parochial school option that Oregon's law had allowed since 1889 and would have compelled the closure of church schools serving children of those ages. It was the most far-reaching measure any state adopted against nonpublic schooling.

ancillary.instrument: Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, 597 U.S. 507 (2022)
ancillary.summary: The Supreme Court held that the Free Exercise and Free Speech Clauses protect an individual's personal religious observance from government suppression, and that the Constitution does not permit the government to single out private religious speech for disfavor on Establishment Clause grounds. The Court stated that it had long ago abandoned the Lemon test and its endorsement test offshoot, and directed that the Establishment Clause be interpreted by reference to historical practices and understandings. The case concerned a public school football coach who prayed at midfield after games.

ancillary.instrument: Illinois ex rel. McCollum v. Board of Education of School District No. 71, Champaign County, 333 U.S. 203 (1948)
ancillary.summary: By a vote of 8 to 1, the Supreme Court held that a public school district may not permit religious groups to conduct sectarian instruction inside school buildings during school hours, even where participation is voluntary. The Court found that the arrangement used tax-supported facilities and the compulsory attendance machinery to promote religious teaching, in violation of the Establishment Clause.

By a vote of 6 to 3, the Supreme Court upheld a New York released time program under which public schools released students during school hours for religious instruction at outside facilities. The Court distinguished McCollum on the ground that the program involved neither religious instruction in public schools nor the expenditure of public funds, and that the state neither coerced attendance nor abandoned neutrality.

By a vote of 6 to 1, the Supreme Court held that a state may not require or sponsor an official prayer in public schools, even one that is denominationally neutral and from which students may be excused. The Court held that composing a prayer for governmental use violates the Establishment Clause.

ancillary.instrument: School District of Abington Township v. Schempp, 374 U.S. 203 (1963)
ancillary.summary: By a vote of 8 to 1, the Supreme Court held that no state law or school board may require that passages from the Bible be read or that the Lord's Prayer be recited in public schools at the opening of the school day. The availability of an excusal with parental permission did not save the practice from the Establishment Clause.

The Supreme Court unanimously struck down an Arkansas statute forbidding teachers to instruct students in the theory of evolution, holding that the statute singled out a scientific theory to protect a particular religious reading of human origins. The First Amendment forbids a state to exclude a subject from the curriculum for reasons rooted in religious doctrine. The opinion does not report a vote count.

In a per curiam opinion summarily reversing the state court, the Supreme Court struck down a Kentucky statute requiring the posting of the Ten Commandments in every public school classroom, holding that the statute had no secular legislative purpose. Chief Justice Burger and Justice Blackmun would have granted plenary review, and Justices Stewart and Rehnquist dissented.

By a vote of 8 to 1, the Supreme Court held that a state university that has created a generally open forum for student groups may not exclude a religious group on the basis of the content of its speech absent a compelling interest narrowly served. The Court held that an equal access policy does not offend the Establishment Clause and that a state interest in separation of church and state beyond what the federal Constitution requires is not sufficient to justify the exclusion. The decision was the direct antecedent of the Equal Access Act of 1984.

ancillary.instrument: Equal Access Act, Pub. L. 98-377, title VIII, 98 Stat. 1302 (20 U.S.C. 4071)
ancillary.summary: Congress enacted the Equal Access Act, making it unlawful for a public secondary school that receives federal financial assistance and has a limited open forum to deny equal access or a fair opportunity to, or discriminate against, students who wish to conduct a meeting within that forum on the basis of the religious, political, philosophical, or other content of the speech at the meeting. A school creates a limited open forum whenever it grants an opportunity for one or more noncurriculum related student groups to meet on school premises during noninstructional time. The Supreme Court upheld the act against an Establishment Clause challenge in Board of Education of Westside Community Schools v. Mergens, 496 U.S. 226 (1990).

By a vote of 6 to 3, the Supreme Court struck down an Alabama statute authorizing a one minute period of silence in public schools for meditation or voluntary prayer, holding that the legislature's sole purpose was to return voluntary prayer to the public schools and that the statute therefore lacked a secular purpose.

By a vote of 7 to 2, the Supreme Court struck down Louisiana's Creationism Act, which forbade the teaching of evolution in public schools unless accompanied by instruction in creation science. The Court held that the act lacked a clear secular purpose and instead sought to advance the religious viewpoint that a supernatural being created humankind.

ancillary.instrument: Board of Education of Westside Community Schools v. Mergens, 496 U.S. 226 (1990)
ancillary.summary: By a vote of 8 to 1, the Supreme Court held that the Equal Access Act bars a public secondary school with a limited open forum from denying recognition to a student Christian club on the basis of the religious content of its speech. The Court held that the act does not violate the Establishment Clause because it extends equal access to religious and secular student speech on a nondiscriminatory basis.

By a vote of 5 to 4, the Supreme Court held that the Establishment Clause forbids a public school to include a clergy led invocation and benediction in a graduation ceremony. The Court held that the school's direction of a religious exercise placed subtle coercive pressure on students at an event of major personal significance from which they could not reasonably be expected to absent themselves.

ancillary_note: These entries concern religion inside public educational institutions: prayer, Bible reading, released time, posted texts, student clubs, and a teacher's own observance. They are held apart from the main register, which measures the room a Christian school or a Christian family has to operate, and they are counted on their own page rather than in its totals.

federal_program.name: Education Freedom Tax Credit
federal_program.citation: One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Pub. L. 119-21, sec. 70411; 26 U.S.C. sec. 25F
federal_program.eligibility: families at or below 300% of area median gross income
federal_program.mechanism: The state elects to participate by filing IRS Form 15714 and a list of qualified scholarship granting organizations with the Treasury.
federal_program.note: Elections are recorded from a dated secondary tracker at tier C and are to be re-coded from each state's own filing or the Treasury's published list. A jurisdiction shown as neither elected nor declined has no election recorded here yet, which is not the same as having refused one.

note: Latitude describes the room the law leaves a Christian school. It is not a forecast, it is not an endorsement, and it is not a claim that latitude produces schools or attention. It is published as a rank and as a ratio to the median jurisdiction, never as a level, because a composite of ordinals carries no unit.
incomplete_note: A jurisdiction is ranked on the components that have been coded against a primary instrument, and a component with no instrument is left uncoded rather than guessed. An index that fills its gaps with the average has quietly published fifty-one opinions. Every jurisdiction is presently coded on all five components, and the rule stands regardless: a component that loses its instrument loses its score.
